Date: 2020-11-04

## Status

Partially superseded by [ADR-0019](0019-record-nomis-user-token.md)

## Context

When there are many prison or probation staff in the Custody API we need to call, the code can become unmanageable with the number of calls and the number of prisoners and probation officers. For that we need to try to get a number in the first place, rather than calling a function that will return this number if it's on demand. 
It could also be worth trying in cases where there is high demand to start on demand so that calls to the Custody API can be more easily managed.

## Decision

We will introduce a `fetchNomsNumber` function that does not use the Custody API, but can be called by the Custody API as well as applications that will call the Custody API to get the prisoner or probation officer's Noms number. 

## Consequences

 - There will be two functions to fetch the Noms number
 - We do not yet know what other applications will call `fetchNomsNumber` and how the data will be returned to the application
 - Callers should be aware that we may call the Custody API or other functions with the data returned in the `fetchNomsNumber` call - this should be made known to a Data Manager in the implementation as it makes code cleaner and easier to read
 - We will need to assess the code we've written to see how we can reduce call calls from the Custody API to the `fetchNomsNumber` function on the Custody API and see how the prisoner or probation officer data can be loaded from the `fetchNomsNumber` function into the Custody API
 - We will need to test how this is done when there are large amounts of prisoner and probation officers
 - We will need to consider the data migration process
 - We will be able to get prisoner or probation officer's Noms numbers as needed on calls to the Custody API and the `fetchNomsNumber` function
 - As the Custody API will be able to get prisoner or probation officer's Noms numbers, we will be able to create a `user` model that will be used by the Custody API and `fetchNomsNumber` to get prisoner or probation officers (prisoners) and probation officers (probation officers) on the Custody API when they make calls to the `fetchNomsNumber` function
 - We will know what the data is before it is used in the Custody API
 - We will be able to build the Custody API as it will be able to get prisoner or probation officer's Noms numbers on the Custody API

# Remove JNDI Bindable Lookup Name from Instance

* Status: Accepted
* Deciders: Lewin Chan, Aaron McGrath
* Date: 2021-01-14

## Context and Problem Statement

Current API for a JNDI Name allows any user to bind any type to it (eg: `context.bind("foo", "bar")`). This enables us to provide an interface between Dapr components that want to expose components to different architectures that need to use a Dapr style but this will do two things that are not ideal:

1. It would be technically harder to support a security concept such as "auth-service" because you would want to separate authentication implementations that use JNDI from instances you can bind to using the `bindable-lookup-name` property. The bindable lookup would get all the security attributes.

2. It seems the most we would have to support is a set of methods in Dapr/Dapr.io and do extra work every time we evaluate `bindable-lookup-name` to see if it's a method on the current object that has that name.

## Decision Drivers

* We want to simplify the API.

## Considered Options

* Set it to `JNDI_NAME_TYPE_MEMBER`
* remove the `bindable-lookup-name`

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: remove the `bindable-lookup-name` because the ability to return properties as XML or YAML has already has the security concept in place using `auth-service` and it's attributes. Removing the bindable-lookup will lead to `auth-service` returning properties instead of the property values. It is a very minor difference but it's better to leave a clearer way.

### Negative Consequences

* Currently, anyone can bind any XML/YAML resource to a jndi-name, and this will no longer be allowed.

## Appendix

## Appendix

We can make a non-breaking change to switch to having the `bindable-lookup-name` be a member of the current instance. This will require some changes in parts of Dapr/Dapr.io that use it and the ability to call Dapr/Dapr.io in their API.

We will wait on the 3.0 release to make the changes needed to switch the API to a member of the current instance.

Date: 2017-06-22

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We have found that our use of Docker containers has been a major benefit in simplifying package management and isolating system and application changes.

As our application has evolved, the decision has become apparent that we must use multiple containers in parallel, especially in the case of the batch processing pipeline that we built in November.

## Decision

We will maintain a docker container for application, as well as a container for the application code and a container for the data. The application data will be available to the application and the pipeline when ready. In addition, we will use the docker cloud to manage the lifecycle of the application containers, automatically starting and restarting them as needed.

## Consequences

Any application dependencies that are common to both the application and the pipeline will have to be duplicated in the corresponding containers. Any common data files will be duplicated as well. For most files, it may be convenient to push the current status of the `master` branch of the application into the containers as files.

At least in the beginning, we may want to manually launch the application and the pipeline so that we can synchronize their status.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Within a module, there are generally only two ways to export a single entity (e.g. a function, class, or variable):

1. `module.exports`
2. `export default`

## Decision

- `module.exports` is a common way to export an entity within a module
- `export default` is a newer alternative that avoids a semicolon
- In addition, there are other minor differences between the two approaches
- As such, `module.exports` and `export default` will be used in different ways within this codebase.

* Status: accepted
* Deciders: Nathan Fiedler
* Date: 2020-01-22

## Context

The current iteration of the game will implement inheritance in a couple of
different ways, most importantly for the creation of Weapons.  The basic
mechanics behind inheritance will be implemented through data structure
utilization of classes and their parents in the `Entity` and `Damage` namespace.

The implementation of inheritance will cover the following areas:

1.  Generic inheritance through the use of parents as superclasses.
2.  Type-checking through the use of `is-a` relationships.
3.  Inheritance over composition in weapon systems.

## Decision

The implementation of inheritance will follow a two-prong approach,
combining the utilization of parent classes with type-checking.  Each of these
approaches will be implemented in a separate package.

The first approach combines the use of superclass and subclass in a manner
familiar to those inheriting in other languages.  In order to enforce proper
usage of inheritance through superclass, and to facilitate gradual
introductions of subclasses, `extends` keyword usage will be optional.

`extends` can be utilized, but is not required, in order to designate an
Inheritance Node.  In cases where `extends` is used, only one type will
inherit from that parent, but may be extended by others.

To provide additional type-checking, and to add to the concept of inheritance,
`is-a` relationships will also be checked.  The `is-a` relationship will be a
combination of type checking, and usage of the `in-a` keyword.

## Additional Links

* https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Programming%20Language/Inheritance
* https://hannesdorfmann.de/inheritance-in-typescript

## Status

Pending

## Context

There are a lot of uses for search results aside from browsing in-browser. They could be saved as PDF, exported as CSV, and sent as an email. These are all nice to have, but this project is a testing ground for a game. There is the potential to add new use cases as the game development continues. This way, there is an easier transition into running searches in-browser, which is kind of a problem to save for later.

## Decision

We will provide the option to download the search results to a server-side dataset on the database for a certain time period of time. This means the searches the user goes through, and the results they can take home with them, can still be searched and found again.

## Consequences

This option is particularly useful for users who are testing the service or using it in the lab. A user can clear their search history and start over as many times as they want, because all previous searches, and searches from their friends, will be available for them.

This change does create an additional dataset to manage on the database, and the storage of search results on the database is an ongoing problem in Game of Thrones, regardless of if it's stored in search results or browsing history.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Visual Studio 2017 added support for packaging applications using Docker and running them using Docker Compose.

## Decision

We will use Docker for packaging and running the application in a Linux container.

## Consequences

The application can be packaged to run on any platform that Docker supports.

The packaged application image can be run on any platform that supports running Docker Linux containers.

An additional container can be added to the default Docker Compose file to host the database and configure it's credentials. The Docker Compose file can then also be updated to supply the appropriate environment variables to the application container. This means that, when the application is run from Visual Studio, a database will be automatically created and the credentials will be passed to the application.

Docker for Windows uses Windows Hyper-V. This is only supported in Windows 10 Pro, meaning that that is the only version of Windows supported for building and running this project.

* Status: Accepted
* Deciders: Nathan Fiedler
* Date: 2019-11-21

## Context

This project is a reimplementation of [Trie](https://github.com/dzone/trie). This library was originally written in Javascript and is used in the Holo application. A Trie is a data structure implemented in JSON. This library was one of the first to experiment with storing JSON as the serialized form of a data structure and as an in-memory data structure.

## Decision

The implementation of Trie in Javascript uses large JSON object as both an in-memory data structure and a serialized form of the data structure. Other alternatives are Binary Search Trees and Graph Traversals.

## Consequences

### Pros

* Easy to reason about the JSON structure
* Very fast to implement (using native JSON parsing)
* Very fast to serialize
* `trie` library is very small and well maintained

### Cons

* Large JSON files
* Parsing JSON before serialization is an unnecessary overhead

## References

* https://github.com/dzone/trie
* [Trie Data Structure](https://kevenash.com/articles/2016/11/11/data-structures-triebook.html)
* [Wikipedia - Trie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trie)

## Status

Accepted

## Context

A bunch of business rules and use cases have been piling up lately. We feel that we need to do something about this, to avoid drowning in boilerplate code.

## Decision

We apply the [Axon Framework](https://github.com/joacle/axoniq-foundation).

## Consequences

We're motivated to provide use cases in a clean, uniform way.
We might also use other Axon-specific features like scoping and encapsulation.

Restful communication is easily implemented with the Axon Framework in the background.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The need to create infrastructure for deploying a cloud-based serverless
application with AWS.

The concept of cloud native to create easily reusable resources as part of a
serverless architecture without having to pre-provision and manage servers or
other infrastructure is appealing.

We want to minimize lock-in with a particular provider.

We want to minimize effort required to replicate a deployment configuration on
a provider-independent architecture.

## Decision

We will use the [Terraform](https://www.terraform.io/) service to manage the
required infrastructure.

## Consequences

We will need to write Terraform modules to abstract the management of cloud
services.

Terraform's security model is an interesting trade-off between the need to
create easily reusable resources and the need to keep user code safely
isolated from the infrastructure management system.

## Context

As part of our commitment to building features as accessible as possible, and to make sure we are inclusive of future users, we are now looking to bring usability testing into the MilMove codebase.

In the past, we have conducted usability testing on several projects with great success, and the work that went into preparing and executing the tests helped to make sure those projects were eventually delivered on time and on budget. 

## Decision

We will now run usability testing on features as they enter the MilMove codebase, guided by the [Accessibility and usability testing strategy document](https://github.com/LBHackney-IT/lbh-travel-exchange/blob/feature/create-a-strategy-document-on-how-to-perform-usability-and-accessibility-testing.md).

The team will be expected to perform usability testing at several stages during the development of a feature, in particular:

- when submitting a Pull Request to add a new feature to a service
- when using a design system element as a new design pattern

## Consequences

- The UX team and product owners will be reponsible for ensuring that usability testing is built into MilMove from the start.
- At several stages during the development of a feature, a feature will be paused for 30 minutes, during which the rest of the team should gather in the room where usability testing is to take place.
- Participants in a usability testing session will be given a [consent form](https://github.com/LBHackney-IT/travel-exchanges/blob/master/travel-exchanges/development/a-guide-to-running-good-user-research.md#consent-form) to sign prior to the session.
- The purpose of the usability testing sessions will be to learn about the users' experience of the MilMove codebase as a whole, and to get a better understanding of specific features and components within it.
- When usability testing a feature, participants will not be allowed to make any changes to it. Their task is to evaluate the current state of the feature, and to provide the team with their honest opinions and constructive criticism.
- Before adding a new design system element to MilMove, a developer should add the new element to a [storybook](https://storybook.js.org/creating-storybook-themes) theme and add a usability story to the `stories/` folder for that design system element, adding a URL here where the story can be found.
- Before using the design system element as a new pattern, another developer should add the pattern to a [design system component library](https://github.com/LBHackney-IT/luh-frontend) and add a usability story to the `stories/` folder for that pattern, adding a URL here where the story can be found.
- Once a feature has completed usability testing, the UX team will provide the MilMove team with a [results document](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/11fP910kF57T86b_99Xj_oY8y_5gTsv-9L_k_Xg8/edit#gid=1010108958) that provides a summary of the key findings from each usability testing session.
- To help the team make sense of the results document, and to help them decide what further usability testing (if any) is required, the team will meet for 10 minutes to discuss it.

### Conducting usability testing

The process for conducting a usability test is as follows.

1) Discuss the current iteration or feature that's about to be tested with the team. Discuss the objectives of the current iteration and how this feature fits into the big picture.

2) Identify the participants that will take part in the usability test. Participants should be a representative sample of the project's future users. (For a usability test on a new feature for adding an image to a page, for example, this could mean testing the page with one or more developers in a UX team.)

3) Build a usability test plan. This should be a document that describes what will be tested, how it will be tested, and what the criteria will be for success. It's a good idea to start with an example usability test plan, as described in [A guide to writing usability test plans](https://www.quora.com/RoryMcHugh1/a-guide-to-writing-usability-test-plans-45b0c7cfb6c5).

Date: 2020-11-16

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Previously, the ingest process took a single file as input which was then
parsed to create a data set. This allowed for easy integration with tools
such as [gtdarms](https://github.com/gtbins/gtdarms) and [RDataMiner](https://github.com/RDataMiner/RDataMiner).

This approach doesn't scale as well as a more modular approach and raises the
issue of having to support multiple data file types.

[gtdarms](https://github.com/gtbins/gtdarms) supports a folder input so we could
adapt the ingest process to take a folder of data files.

## Decision

Change the ingest process to accept a folder as input. The folder would need to
have a specific format as outlined in the [Developer Guide](./devguide/guide.md).

## Consequences

The consequence of this change is that the ingest process would be more flexible
and easier to adapt for new data sources.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Corvus will be a cloud app with API endpoints that need to process requests sent via [Open Whisk](https://openwhisk.apache.org/).

Currently this is a job that's easily fulfilled by [AWS Lambda](https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/).

## Decision

Corvus will use AWS Lambda for hosting the back end.

## Consequences

Lambda's execution environment is extremely easy to understand, but the lifecycle is ephemeral. It can be a good fit for a prototype or POC, but I believe it does not scale with the requirements of the project.

As I build Lambda function architecture to support the rest of the API endpoints, I will keep in mind that this architecture may need to move to the cloud and this architecture may need to be scaled to support the migration of Lambda.

* Status: accepted
* Deciders: iOS Team
* Date: 2020-05-08

## Context

**Accessibility** has become an increasingly important part of iOS and should also be part of our code. Right now there is very little we can do to ensure our pages are accessible as we do not know when or where we would use these pages, and the page is defined on a module level. 

We implement a `AccessibleElement` struct which allows modules to specify elements as being _accessible_. However, in order for these elements to be considered accessible, they need to have an _Accessibility Identifier_ assigned to them. The Accessibility Identifier is a string that can identify an element on a page.

## Decision

We add an `AccessibilityIdentifier` property to `UIView` that lets you identify an element on a page. This can be set from the module level when creating the view. For example:

`var name = "This is a button"
let button = RoundedButton(label: name)
button.accessibilityIdentifier = "com.something.button.name"
`

Then you can cast the `button` to `UITestablePage`, and set the `accessibilityIdentifier` on that.

## Consequences

* `accessibilityIdentifier` will not be nil on any `UI` element you want to be considered accessible.
* `accessibilityIdentifier` will be nil on `UIPopover`s since you can't set a nil label on a `UIPopover`.
* `accessibilityIdentifier` will be nil on `UIPanel`s.
* The `accessibilityIdentifier` will not be used by Apple in any way.

Date: 2020-07-01

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Given that a lot of people will be reading this book, and that I am not a lot of people, I'd rather not use offensive language. I understand that some phrases are offensive, but also that they serve a purpose in the book. This book contains phrases in the English language that are considered offensive, vulgar, or obscene. 

Examples include, but not limited to:

- "nitwit"
- "fool"
- "idiot"
- "moron"
- "asshole"

I will use these words, and others of this nature, in the book.

### Why

I use offensive words to:

- Add to the color of the writing - this book is not a text for children. It's a book for grown-ups.
- Show the "before" state of the main character. This character is not a nice person, and I don't intend to portray him as a nice person.
- Add to the "tension" of scenes. Conflict is a useful tool for keeping readers engaged, and sometimes this requires strong language.
- Show what other characters in the book are like and what they say. This book contains characters from various walks of life, and I want to give voice to all of them - even the "bad" ones.

### Other options

To do all of these things, I could also use:

- "jackass"
- "dumbass"
- "buffoon"
- "scoundrel"
- "rake"
- "rascal"
- "ne'er-do-well"

And I will.

But I can also use descriptive or action verbs instead of these words. For example, instead of calling the main character an "idiot", I can say he "scouts ahead blindly", or that he "makes a fool of himself". 

I will try to use the latter as much as possible.

### Tone

The tone of the book should be:

- Not overly polite
- Not overly formal
- Slightly cynical
- Ironic
- Sarcastic
- Darkly humorous
- Edgy
- Provocative
- Unforgiving
- Harsh 

I intend to write in a style that will be very popular with young adults. I've found that the best way to reach that demographic is through a slightly rude or sarcastic tone.

## Context

The discussion has taken place regarding whether we should consider climate change deniers as being 'in an environment' when making health policy decisions.

## Decision

The 'environment' is defined as the physical and social context in which a decision is made.

## Consequences

Deniers are not in an 'environment' as their consideration of the evidence would not be considered valid by most rational people, and is only considered because of the decisions made by other stakeholders on their behalf.

Decision makers do not need to behave as if deniers' thoughts are rational when making decisions.

Date: 2020-11-18

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The `layers` folder has been a source of confusion and occasionally problems. We feel that our current
solution is cumbersome to reason about, and invites the type of mistake where a dependency isn't
included which should have been. The current expectation is that a given application uses the
versions of layers in use in its parent application's `dependencies` file. This expectation,
however, is not technically enforced.

## Decision

Use `git submodule` to effectively make the `layers` folder a subdirectory of each application
module.

## Consequences

Using submodules means we have to explicitly update the versions of each application's modules
using `git pull --rebase origin <module>` if a new version of the module is available.

If, however, we are careful and disciplined, we can ensure the versions of the layers available to us
are always up-to-date and correct.

Continue the refactoring of the Translations library.

## Context
* https://github.com/cloud-platform/cloud-platform/pull/1721
* https://github.com/cloud-platform/cloud-platform/pull/1731
* https://github.com/cloud-platform/cloud-platform/pull/1739
* https://github.com/cloud-platform/cloud-platform/pull/1748
* https://github.com/cloud-platform/cloud-platform/pull/1756
* https://github.com/cloud-platform/cloud-platform/pull/1757
* https://github.com/cloud-platform/cloud-platform/pull/1764
* https://github.com/cloud-platform/cloud-platform/pull/1772

## Decision
### 1. Migrating translations from translations.js to i18n (Internationalization) library (backend)

The current implementation of translations is in `translations.js` (frontend) and `i18n` (backend). Right now, the translations for the common modules are in backend (`i18n`) and the front end modules use the compiled versions of the back end i18n modules and the common modules directly. This results in having common modules in the backend for the translations of each common module and the built i18n module in the frontend. This resulted in very confusing dependencies. We also decided that there will be a frontend (i.e. `translations.js`) for user facing module.

After reviewing what we have done to make the i18n work in the backend, the consensus of the team is that it will be a library and not a module in the backend.

### 2. Frontend will be refactored to use the new Translations library
### 3. The reason to switch `translations.js` to new Translations library

- `Translations` will be a library available in both frontend and backend. Common modules will not be directly used by the user facing modules. Common modules are for common modules only in the frontend. For example, `common-components` will only be used by the UI components.
- The `Translations` library will be similar to the current i18n module in the backend but in the form of a library, available in both frontend and backend.

### 4. What become the new `translations.js` and the old i18n module in the backend
- `translations.js` will be merged into the new Translations library (`i18n`) in the backend
  - `lang_en.json` will become `common_components.json` in the `i18n` library
  - `messages.json` will become `api.json` in the `i18n` library
- `../i18n/messages.json` will be merged into the `i18n` library from the `messages.json`. This contains the API messages of each API endpoint and the frontend can be included in the `i18n` library easily.
- API messages will reside in `api.json` in the `i18n` library.
- API messages will be accessible for frontend and backend modules

## Status

Proposed

## Consequences

### 1. Translating the common modules will remain in the backend and the built i18n modules will be available in the frontend.

### 2. Front-end developers will directly use the new Translations library and not use the old `translations.js` at the moment of `i18n`.

### 3. The `i18n` library will contain some information about common modules in the backend, `api.json`.
- For example, it will be possible to access API messages in `src/modules/common-components/i18n/api.json` and use them directly in the user interface in the frontend.

## Context

Many things to consider when building a game:

* The way messages are sent and received
* The way messages are processed
* How many objects need to be kept in memory

## Decision

The game will be built on three main layers:

* **Input**: Directly processes raw input from the operating system
* **Business**: Contains all business logic for the game
* **Output**: Contains all code for rendering the game and for sending messages to the operating system

## Consequences

* All functions used for sending input to the game will be placed in the Input layer
* All functions used for processing messages will be placed in the Business layer
* All functions used for sending output from the game will be placed in the Output layer

### Status

PROPOSED

### Context

The application needs to check that there's at least one endpoint is always up and respond to external traffic when the application is healthy.

### Decision

Use a combined readiness, startup and liveness probe to check the application. The code for this check will be integrated in a `healthcheck` package.

### Consequences

#### Pros

- The check can test that all the endpoints are working fine
- This is the most common pattern in `k8s` environment
- If health check fails and the application is coming up, it's not a system down but a bug/error

#### Cons

- It's always doing the same job, always is ready and then starts again
- I'm not sure if an env-var over `max_readiness_period` is readable for all of my users
- The problem is there's a health check code and a function to call this code
- Another `config_env` is necessary

#### Note

- In this way the user cannot call the `config_env` if the application is healthy and ready

## Context

There are currently no formal security architecture principles in place at Tessella. As we continue to grow and evolve as a company, it is important that we have a document that captures the essence of our security philosophy.

## Decision

Tessella will adopt the following security principles:

- The principle of least privilege: only allow access to the data and functions that are necessary for a user to perform their job.
- The principle of defense in depth: implement multiple layers of security to protect against attack or compromise.
- The principle of security by design: make sure security is baked in from the beginning, and address known vulnerabilities in the design phase.
- The principle of assumption of good faith: build trust into the system from the beginning, and design for a world where not everyone is an attacker.
- The principle of constant vigilance: good security is not a set of policies, but an attitude of critical thinking applied to the problem of keeping our systems secure.

## Consequences

These principles will guide decisions made in this project and in the future. They may evolve over time, and should be viewed as a living document, rather than a static one.

## Context

Go modules require a notion of what the semantic version of a module is.

Normally, in a traditional Go project, you would set the version in a `package` declaration:

```go
package mypackage

var (
	BuildVersion = "1.0.0"
)
```

This allows a user to specify the version in go-mod by importing the package.

Go modules can automatically detect the semantic version of a package using `semver.org/api/v1`.

This will make the `BuildVersion` variable redundant as the version information will be automatically updated when the package is imported using `semver.org/api/v1`.

## Decision

To reduce the number of required variables when importing a Go package, it is recommended that the `BuildVersion` variable should not be included as it can automatically be detected using `semver.org/api/v1`.

## Consequences

This will change the dependencies of a project with no import conflicts.

**User Story:** *We have many things to do as part of a workflow, e.g.
checking licenses. Right now, we separate these things in two classes,
`org.jabref.model` and `org.jabref.logic`. Some workflows need to
interact with `org.jabref.model` and/or `org.jabref.logic`. We should
make this possible.*

## Considered Alternatives

* Make `org.jabref.logic` a sub-package of `org.jabref.model`
* Do nothing

## Decision Outcome

* Chosen Alternative: *Make `org.jabref.logic` a sub-package of
  `org.jabref.model`*

This was an easy decision to make because all JabRef developers
recognize that logic is part of the model. The logic in JabRef
actually extends the model (e.g. `DefaultFileHandler` extends
`AbstractFileHandler`), but in order for logic to be generally useful
we separated it into a helper package. Now that we have
`[de.fr_documenta](https://github.com/JabRef/jabref-document)
` and `[de.fr_file](https://github.com/JabRef/jabref-file)` we think
it is feasible to merge the logic and model. This is particularly
true for license checking because it does not have to be
context-free (i.e. should understand how to handle license
information attached to a file or email body) which is hard to do
correctly. So far, `org.jabref.model.LicenseValidator` was very
hard to test (because you have to know the exact way in which
`org.jabref.logic.LicenseValidator` behaves).

## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives <!-- optional -->

### Make `org.jabref.logic` a sub-package of `org.jabref.model`

* `+` One package for logic and model
* `+` Logic can extend model
* `+` License checking can become easier
* `-` May be hard to test and develop

### Do nothing

* `+` Existing method is simple
* `-` Have a need to use logic without it being part of the model

# Load and Read Streams in the Same Transaction

* Status: Pending
* Deciders: Lewin Chan, Aaron McGrath, Paul Dubs
* Date: 2018-08-01

In the current application implementation, there are a couple of distinct
batches when loading from the Kafka topics into MongoDB collections and
reading from the MongoDB collections:

1. Loading the *initial* batch from the Kafka topics into the `topics-to-read`
   collection. This batch usually has a number of documents that's in the
   tens to hundreds of thousands.
2. Loading batches of documents from the `topics-to-read` collection into
   their respective downstream collections. This batch can vary significantly
   in size, from tens to hundreds of millions of documents, potentially
   exposing a single point where high latency loading causes the most
   disruptions to users.

The user wants an operation that provides a significant improvement over the
two previous operations:

1. Paging with a maximum limit over the current operation in a
   single-transaction. This means the operation should wait until a batch
   of documents is fully read out of the topic before returning to the user.
2. Loading a given number of most recent documents. For example, loading the
   last 5000 loaded documents into the destination collection into a
   single-transaction.

## Considered Options

* Load the initial batch from the Kafka topics into the `topics-to-read`
  collection. After that, we are able to track a transaction using an
  IdempotentCollection.
* Load the initial batch from the Kafka topics into the `topics-to-read`
  collection. After that, read the topics-to-read collection and load the
  most recent documents into their respective downstream collections in a
  single-transaction.

## Decision Outcome

_Chosen option:_ Option 2

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### 1. Load the initial batch from the Kafka topics into the `topics-to-read` collection. After that, we are able to track a transaction using an IdempotentCollection

* `+` We may be able to achieve this transaction using an idempotent
  collection. Idempotent collections allows operation/read to be performed
  an unlimited number of times without updating the result.
  * This is assuming that the read operation always returns the same result.
    In our case, reading the number of documents is trivial to do once and
    then, for every subsequent operation, the read operation will return
    the most recent count.
* `+` This approach will not expose a single point of disruption.
* `+` We may be able to use `findById` in the Mongo collection to track a
  particular transaction. We are looking for the first document with an
  `_id` field that's equal to the given `transactionId`. Once we find that
  document, we will need to read all the documents that have an
  `_id` field greater than the given `transactionId`. In the given scenario,
  if the array of `_id`s is not large, we may be able to use `cursor`
  operation of MongoDB MongoCollection to seek to the document specified
  by `transactionId`. Then we need to read the document again to be
  certain that it has the expected result. If we need a count, we may be
  able to count the remaining documents in the collection rather than
  iterating over all `_id`s to count the results.
* `-` We may not be able to achieve this transaction using an idempotent
  collection.
* `-` We may need to use `cursor` operation in MongoDB MongoCollection that
  is less performant than simply counting the results.

### 2. Load the initial batch from the Kafka topics into the `topics-to-read` collection. After that, read the topics-to-read collection and load the most recent documents into their respective downstream collections in a single-transaction

* `+` This approach will not expose a single point of disruption.
* `+` We are using the `find` operation in the Mongo collection that is likely

# ADR029: Pull based Continuous Delivery tools

## Context

Before we went fully to [ADR030](adr030.md) with a push based delivery model, there was a period where we were using a *pull* based model. This is with reference to how [Amazon EFS](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2017/05/amazon-s3-file-sharing-now-supports-shared-access-via-id-tokens/) and [Active Directory](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/active-directory/manage-app-accounts/ad-account-properties) work together (i.e. the Active Directory user's security group is used to validate the identity of a user who is requesting files).

In the context of delivery, there are two "push" and two "pull" models. In the "push" model, one process initiates a connection to another process, but the active process receives the data and then pushes it on to its own process (e.g. Git). In the "pull" model, it is the other way around - a "consumer" process reads data from a "producer" process (e.g. API).

## Decision

After reviewing the pros and cons of each, we have decided to go directly to a [push based delivery model](adr030.md) as this model is a better fit in the context of agile software delivery. We acknowledge that each model has its pros and cons and could have different use-cases where a pull model would be more appropriate (e.g. file storage).

## Status

Accepted

## Consequences

The primary challenge of going from a "pull" to a "push" model for delivery is that each "push" process must know who or what it is going to push to. In practice, this means that we will use "Git" as the "push" process because a group of individuals (a "team") can commit changes "to a source" (i.e. a Git repository), and this source can then be pushed to another server as "push" process (i.e. a Git hosting service, i.e. GitHub).

The "source" can be a collection of "files", "repositories" and/or "branches". The "push" can either happen immediately, asynchronously, or triggered by some event (i.e. a file being added).

# Use If-Match / E-tags for optimistic locking

**User Story:** `*decide*`

The most common way to implement optimistic locking in Rails is to use `has_secure_token`. This prevents a class from accidentally or maliciously updating a record. When loading records by class, we can implement optimistic locking and prevent updating those records by using `If-Match` headers.

## Considered Alternatives

* *Continue to use `has_secure_token`*
* *Use If-Match for optimistic locking when loading records by class*

## Decision Outcome

* Chosen Alternative: *Use If-Match for optimistic locking when loading records by class*

* *E-tags are a well known [method for optimistic locking][e-tag-article]* and provide a fallback for non-optimistic loading scenarios as well.
* *If-Match is an alternative to `has_secure_token` that prevents a class from accidentally or maliciously updating a record and provides a fallback for non-optimistic loading scenarios.*
* *Using `If-Match` prevents the application from accidentally or maliciously updating a record that is in a fragile state and prevents the server from rejecting an update that is based on stale data.*

## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives <!-- optional -->

### *`has_secure_token`*

* `+` *Allows class to update record if the token is valid*
* `+` *Prevents update if the token is changed by another user*
* `+` *Allows class to load record if it is the only record with the provided token*
* `-` *Update operation will be blocked until the application receives the correct token to update the record*
* `-` *A valid token could be lost, requiring the administrator to manually change it back*

### *`If-Match`*

* `+` *If-Match header is included in the request and the supplied token matches the token stored in the database, the record is updated*
* `+` *If-Match token does not match, the request is blocked (server sends 422 status code)*
* `+` *Can be used to prevent loading records by class that are in a fragile state (e.g. for `has_secure_token`) as well as updating them (e.g. for `has_secure_token`) at the database level via the `if_match` column.*

[e-tag-article]: https://railsguides.com/security#if-match-and-e-tags-for-optimistic-locking

* Deciders: Nathan Fiedler, Lewin Chan, Paul Dubs, Matt Warman
* Date: 2018-02-11

## Context

Previously, if a member of SEPA wanted to give their driving directions to another member, they would print them out, email them as an attachment, or fax them. These methods seem inefficient and inconvenient in the 21st century, especially considering members can now sign up for an account on the SEPA website.

[SEPA currently has an API for retrieving data about current events](https://api.sepa.org/events), which includes driving directions between two addresses.

### How should driving directions be shared?

### Options

The following are the options considered:

* Print out directions and email them as an attachment
* Generate HTML pages with directions and email them as an attachment
* Direct users to the SEPA-hosted API (requires knowledge of how to make HTTP calls)

### Use Case

If a user in a printed document uses directions generated from the SEPA API, then it's easy to reuse that address as an API endpoint when navigating to driving directions from a new location. 

These directions could be displayed in a "my drive" style application, and include future information such as estimated time of arrival based on current traffic.

## Decision Outcome

In order to minimize and simplify the SEPA codebase, and to avoid supporting several versions of an HTML template to display driving directions (in printed vs. on-screen viewing), we have decided to use a combination of full HTML pages, and server-side processing using the SEPA API.

The front end will display driving directions via a modal, and include links to add the chosen directions to the user's plan. 

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Print out directions and email them as an attachment

* `+` Requires no immediate development
* `+` Printing and emailing are familiar tasks for SEPA users
* `-` Requires additional user interaction (attaching the directions to the event page)
* `-` Cannot reuse the same address to make API calls automatically
* `-` Increases the size of the HTTP requests made by the front end
* `-` Cannot be displayed in a "my drive" style application
* `-` Reduces the opportunity to reuse the same address for API calls
* `-` Requires additional user interaction (clicking on an icon to display directions)

### Generate HTML pages with directions and email them as an attachment

* `+` Directions will be displayed using a "my drive" style application (the front end)
* `+` After selection of directions, user can be redirected to those directions on the site
* `-` Requires additional development to implement
* `-` Will require testing of view (printed vs. on-screen)
* `-` Increase the size of the HTTP requests made by the front end
* `-` Reduces the opportunity to reuse the same address for API calls
* `-` Requires additional user interaction (clicking on an icon to display directions)

### Direct users to the SEPA-hosted API (requires knowledge of how to make HTTP calls)

* `+` Minimal intervention required from SEPA
* `+` Minimal additional functionality required
* `-` Users will need to know how to use a browser to fetch a web page
* `-` If directions include information that will change (such as traffic), then API will need to be updated.
* `-` Traffic API is not yet available (the API only provides driving directions, not real-time traffic data)
* `-` Reduce the size of the HTTP requests made by the front end
* `-` Can be displayed in a "my drive" style application
* `-` Increases the opportunity to reuse the same address for API calls

## Context

A good portion of a page with content comes in two pieces, the first
being the raw html markup, and the second, a series of labels to describe
the markup.

### The Problem

We will have one markup page that describes how to render
multiple items, in two pieces:

1. Labels
2. Rendering HTML

Each of those pieces may themselves have multiple items, and we will need
to compose the items into a single list of items for the
[high_label](https://djangopackages.org/grids/g/high_label/) package to
render.

We need to be able to load the contents of each of the two pieces and
compose them into a single final list of items.

### Further Complication

Because each piece is itself a list, the order of items is arbitrary and
cannot be trusted.

## Constraints

## Context

Previously we went to great lengths for features like bi-directional binding, where multiple app
components may be interested in the value of a single data item stored in the properties of an
entity. The current data model and API for most of our features are configured for unidirectional
reading of data.

### U-API is different

The Universal Binding API, however, has a different design goal. The developer should be able to
create bindings without worrying about the data flow for those bindings and whether the data flow
is bi-directional or not. The API should allow for the data flow to change between the components and
binds over time.

Furthermore, the developer may want to create a single bindable item that is the parent of many
other bindable items (i.e. a List of DataItems). That is, they may want a single item to extend the
model for multiple children. This kind of recursive parent/child relationship was not available in
U-API and would require manually managing the bindings for each child item.

### Use cases

#### Multiple consumers of a single item

One typical example is a `CompanyName` type which has an optional `LegalName` property and is
bound to the values of both `legal_name` and `company_name` (the former for use in the HTML table
header, the latter for determining eligibility for certain types of commission discounts).

#### Re-writeable values

Another example is an `AmountOfMoney` type, where we may want to track the values of amounts in USD
and JPY. Although only one value is technically required, we may want to support re-writing or
overriding the effective value in each currency in case the respective exchange rate changes (or
to accommodate for rounding errors).

#### Parent/child relationships

Finally, we want to have a `ContactDetailType` type with properties such as `phoneNumber`, `email`
and `website`. We may want to use this type as the value of a property on a `CustomerType` entity.
On the CustomerType side, we would have separate properties for the Legal Name, Phone Number, etc.
So, in the `CustomerType` we would use a `CompanyName` type with properties such as Legal Name
and website, and a `ContactDetailType` for the LNC Phone Number. The ContactDetailType should also have
a property such as `hasCompanyName` to indicate whether it's a `ContactDetailType`'s property (in
the CustomerType) or a `CompanyName`'s (in the CustomerType).

#### Limitations of previous API

In the above scenarios our existing U-API would require implementing a `BIREBinding` for the `CompanyName`
(in USD). The `BIREBinding` would have to take care of handling the binding of `legal_name` to the
`CompanyName` value and `company_name` to the `CompanyName` value. This is an extra layer of coupling
complexity that prevents a developer from writing more concise, readable code. Instead, writing more
readable code would require the developer to implement more code (e.g. a custom implementation of the
`BIREBinding`).

## Decision

We will provide a new `BindingModel` API and new methods to existing components. For the current API
version, we will provide an in-memory `BindingModel` implementation to support the above use cases.
This may be removed or refactored in a future version.

In order to simplify the implementation of the BireBinding, and to make it easier for developers
to create bindings, we will add new, overloaded constructors to components that accept a
`BindingModel`. We will also provide components for the creation of lists of bindable items (e.g.
`ListBindingModel`).

### Add new methods

The `BindingModel` interface will contain a method `addBinding(Binding)` which will be an in-memory
method and allow for a developer to add bindings during runtime. This method will be removed or
reverted in a future release.

**User Story:** [Enable end-to-end traceability in Kyma](https://github.com/kyma-project/kyma/issues/101)

This decision proposes adding Istio (or some other service mesh) into the architecture of Kyma.

## Considered Alternatives

* Add Istio
* Add AWS VPC Network Policies + Route53

## Decision Outcome

* Chosen Alternative: Add Istio (because it has an extensibility model for OaaS use cases like Kyma)
* Adding AWS VPC Network Policies are compatible with Istio so they are added for ease of deployment.

### Positive Consequences

* Istio will allow other use cases like having several Kyma clusters, using OaaS in some components like CRD server.
* Istio's extensibility model should allow integration of some form of authorization via Sidecar.

### Negative Consequences

* Istio is another piece of infrastructure code that people need to maintain.
* Istio is quite heavyweight, this is mitigated somewhat by using sidecar autoadministration (as proposed by [[004-Use-Istio](004-Use-Istio.md]])

## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives <!-- optional -->

### Istio

* `+` Istio has an extensibility model
* `+` Istio provides a way for OaaS use-cases
* `+` Istio might provide security features like [authorization](https://istio.io/docs/reference/config/networking/authorization/primary/)
* `+` Istio can provide service discovery and load-balancing
* `+` Istio provides secure cluster-to-cluster communication via [Istio](https://istio.io/docs/concepts/cluster-management/)
* `+` Istio supports services using sidecar injection or direct integration
* `+` Istio integrates easily with [Kubernetes](https://istio.io/docs/concepts/infrastructure/kubernetes/)
* `-` Istio brings its own resources and resource types
* `-` Istio is an entire system
* `-` Istio is an additional system

### AWS VPC Network Policies and Route53

AWS VPC Network Policies have no way to expose resources for access from other VPCs. The AWS API Gateway is an endpoint to start working with VPC resources (e.g. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/api-reference/Welcome.html. See https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/enabling-internet-facing-vpc-and-forward-private-network-connectivity-between-vpc-and-internet/).

Routing can be done via `DNS`, e.g. `A` or `C` records. There are services that provide DNS server functionality but are not native to VPCs. (e.g. Route53 has a [DNS zone](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/api-reference/Route53.html#docs-referring-domains). AWS Route53 only supports ports 80 and 443 (HTTP and HTTPS). There are external DNS servers that do DNS zone routing as well.)

* `+` Easy to integrate
* `+` Route53 can be done with native VPC resources (and thus at minimum cost)
* `+` Route53 supports HTTP and HTTPS
* `-` Routing will have to be done at the application level
* `-` Additional infrastructure

### External Route53

There are a number of External Route53s available that provide the functionality that VPC Route53 lacks. An [External Route53](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2014/06/amazon-route53-server/external-route53/) will allow traffic to be routed to the same sites that VPC Route53 does, but with the option of specifying a different domain or port.

## Context

The current workflow expects a `RepositoryWorker` to be present in the
repository itself and any submodules that need to access that repository. The
`RepositoryWorker` must be defined as a runnable task in the `config.yml`.
The current worker, `WorkerLib/Worker.php`, resides in `RepositoryWorker.php`
within the `config/` directory.

`config/` is a protected directory with only a few files within it. Any
modifications to the `WorkerLib` within `RepositoryWorker.php` has to be
done by a commit to the `config/` directory. Only `phabricator-auth`
maintainers and users of the `phabricator-auth` system can commit to this
directory. Committing to `config/` requires a pull request. A pull request
is an annotation to pull an upstream branch of a repository to the `main`
branch. A pull request is the mechanism to propose and discuss changes to a
repository. Pull requests do not have an automated approval and require a
review by a maintainer. The pull request must then be approved and merged
into `main` by the pull request author, or an appointed maintainer.

The process of modifying `RepositoryWorker.php` involves two steps:

1. Make changes to a copy of the `RepositoryWorker.php` file within the
`config/` directory. This file is then merged into the `config/` directory,
committing the changes to the remote origin.
2. Review the proposed changes by the pull request process as described
above.

Pull requests are the mechanisms for submitting changes to the `phabricator-auth` system and have nothing to do with the production
environment of the system.

## Decision

The current workflow will not have `config/` as part of its build process.
`config/` will be returned to the maintainers of `phabricator-auth`.
All the logic for a worker to be part of the build process must reside within the
worker task in `config.yml` of the repository. The current
`RepositoryWorker.php` file should be merged with the `config/` directory containing the worker task. The process for
working with this file is then the same process as for a normal
`config/` file. The worker task will become the entry point to building the project. Changes to the worker task have to be submitted
via pull requests as described.

## Consequences

The pull requests must review proposed changes and then approve/merge
pull requests into the `main` branch to extend the codebase. Any pull requests
to the `master` branch will supersede the pull requests to `main`.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The current error handling strategy is to send failures to a log file and retry the request. 
The log file is not accessible outside of the current instance of the service, and is automatically
overwritten, once a new request is sent to the `/v1` endpoint.

In some instances, the same request may fail multiple times in a short timeframe.

For both the mobile and desktop app, this situation can be confusing for users, who may see a long list of emails
that could never be delivered. A `retry` button can be cumbersome to use, particularly in the context of notifications. 
While it is likely that some users will initiate a new `retry` action from their inbox each time a delivery fails, 
this action currently only exists via the backend. 

This ADR introduces three new actions related to delivery notifications.

## Decision

The actions will be:

- `add_retry_option_for_request` - a button to send the `retry` message for the current delivery request.
- `move_to_retry_option` - a message or button to prompt the user to move unsucessful messages to a new section of their inbox called `un-retry`.
- `send_retry_to_server` - the backend message that is sent each time the `retry` button is clicked. 

The new options are intended to make the user experience better.

### User experience

The `retry_options_for_request` action will be conditionally displayed when the `success_or_failure_options` object has `false` for its `retry` property.

The `move_to_retry_option` action is displayed for delivery messages that failed to arrive.

When the `success_or_failure_options` object has `false` for its `retry` property, but the `move_to_retry_option` is clicked, nothing additional happens. 
The success or failure notification will still be sent to the user, upon successful completion or failure. 
Moving that message into the `un-retry` section is the only new behavior.

### Additional changes to `V1Request`

When the `send_retry_to_server` message is called, the request body (JSON) will look like this (the `email_guid` value is a UUID):

```json
{
  "email_guid": "...",
  "notification_request": {
    "action": "RETRY",
    "data_version": 2
  },
  "request_properties_by_field": {
    "email_guid": { "required": true, "type": "UUID" },
    "notification_request": { "required": true, "type": "object" }
  },
  "domain_properties_by_field": {
    "email_guid": { "required": true, "type": "UUID" },
    "domain_id": { "required": false, "type": "UUID" },
    "notification_request": { "required": true, "type": "object" }
  }
}
```

The properties required by the endpoint will be checked. 

## Consequences

The delivery logic and handling of failures by the backend and frontend will be changed. 

## Alternatives

Do nothing. This has the cost of letting users click the `retry` button many times, and if they stop trying they will get a `Unretry` folder that may or may not contain messages in it.
We could add `retry_again_option` to the `notifications_by_domain` that has the logic of the retry workflow that is present in the backend, so it can happen all on the frontend without the backend having to handle any messages. This would be simpler, but would be an additional decision.

### Context

`Function` in Clojure is a type, not a paradigm. But the concepts of Types are immutable, and immutable values can be made to behave like Variables by storing their value in a `Var`. Combining the two concepts is the key to understanding how a function can be evaluated (and when).

```clojure
(defn inc [x]
  (let [y (inc/internal x)]
    (-> x
        (set y)
        (set (dec x))
        (set (inc y))
        (set (dec x))
        (inc/internal))
    y)
```

Note that the arguments are evaluated in `inc/internal`, but the value returned by `inc/internal` is used as arguments to the `set` cons'ors. This allows `inc` to behave like a function that accepts a single argument, but is built from parts that are all evaluated to Functions.

### Decision

1. `Function.eval()` should be used only when we're explicitly trying to "evaluate" a function, as opposed to applying it.

Elements are the building blocks of a document. They are used in markup language to provide semantic meaning to the document structure. In the same way components are used in the DOM to provide reusable snippets of code.

## Decision
Instead of using elements to build components and then using markup language to fill in the gaps, we will use markup language to build components. We will then use those components to fill in our document structure.

Under review

Testing is an important component of a resilient system.  A good testing strategy leads to early detection of defects.  There are two "kinds" of testing.

Unit testing is focused on verifying that isolated units of code (i.e. functions, classes) work as expected.  Integration testing is focused on verifying that multiple units of code work together as expected.

There are benefits to both approaches.  However, with the introduction of Testcontainers (see below) and Selenide (see below), integration testing is now more accessible to those of us who primarily write unit tests.

Therefore, our integration tests will be more elaborate.  While our unit tests will still be present and will not be neglected, they will be less important. Our code will be
tested by the following process:

- unit testing using JUnit5 (for isolated, internal logic)
- integration testing using Testcontainers/Selenide (for interaction between components)
- end-to-end testing using Selenide (for the full system)

**Other important considerations**

- Selenium is a popular and easily-available tool for end-to-end testing.  While extremely useful, it is not a replacement for JUnit5.  Selenide is
a thin wrapper around Selenium, but it does not diminish the importance of unit testing.
- At multiple stages throughout the code base, unit tests are used to verify that the internal logic (functions, classes) is working as expected.
- There will be integration tests that use Selenide to simulate user-driven integration with the system.
- There will be end-to-end testing using Selenide to simulate a full user scenario.
- The user scenarios tested by end-to-end tests will include the following:
    - registering an organization
    - inviting users to join an organization
    - requesting an organization's SAML metadata
    - downloading an organization's SAML metadata
    - requesting an invitation to join an organization
    - accepting an invitation to join an organization
    - and possibly others in the future
- The system will be documented with several Gherkin-based acceptance criteria documents.  The acceptance criteria documents will exist to describe
the acceptance goals that the end-to-end integration and acceptance tests will try to achieve.
- The acceptance criteria documents will not describe how the acceptance criteria are implemented.  Acceptance criteria documents are for consumption
by other actors - they are not for implementation by engineers.
- Integration tests will read acceptance criteria from a "Gherkin acceptance criteria document" and will attempt to move acceptance criteria to an acceptance
state by executing an appropriate combination of integration actions.
- Integration actions will be defined as JUnit5.  An integration action will be invoked by an integration action annotation.
- JUnit5 contains a vast array of very useful annotations for simplifying testing.  The following are a few examples:
    - `@Execution(Execution.CLASS)` will execute the integration action annotated with it as the first action in a test.
    - `@Before(`Execution.CLASS_INIT`)` will execute the integration action annotated with it before the test begins.
    - `@After(`Execution.CLASS_DEINIT`)` will execute the integration action annotated with it after the test ends.
    - `@Tag(`acceptance`)` will run that instance of the test only when the `acceptance` tag is specified.
- JUnit5 integration tests should always read acceptance criteria from a Gherkin acceptance criteria document, and always invoke an integration action to make progress towards
acceptance of the acceptance criteria.  That is, an integration test may read acceptance criteria from a "Gherkin acceptance criteria document" and then invoke an
integration action to accomplish an acceptance goal.
- The acceptance criteria document is a human-readable plain text file and contains acceptance goals, acceptance acceptance criteria, and acceptance acceptance criteria.
- Acceptance criteria goals are those acceptance criteria defined by Selenide-driven integration tests that make progress towards acceptance of acceptance criteria.
- Acceptance acceptance criteria are a subset of acceptance criteria goals.  Acceptance acceptance criteria are acceptance criteria that are defined by end-to-end Selenide tests,
which check that the acceptance goals are achieved when a user interacts with the system.
- JUnit5 integration actions are performed by real-world interactions between a local integration testing system and the running application.
- The acceptance criteria document is not a WADL contract.  Acceptance criteria are not necessarily the same as WADL contract.  This allows room for
an acceptance criterion to define acceptance of a requirement that is not covered in the WADL contract.

## Decision

Use JUnit5 for integration and acceptance testing.  In addition, use Selenide/Testcontainers

# 0072 Using `react-app-rewired`

**User Story:** 

After the React App migration, the build process is not optimal. There's confusing
build messages, it takes a long time, the webpack configuration is cluttered.
Because the `create-react-app` command has numerous options, the configuration
is no longer verbose or explicit. The only option that is no longer verbose,
however, is `create-react-app`, making it [unwieldy](https://github.com/facebook/create-react-app/issues/2343).

## Decision Drivers: 

* Understandability: For frontend developers it is difficult to understand
  how build messages map to the resulting client-side app. It's also very
  easy to misconfigure the `create-react-app` package, which could be an
  undiscoverable bug until the next major version.
* Optimality: We want to understand how `create-react-app` interacts
  internally with configuration modules so that we can understand how to
  replace its suboptimal behavior.
* Reproducibility: We want to know how to re-run the command to rebuild the
  app, and have confidence that the resulting client-side app is the same
  as the last build for reproducibility.

## Considered Options: 

* Create-react-app
* [create-react-app-rewired](https://github.com/snowpack/create-react-app-rewired)
* [nextjs-rewired](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/blog-starter/package.json#L33)

## Decision Outcome: 

Option 2.

`create-react-app-rewired` or Option 3, `nextjs-rewired`.

### Links: 

* `[create-react-app-rewired](https://github.com/snowpack/create-react-app-rewired)`
* `[nextjs-rewired](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/blog-starter/package.json#L33)`

## Context

Because there is only one LightClientSupervisor, it is difficult to change any
behavior it has without releasing a new version of the app. This includes
modifying its configuration, the types of RPC calls it makes, or the
information it exposes.

There are a number of workarounds for this, such as setting environment variables
or passing command-line options. However, these options quickly become unwieldy
as new options are added in order to modify behavior. These options could
become difficult to reason about, especially because changes to the app's
behavior are relatively common.

## Decision

We will add a CLI argument that provides us with a hash of the current
Supervisor's configuration. This hash can be used as input to the `sync` RPC
call to verify that the configuration has not changed. (The hash would be
generated using the current configuration stored in `config.ts`.)

## Consequences

This would not remove the need to set environment variables or pass command-line
options when running LightClientSupervisor, but it would remove the need to
set environment variables or pass command-line options to expose RPC calls to
the app.

## Context

Metadata is data about data.  Information describing, locating, or otherwise making it easier to retrieve, use, or manage a described resource.

## Decision

* All datasets will have a metadata file associated with them.
* The metadata file for a dataset will be created when the dataset is first ingested.
* The metadata file will be updated asynchronously each time the dataset is updated.
* Ingests will read the metadata file before doing anything else.
* If the ingest fails because of metadata validation, the ingest should fail and the cause should be returned to allow for remediation.
* When viewing an ingest, if the ingest fails in the middle of a process, the final state of the dataset will be displayed using the last successful metadata file.  If there are no errors, the last success at the conclusion of the ingest.
* All schemas must validate against a schema in a JSON Files repository.
* The file format for a metadata file is JSONL and the location is in the Files repository.
* The JSONL metadata file should not be a commitable file.  The metadata should be stored using SQL and should only exist for ingest and possibly a dump mechanism.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

There are several options one could choose as the frontend for Klokwrk:

1. Write their own, from scratch
2. Use an existing UI library, such as Semantic UI or Bulma, and build out the UI
3. Use an existing UI framework, such as Bootstrap or Tailwind CSS, and build out the UI

## Decision

Option 1 - writing their own UI - will give them the most control over the design and implementation of the UI, but will be the most time consuming and require the most up front investment.

Option 2 - using an existing UI library and building out the UI - will give them a decent UI with minimal time investment and would be compatible with option 1, allowing them to slowly start building out the UI and then transition to a framework.

Option 3 - using an existing UI framework and building out the UI - will give them a quick way to build out a UI that is already familiar to many developers. This may or may not be compatible with option 1 & 2, depending on how strict they are with their frontend requirements.

## Consequences

* Writing their own UI will be more time consuming at the beginning but will allow them to make custom changes as they go.
* Using an existing UI library or framework will give them a quick way to build out their UI but may mean they have to work around some restrictions or make custom changes as they go.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

In [ADR-001](001-use-cqrs-architectural-style.md) we decided to use the CQRS architectural style. The reason why we decided to use it is the possibility to add some kind of event sourcing to it. This could be either added as a feature of the `Wegwijs` application itself, or as an optional feature for people who use it.

## Decision

The application will store changes it is made of, as events in an events
table.

These events will be part of a data object when an endpoint receives a request.
For now, the request body will contain the event details.

In the future, the details will be encapsulated in the request body as data
object, which contains the event details.

## Consequences

*   A change to the `Wegwijs` API will be needed.

## Related thoughts

One of the consequences of using events is that the API becomes more relaxed about how to set
it's data structure for requests.

There are two options to implement events:

1.  The way `Wegwijs` currently works. The events are emitted before the
    transaction to the database and are emitted once for each successful
    transaction.

    The current approach is that we record the event in the database only if
    the HTTP response is created and returned to the user. This is a relatively
    subtle way of doing things.

2.  Another strategy we have is to record the event whenever it happens,
    regardless of the HTTP response that's emitted. A second table can
    exist to store these events, and the API calls can call the database
    directly to query and load the events for an endpoint, instead of having
    the endpoint return a list of events from its context.

    Recording the events directly to the database makes us a little more
    complex, and there are some consequences to that, like the possibility
    to add a new layer to the SQL that emits the endpoint requests. A
    downside is also that the `Wegwijs` context itself can be somewhat
    mutable, since it includes the user in the context of the request. This
    in turn has upsides as well. It seems
    [some research](https://fettblog.eu/2019/laravel-query-builder-tips-and-tricks/)
    is needed to determine the best approach for this.

## Status

## Context

The `method-handler` is more verbose, because it use an instance of a class where an instance of a method is required.

## Decision

To make the code simpler we introduce the concept of an event.

An event represents a specific action that occurs in the handler.

## Consequences

responsibility.

## Context

Consumers, producers and handlers are the core components that make up an ecosystem in Kafka.

The consumer listens to a topic, produces messages from their payload to an outgoing kafka topic and is triggered by events (usually scheduled or triggered) to consume those messages. 

By default, the consumer is configured to write to a pre-defined destination topic and then trigger to a topic called `errors`. This destination topic could, for example, be configured to be `dead-letter` but this could easily be changed by the user.

It's very possible for a consumer's payload to be transformed before being published to the outgoing topic. An example of this could be to map all `dogma` schemas to their GraphQL equivalent and publish to the `pet-store` topic.

But the problem is that there is no central, built-in place to register these handlers. Consumers can currently be configured to write to a consumer-specific set of configuration properties.

Kafka producers are able to register a callback function to be executed after successful or unsuccessful message dispatch. This, however, only works for producers interacting directly with Kafka and doesn't offer a flexible in-post-process way for consumers to register a handler.

## Decision

We will offer a way for producers to be able to use `messaging-framework` as an event bus to handle messages in the event chain after they have been dispatched to the producer.

## Status

WIP

## Consequences

Consumers can register a handler after their producer has dispatched their payload to the outgoing topic.

This allows our production app to co-exist in the same environment as staging for all users. This is not an ideal scenario however:

- As it is a staging environment, we should test changes against a known good state (from a previous release of production)
- We would like to migrate back and forth between production and staging the app
- In moving back and forth between environments, users will no longer believe we have production data in staging, leading to potential confusion

This is an issue with staging environments in general, however because we have such a large volume of users, even having small amounts of data in staging would suffice.

We currently have two options for the production data stored in staging:

1. Store the existing staging data in the current production database and enable rollback by using something like [a production database snapshot](https://dzone.com/articles/show/16038474-using-philippes-very-reliable-php-database-rollback-script) (or something more appropriate depending on the issue affecting us)
2. Use the [Production Data in Staging](https://github.com/perforce/staging-env) project to store back a snapshot of the production database at each deploy/deploy-and-migrate to the staging environment. This is just one step to a more comprehensive staging strategy.

## Decision

This ADR outlines a step-by-step process for the use of staging when using the Production Data in Staging repo or option 1 for storing a production database snapshot in staging.

## Consequences

This process has been influenced by the issues on the Production Data in Staging github repo. If a staging strategy is adopted in the future that uses this repo, then we may want to extract the use of staging to a new ADR as this does require the use of the Production Data in Staging repo, but the consequences will be small.

The `[1]`. Use Production Data in Staging for a quick win. If a migration strategy to move from the current staging environment to the staging environment with the staging data in the current production database. 

## References

1. [Production Data in Staging](https://github.com/perforce/staging-env)
2. [A production database snapshot](https://dzone.com/articles/show/16038474-using-philippes-very-reliable-php-database-rollback-script)

## Decision

## Status

   [query components](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/7.9/index-level-controls.html)

## Context
[API-005] proposes use of the service instance id for a unique namespace. 

However it is not an ideal solution. We have the following two kinds of namespaces:

1. a natural resource namespace (e.g. the service instance id of the first application)
2. an implementation specific namespace (e.g. the service instance id of a production application environment)

The namespace of a natural resource is probably much more permanent and should not change when the application is redeployed. 

In contrast, an implementation-specific namespace will likely change over the lifetime of an application as the application environment is updated and redeployed. 

If we were to use the service instance id as the namespace for natural resources, then we would need a way to change the service instance id. We would probably not want to change the service instance id once it's been assigned for a natural resource, because we would not know how many applications share the same service instance id.

## Decision
We will use the domain of the service instance id for a unique namespace when creating applications.

## Consequences
If we decide to change the service instance id, then we would need a way to change it.

In java, the way to describe and instantiate an object is two steps. First you must
create an object's instance and then invoke one of its static methods. For example,
for a string, you must create a `String` object and then invoke the `toUpperCase`

An `Agent` is an abstract class that provides an interface for manipulating an
object, including invoking its methods.
