## Context

A Rust crate is in release when you can independently verify that each binary behaves correctly
using one or more test suite. This is something we take advantage of every time to guarantee
functionality. For `testsuite` this will mean a few things:

1. When compiling for all target architectures, `testsuite` will produce a binary.

2. When creating a `testsuite` executable in the [binary-cache](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-lang/tree/main/binary-cache) (as used by cargo's `--release` flag) you will be able to run it without depending on any external file that `testsuite` has always published.

## Decision

These two things have to happen but they will occur in slightly different steps:

### Phase 1: Produce binaries without having to depend on external files

We will make it clear that every binary that contains a `testsuite` is used for testing. We will not, 
however, force every Rust crate to depend on `testsuite` in its `--release` flag to make publishing a cargo-friendly package a lot simpler, especially in the early work stages as this crate matures.

When you're compiling and using the cargo `--release` flag, and you're using `testsuite`, you will be able to run the generated binary and have a set of commands automatically picked out.

We still want you to be able to verify the binaries produced by `testsuite` and a bit of a workflow is already available for this in `docs/verifying-and-using-binaries-for-testing.md`.

### Phase 2: Dependencies on `testsuite`

Once `testsuite` is in `testsuite`/`src/` or moved and refactored out, and when you're ready to publish an updated package, we will introduce two changes for the sake of `testsuite` publishing:
- Make sure the release binary that contains `testsuite` doesn't depend on `testsuite` in its `--release` flag. This could be a simple `cargo lipo --release` command to add your binary when using `testsuite`.
- The release binary that contains `testsuite` is in `testsuite`'s `/src` directory. This should have a one-to-one correspondence with which architecture's binary is created in the binary cache (see `docs/using-binary-cache.md`). When you push `testsuite` to GitHub the release that contains the changes must be in `testsuite`'s `/src` directory.

## Consequences

When we release a new `testsuite` version there will be two separate files you need to push to `testsuite`'s `/src` directory:
- The release that contains `testsuite`. This release is compiled for all architectures, including `i386`, `x86_64`, `aarch64` and `windows`.
- The release that does not include `testsuite` as the release/use case. This release is compiled for all architectures, including `i386`, `x86_64`, `aarch64` and `windows`.

## Context

 - The current approach to handling requests and sending emails in MICO is such that a large number of threads are blocked waiting for the operation of the Mail Queue or LDAP Service. This has been exacerbated by the decision to make the service respond to both web and gRPC requests by deploying a single instance of the service. A message broker would remove the need to have threads waiting between these two responsibilities.

## Decision

It is an intention to implement MICO as a node module in such a way that a message broker may be easily swapped in. This will involve the removal of the direct HTTP and gRPC connections from the central server application and the sending of requests via a message broker. In the initial implementation, this module will accept requests and send them via the existing channels to both RabbitMQ and the LDAP service. 

A single application will be used which handles requests via an in-memory message queue. 

## Consequences

 - A message broker must be included in the application package.
 - Calls to the LDAP service and calls to the Mail Queue must be migrated to use this module. 
 - The current implementation of the application must be refactored so that the central server application is no longer a gRPC endpoint.

## Status

Proposed

## Context

We can think of an ordered list of items and a set of items in two distinct flavors:
- `Iterable<T>` is an ordered list, the elements have an order and are iterated in a specific order.
- `Collection<T>` is a set of items, the elements are unordered and iterated in some arbitrary order.

This distinction is not specific to Scala. Java makes this distinction very explicit.

## Decision

In a situation where a type does not have an explicit order, e.g. a `Set` or a `Map`, the
`order` parameter should be made optional.

When encountering situations where the order of items is important e.g. a `List` or a
`TreeSet`, e.g. where ordering by some projection is required, the `order` parameter should be
required.

## Consequences

Situations arising where a type `T` has both an order and no order:
- when `T` is an `Iterable`, `T` can be made `Collection` by casting.
- when `T` is a `Collection`, `T` can be made `Iterable` by casting, losing the ordering.
- if `T` has a `Comparator`, this can be used to sort the items without lose of ordering
- if `T` is an `Ordered` (has `head`, `tail`, `isEmpty`, `size` and a `sort` method), it can be made `Iterable` by casting.

### Context and Problem Statement

We are migrating from the version-based URL structure to a path-based URL structure for the API. Before this, any new API endpoint was added by just creating an HTTP verb endpoint, and the resource was versioned through URL paths.

### Decision Drivers <!-- optional -->

* Clean, simple URL structure
* Easily understandable for user
* Easy to parse for applications

### Considered Options

* Option 1:
  This is like the option that was used before. A resource can be versioned by its location in the path. A resource can come from multiple versions of the endpoint via multiple paths.
  
* Option 2:
  This adds another HTTP verb and gets the resource from the application. A resource can only come from one HTTP verb at a time. So the correct path would be `/v1/resources/{id}` to get the version 1 resource, and `/v2/resources/{id}` to get the version 2 resource.
* Option 3:
  This is like option 2, but HTTP GET method is used for the path to get the resource. So any resource can come from multiple versions of the endpoint via multiple paths.

### Decision Outcome

This adds another HTTP verb and gets the resource from the application. A resource can only come from one HTTP verb at a time. So the correct path would be `/v1/resources/{id}` to get the version 1 resource, and `/v2/resources/{id}` to get the version 2 resource.

#### Consequences <!-- optional -->

This option can bring a lot of consequences in a single move. It is the easiest for the developer and user to understand, and will lead to creating a clean and simple URL structure. This will also be easier to parse for applications. However, it may require the user to call the endpoint twice to get the same resource, once for each version.

## Context

Every system has a primary key, in fact we have a primary key in two cases for the citizen:
- the mandatory _citizen identifier_
- the optional _connection identifier_

The mandatory _citizen identifier_ is the same for all citizens, and is already provided by the DVS (the Dutch Identification Service).
We use the mandatory identifier as the primary key for all citizen data systems.

For the optional _connection identifier_ the rules for "primary key" are different.
In this case there is no single well defined mandatory identifier, but a selection of rules and conventions.
Since this is not an easy to reason solution, we postpone the choice of solution until we actually have the data.

## Decision

- Use the _mandatory citizen identifier_ from DVS as the primary key for all citizen data systems.
- Use a _unique system citizen identifier_ in _all_ cases. This will be the same for the mandatory identifier.
- In the future, if a _connection identifier_ needs to be added, we will use a _unique system citizen identifier_ in _all_ cases.

## Consequences
- If we decide to add a _connection identifier_ later, this will already be a well defined primary key.
- The _unique system citizen identifier_ allows other systems in the citizen ecosystem to have this as a primary key, e.g. the [citizen account platform](https://github.com/ministryofjustice/citizen-account-platform).

## Status

## Context

The [Application Layer][sec-layers] uses text for many purposes. In order to make an
informed design decision, a number of candidate encodings are evaluated, with a particular
focus on those that have wide adoption and are easily worked with in JavaScript. The
encodings evaluated are
- [UTF-8](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTF-8)
- [Base64](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base64)
- [Shift-jis](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shift-jis_encoding)

## Decision

The decision was made to use UTF-8 for the following reason:
- The encoding is extensible.
- Characters can be created that fall outside the [Basic Multaniplity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_Multi-byte_Sequence_(EMBMS)), making it easier to merge datasets from different source.
- UTF-8 is [natively supported by modern browsers](https://www.w3.org/TR/encoding/).

## Consequences

The main consequence for the application will be an increase in the [available character set](http://www.w3.org/TR/encoding/#encoding-notation). It is likely that the application will have support for several languages.

The TOSCA YAML builder is a programmable generator and transforms a [TOSCA YAML](toscana/toscana-yaml.md) specification into a Java model. ## Decision Outcome

* The `DefaultTOSCABuilder` transforms complete YAML files into Java models

* `TOSCAYAMLBuilder.build(..)` calls `DefaultTOSCABuilder.build()` internally
* `TOSCAYAMLBuilder.isComplete()` checks if the Java model is `null` (in case of errors) or `true`

designed to support and improve internal-only access to MediaWiki resources.
Some internal-only resources do not actually use HTTPS and thus cannot
benefit from using Fetchable. For most external resources it is hard to
replace the fetch-api with the Fetchable protocol.
HTTP error handling is not currently a part of Fetchable protocol: in such
cases the response status code will not be returned to the caller.
Therefore, in this job we would want to:

* Handle DNS errors:
  * Ensure that there is only one DNS server in the `/mediawiki/core`
    domain (which uses both internal and external hostnames).
  * Ensure that each internal hostname can be resolved.
  * Ensure that each external hostname can be resolved.
* Handle HTTP errors:
  * 2XX: return the response status code, along with the content of the
    response.
  * 3XX: forward the request to the URL provided in the header. Return the
    status code returned by the fetched URL.
  * 4XX: return the response status code, along with an error message in
    the response headers.
  * 5XX: return the response status code, along with an error message in
    the response headers.
* Forward the original request when the protocol is not supported.

## Considered Options

### Implementation using internal-only resource support

Option 1: Extend internal-only resources to support custom error handling

The second version of the `internal-only-resource` endpoint (which only
supports upload and internal-only resources) will support custom error
handling by relying on the `mediawiki-extensions-Popups` endpoint. This
allows the upper-level endpoint to decide how an error should be handled.

For example, if DNS issues occur when resolving an external resource, the
error message "DNS error: cannot resolve hostname" will be returned to the
caller.

#### Pros

* In progress; no more than minor code changes
* 0% of the feature is implemented in the `internal-only-resource` endpoint,
  which is already complete.

#### Cons

* 55% of the feature is implemented in `mediawiki-extensions-Popups`,
  including some API changes that would need to be merged.
  * 40% of the feature is implemented in `mediawiki-core` and may still
    be incompatible.

### Decision rejected

Option 2: Introduce new `mediawiki-fetch-server` endpoint

We could introduce a new endpoint that takes care of all fetch operations
and introduces custom error handling, but would not be required as we
already have an endpoint for the same.

Option 3: Introduce new `mediawiki-extensions-Popups` endpoint

We could introduce a new endpoint in `mediawiki-extensions-Popups` that
handles external-only resources and introduces custom error handling, but
this will likely be the preferred solution.

#### Pros

* Clear separation of concerns
* `mediawiki-extensions-Popups` would still handle both internal-only and
  external-only resources.

#### Cons

* 55% of the feature is implemented in `mediawiki-extensions-Popups`,
  including some API changes that would need to be merged.
  * 40% of the feature is implemented in `mediawiki-core` and may still
    be incompatible.

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Implement using internal-only resource support", because
this option is the most mature.
In the future, the `mediawiki-fetch-server` endpoint could be introduced
and the internal-only resource support could be merged to it.

Technical Story: PLATUI-905

## Context and Problem Statement

The tracking consent banner will be displayed in multiple languages.
The tracking consent preference will be stored as an attribute on the user.

## Decision Drivers <!-- optional -->

* Quick and easy to understand

## Considered Options

The tracking consent banner has three possible locations:

1. On the frontend application:

The tracking consent banner will be displayed on the website as an information bubble at the top
of the page (left or right side). The location of the bubble should be driven by user's
locale.

This is the most common location for tracking consent banners used by third party service providers:

- [PropertyLink](https://propertylink.co.uk/tracking-consent/) - Bubble on right
- [HubSpot](https://kb.hubspot.com/tracking-consent-banner/) - Bubble on left
- [Trustpilot](https://tracking-consent.com/blog/review-trustpilot-tracking-consent-banner/) - Bubble on left

2. On the backend:

The tracking consent banner will be displayed on the backend (administration) in a drop-down menu,
when the user is accessing the website for the first time. The chosen option will set the `TrackingConsent`
parameter on the user, which will then be used to display the tracking consent banner on the website.

This is the most common location for tracking consent banners used as part of the user journey:

- [GP.UK Frontend](https://github.com/alphagov/frontend/tree/master/govuk/settings/trackingconsent) - Drop-down on backend
- [GOV.UK Frontend](https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-frontend/tree/master/docs/tracking-consent.md) - Drop-down on backend
- [NHS.UK Frontend](https://github.com/nhsuk/frontend/tree/master/docs/tracking-consent.md) - Drop-down on backend
- [Public Goods Frontend](https://github.com/alphagov/public-goods-frontend/tree/master/docs/tracking-consent.md) - Drop-down on backend

3. In a modal:

A modal tracking consent will be displayed on the website when the user navigates to `/tracking-consent`,
which will set the tracking consent parameter on the user. This modal can then be displayed on
the backend when the user is accessing the website for the first time.

This is less common than options 1 or 2, but it is also not unheard of:

- [LogRocket](https://logrocket.com/tracking-consent-banner/) - Modal on front end, tracking preference set on user
- [Cookie notice](https://github.com/superwerker/cookie-notice/blob/master/docs/tracking-consent.md) - Modal on front end, tracking preference set on user

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: 1.

We chose to use data attribute to set tracking consent language when display on the frontend,
because the tracking consent preference will be stored on the backend,
so this method will prevent having to maintain the tracking consent preference on the backend.
This method allows us to implement the user-centric approach of tracking consent.

## Pros and Cons of the Options <!-- optional -->

### 1. On the frontend

- `+` Simple and common pattern used by third-party tracking consent service providers

### 2. On the backend

- `+` Allows to control user-centric approach of tracking consent

### 3. In a modal

- `+` This method can be applied to the backend to add a new tracking consent flow on the backend at
first access, which will allow this to be displayed on the frontend.
- `-` We have to learn a new pattern for tracking consent flow on the backend.

## Status

## Context

The current rpi-con system has used several libraries to map GPIO pin values to physical pins, some of those libraries are rather old and others are based on the assumption that only a single shared GPIO port is used.

Previously we have run into issues with the [wiringpi](https://wiringpi.com/) library, there for we must adopt a more universal method for mapping pin numbers to physical pins.

The [ngxctl](https://github.com/ngi.org/ngxctl) library uses a somewhat complicated and unintuitive protocol to control the GPIO pins on the Raspberry Pi. In order to make this library useful to more people we felt that it would be useful to develop a wrapper which could reduce the complexity and hopefully make it somewhat more intuitive.

## Decision

In order to make this wrapper easier we are going to develop the [pxt](https://pxt.readthedocs.io/) library. This library was previously only available for Arduino's but now we have developed an ARM Cortex-M7 wrapper.

## Consequences

Now using `ngxctl` for the rpi-con library is entirely possible. Using the wrapper will be a relatively trivial undertaking, as `ngxctl` uses the GPIO port and only a few pins of the Raspberry Pi. The GPIO wrapper will have its own issues to deal with in regards to the usage and mapping of pins. This wrapper is not intended to be used by itself but as a tool to add to the rpi-con library.

As there will be overlap between the `wiringpi` and `pxt` libraries in regards to pins and functions it might be confusing as to why both libraries are needed. My guess is that the `wiringpi` library will eventually be deprecated in favor of the `pxt` library.

## Context

* Utility classes are in a single place

## Background

After a while using plain object as component, we have made several components using a `classnames` library. These components are also using other NPM packages for functionality. As a result, it is becoming pretty overwhelming to comprehend every detail regarding those components. After giving it some thought, we hypothesise that we can reduce this complexity by changing our approach to using NPM package for every component.

### pros

- Components will need much less lines of code
- Every package will be reusable by other developers
- In future, we can move function to server without creating any logic into client code
- NPM provides a lot of features for package management, like lock file management, package versioning, publishing, reviewing, searching, and updating
- NPM provides a lot of features for making our own package
- As we are using [Create React App](https://create-react-app.dev/), we will need to configure a lot of things for making our own package. We can remove all those steps by selecting a proper NPM package
- We can [migrate an existing project to Create React App](https://github.com/facebook/create-react-app/blob/master/docs/migrating-an-existing-project/step-by-step.md)
- Create React App also comes with [eject](https://github.com/facebook/create-react-app/blob/master/docs/available-scripts#npm-run-eject) command to create a standalone package and setup all of our custom commands. This allows us to have a package that will be a good fit for our use

### cons

- As our own package will be built with NPM, the file structure will need a lot of work to be able to run using `create-react-app` commands

## Decision

We are going to change our approach to using NPM package for every component.

A consistent schema is needed for the REST resources. GraphQL does require a schema to handle resolving input to a resource. However, OpenAPI is a schema that has support libraries for GraphQL and TypeScript. There are multiple OpenAPI schemas that support GraphQL and TypeScript, however, all of those schemas have additional requirements and restrictions that make it difficult to combine them.

[This article](https://medium.com/clever-insights/api-architecture-consideration-1-choose-an-api-specification-1a186803639) discusses various OpenAPI schemas and their pros/cons.

## Decision

Given that there are already resources that use OpenAPI for a GraphQL API, this ADR recommends using OpenAPI specification. The `x-packager` tool (described in [ADR 012](0012-pnpm.md) ) makes it easy to combine multiple plugins, and OpenAPI specification is a simple and straight forward API to work with, making `x-packager` plugin and OpenAPI specification a natural fit.

OpenAPI brings with it additional work to create API specification documents, however that work will be offset by using an API specification that is already widely adopted.

# Use MADR as a Record Format

* Status: Accepted
* Deciders: Lewin Chan, Jonathan Pearce, Paul Higginson, Sebastien Belin, Matt Warman
* Date: 2018-05-08

## Context

The PIMS project is an agile project and will be developed initially during the author's free time (i.e. a few hours/week for each developer).
Development will involve other developers in the near future.
When joining a new team, developers will need quick access to key decisions made in the project as a whole in order to get going on their own area of the development environment.
These decisions are generally needed during the early stages of development of a feature and may be made rapidly as a team responds to changes in priorities.

### Architectural Rationale

In order to be as accessible as possible, the records of key decisions made so far should be accessible via the web.

While the MADR format may not be suitable for long term storage of records, the timeframes involved in the early stages of PIMS development may not extend beyond the period that the MADR format is still suitable for.
In addition, other formats would be possible in the future (e.g. a more detailed textual or JSON format) and there is nothing within the MADR format to prevent this.

## Consequences

The PIMS team will be developing the record of the decisions made to date in the style of the [MADR](http://thinkrelevance.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions).

The benefits of this format are:

* a concise format that should be reasonably easy to understand for non-developers on the team (e.g. product owner and management when reviewing the records of the decision)
* easy to edit and add to (e.g. as the project evolves and more and more decisions are made)
* very easy to create new records for (e.g. most of the team will have been on board at this stage)
* easy to move into other formats (e.g. if we want to use a JSON format for the PIMS API or in other contexts)

## Context

In order to design the system (the ADR has already happened) and implement it, and to communicate the design to others, it is necessary to record the context in which decisions have been made, and the decisions themselves.

## Decision

See [http://thinkrelevance.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions](1) for a useful write-up on how to record and use architectural decision.

## Consequences

Architectural decisions continue to be made that affect the current implementation. This ADR is superseded by [ADR-0002](ADR-0002.md)

## Context

* We are building an application which takes a number of parameters via the URL.
* We believe that these parameters will come from user input, not from the server config.

We need to find a way to separate this URL parameter logic from the rest of the application.

## Decision

We are going to use [gorilla.io/mux](https://github.com/gorilla/mux) as our URL routing package.

This package is very light-weight, but provides a number of additional features over
straight-forward usage of [net/http](https://golang.org/pkg/net/http/).

* automatic HTTP multiplexing (enables a single server to handle multiple web services)
* request rewriting (enables the application to act as if it's multiple applications)
* handling nested URLs
* request body parsing
* middleware support (logging, monitoring, etc.)

## Consequences

* The application will be slightly more complex - we will need to implement middlewares
* in order to use the features of gorilla/mux. These middlewares may in turn
  use other (possibly more complex) HTTP features in order to provide
  functionality such as request rewriting.
* URL structure is still a simple hierarchy - for example: `/questionnaire/:questionnaireId/:sectionId/:questionId`
* We have a list of URLs that we expose and every time we have a new URL we would need to use `mux.NewRouter`.

## Context

1.  Kibana is a critical application for E&I, as well as for the vast majority of Elastic users.
2.  As of the date of this writing, there are a non-trivial amount of users that have access to the Kibana instance that is configured for the E&I environment.
3.  As stated in [ADR-0001](0001-elastic-kibana-access.md), access to the Kibana instance in the E&I environment will be limited to authorized users only.
4.  All users of the Kibana instance will be able to access and utilize it regardless of their team.
5.  As of this writing, all users of the Kibana instance have roles that grant full access.
6.  The only user that currently has a role that limits their access to the Kibana instance is an internal user that is responsible for the maintenance and support of the infrastructure in which Kibana is deployed.
7.  Access to the Kibana instance will continue to be granted on a per-request basis regardless of user.
8.  The `KIBANA_SUPER_USER` permission is available within the Kibana instance.
9.  The `KIBANA_SUPER_USER` permission is a role that allows the use of all the permissions and is configured as a superuser.
10. The `KIBANA_SUPER_USER` permission is already configured for a user with the username `elastic`.

## Decision

1.  Grant superuser permission to existing and future users of the Kibana instance.
2.  Use a managed user for the administrative role of "Superuser" with the username `elastic`.
3.  Set a strong password for the `elastic` user (and/or use an automated password rotation policy, such as is already implemented for other infrastructure in which the `elastic` user exists).
4.  Grant this user access to S3.
5.  Grant this user the ability to provision the access role that is configured as `KIBANA_USER`.

## Consequences

1.  Users in the E&I environment will be able to access and utilize Kibana, regardless of their team (as long as they have a valid username).
2.  Administrators and developers in the E&I environment can utilize Kibana for any purpose without their access being limited to the context of their team (as long as they have a valid username).
3.  A single user is able to access and utilize all permissions within the Kibana instance with a simple password.
    1.  The password can be used to perform the actions of any user of the Kibana instance, including those that possess elevated permissions (i.e., the ability to access the `elastic` user with the `KIBANA_SUPER_USER` role).

This will be the easiest solution to use because now it will not matter where or how the application is running as long as there is a Docker daemon around

## Context

Our patterns are intended for reuse, and a pattern component should fit into any application. We have two other patterns (the builder and the decorator) that are made up of multiple files.

### Builder

We currently understand a builder to be an immutable object that creates a model. The builder is an immutable object that is passed to a creator function (constructor) which returns the model. The builder is then used throughout the application to get to a state where all models have been created and populated.
### Editor

We currently understand an editor to be a collection of classes which build to an immutable object which returns the model. The editor is invoked to start the process of creating a new model, populated with values from various inputs. Throughout the lifecycle of the editor the created models are stored in a single point and used to generate final models and populate an instance of a target model.

## Decision

We will make a pattern library of building blocks which will be available to be combined as and when required. This will be available with a builder and editor implementation for each block.

### Builder

The builder is invoked to generate immutable objects in the application and is invoked as early as possible in constructing a given model. This is invoked on entering an `if` statement block where the outcome of the expression is used to create an object of a given type. The builder can be called with default values and `null`.
### Editor

The editor is invoked when a decision point is made and used to populate an immutable object with values based on various inputs. This is invoked in a `if` statement block following the decision point. The editor can be called with default values and `null`.

## Status

Accepted

### Consequences

#### Pros

This allows us to maintain an API with minimal changes. The ability to nest builders and editors within one another should allow us to cover most nesting requirements. This will reduce code duplication. This will provide a clear separation between the immutable building blocks and the models in the application. 

#### Cons

Users will not be able to invoke the editors which will remove a level of flexibility.

# Use standard gopath for mymove

The location where `mymove` is installed (and therefore its `bin/` directory) does not conform to the standard Linux filesystems for Go packages.

## Considered Alternatives

* Move `mymove` into the `$GOPATH` (where `go` modules are expected)
* Keep current installation location

## Decision Outcome

* Chosen Alternative: **Keep current installation location**

## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives

### Move `mymove` into the `$GOPATH`

* `+` `mymove` would be more 'semantically' correct as it would exist in the root of the project, as it is when shipped.
* `-` Changing directory structure would be required
* `-` `mymove` would also require the other files that the `git command` in the root of the project.

### Keep current installation location

* `-` A `bin` directory under `src` doesn't feel 'correct' for Go packages
* `+` Installation doesn't require a `cd` into a subdirectory of the `GOPATH`

### **Status**

{Proposed}

### **Context**

Providing external Kubernetes clusters (i.e. non-internal domains) exposes endpoints that will be in use over a long term, and as more people use those endpoints, it becomes exponentially harder to understand if a cluster is still worth or feasible to use.

This is especially true in the context of the current [OpenShift deployment](https://github.com/redhat/open-cluster-deployment) which uses a default of 7 "compliant" clusters. Most of the time only a few clusters are ever actually useful at any one time, and there is no easy way to remove or unconfigure clusters that are not.

Historically I have used a bunch of bash scripts I was using to test network connectivity of internal Kubernetes clusters and this has worked very well for checking internal cluster availability. The scripts are simple and easily understandable and I have an easy way of telling if a cluster is still good or not.

But this is a new development effort and my team is not interested in maintaining bash scripts as part of their workflow.

### **Decision**

We will use a couple of kubectl commands to probe the endpoint(s) for an internal (non-public) Kubernetes cluster and update an Ansible variable that indicates whether the internal cluster is still valid.

### **Consequences**

-   The ansible variable that indicates cluster validity will be available for use in all environments
-   New internal non-compliant clusters will show up as invalid with no configuration
-   A non-compliant internal cluster will still pass the probe when it is first configured
-   Non-compliant internal Kubernetes clusters will show up as valid only when all endpoints are configured

**User Story:**

There are different ADR formats with names like:
- Standard
- MADR
- GADR
- etc.

We need unified naming.  
As all ADRs need to be in one place, the decision has to be made, what the universal name should be.

## Considered Alternatives

- Continue with MADR
- Use GADR everywhere

## Decision Outcome

Chosen Alternative:

We decided to just use GADR everywhere.

The reason is simple: 

- all existing ADRs should be moved to a new repository (see [ADR 0000: Move ADRs to Separate Repository](0000-move-adrs-to-separate-repository.md))
- there is no reason to just use some MADR-ish name

## Context

Currently we have two types of tests:

1. Unit tests: Tests a single isolated part of the application.
2. Integration tests: Tests the integration between two or more parts of the application.

These two types of tests are useful in different ways and for different purposes. Unit tests make sure that each part is working. Integration tests make sure that the parts work together.

However, our current test coverage reports show a pretty complete integration coverage, but as we dig in deeper we are realizing that we never actually test the application as a whole.

We have several integration tests which target an entire application workflow:

1. Login and register
2. Password recovery
3. Password reset
4. Sending emails
5. Sending emails (registration)
6. Invites
7. Invite acceptance
8. Logout
9. Admin interface (admin menu, create user, email config, etc)
10. Admin actions (send email, reset password, etc)
11. Create service role
12. Create application user
13. Applications
14. Application form
15. User management
16. Password recovery
17. User email verification
18. Notifications
19. Send confirmation email

This is not a complete list, but it does include all integration tests that are currently in the app.

As we investigate each of these, we've discovered that these tests actually only test a single feature or a very specific user story, which is kind of ironic considering that a user acceptance process is currently in the same process as any other product feature.

I think this is a good use of our integration tests and it should be continued, but we have some additional decisions to make and integrate in the app.

## Decision

1. Create unit coverage reports that reflect the current status of unit coverage of the app as a whole and give specific feedback regarding integration vs. unit coverage. The integration coverage reports will be integrated into the unit coverage reports to give a holistic view of test coverage.

2. Create custom code coverage dashboards for the app as a whole, covering all users. The code coverage dashboards will display the current coverage status, the unit coverage, and the integration coverage status. This will give a view of the overall test coverage and integration vs. unit coverage.

3. Create a new type of test in the app called _End-to-end tests_ that tests the entire application from start to finish, including the acceptance process as a whole. An acceptance process will consist of a user story (including acceptance criteria), an acceptance status, and the acceptance date. An end-to-end test will be triggered on acceptance and will test all acceptance criteria. This will ensure that acceptance criteria is fulfilled and that the acceptance process is understood and followed.

4. Decide what to do about the tests we have in common between unit tests and integration tests. Integration tests that are common with unit tests will be moved to the unit test files.

- Use it to create end-to-end tests in a clean, separate namespace in each environment
- Do not use it to destroy and recreate namespaces between tests

## Consequences

## Context

The [Wikibase Extension] is composed of several bundles. These bundles are 
named according to their functionality, in order to keep the total
installation as modular as possible.

* `mediawiki.extension.wikibase.api`

The behavior of bundles is already defined and covered by a test in

## Status

Partially superseded by [ADR 11](0011-replacing-batch-loading-with-cursor-based-pagination.md)

## Context

Dealing with situations where many objects need to be loaded into the Neo4J database in a highly parallel fashion presents some problems.

First of all, loading batches of objects can be quite computationally expensive because of the overhead of transactions.

This is due to the fact that the cost of loading one node is not the same as the cost of loading 1000 nodes. If, for instance, you need to traverse 1000 links to reach each of the 1000 nodes, the cost of doing this once for a single node is low, but the cost of doing this 1000 times for 1000 nodes is quite high.

This can lead to a lot of delays, if the application is able to load only a single node at a time.

## Decision

The proposed approach is to introduce [http://api.neo4j.org/0.6/org/neo4j/db/util/Cursor.html](Cursor) type of loading into the application.

This allows the user to create a single query and then use this query to load sets of objects from the database.

This method allows the user to control how many objects are loaded at a time, which helps manage any constraints on the database connection pool.

For instance, the following allows the user to retrieve all objects with a `startedAt` date more recent than 2014 and load them in batches of 100:

```java
NodeCursor<String> cursor = nodeStore.find("SELECT value.eventDate" + " WHERE value.startedAt > ?date", new DateTime(2014, 10, 20))
```

## Consequences

The following are the expected consequences of using this approach.

### Positive

- Ability to load large sets of nodes in parallel. This can potentially be quite useful in scenarios where there are multiple nodes which need to be created, but which are already loaded in the Neo4J database.
- The user can control the rate at which objects are loaded.

### Negative

- Users must know how to use this method. The documentation that is used to introduce this method should be clear and concise to reduce the learning curve.

### Neutral

- The initial approach should be fairly simple, as we only need to implement the basic logic of creating a query and then searching for the first value in the results object to see if the `cursor` has been advanced. It's worth noting that the API already contains some basic logic for doing this and so the implementation of this method would sit nicely within an existing query object.

## Context

There are possible entities in the system, let's say I have a Customer, an Order and a Product. All of these entities can have several Properties, say a Customer can have Name, Address and Discount. An Order can have Customer, Product, Quantity and Price. And a Product can have Name, Description, Price and Image.

This information can be used for various purposes:

- Navigating between the items in a graph
- Querying and aggregating data across the items in a graph
- Generating descriptions and metadata for the items in a graph
- Reasoning over the items in a graph

## Decision

To do this, each entity will have a metadata field where you can store information regarding it's properties and relations. The type of this field will be defined by the programming language.

## Status

Proposed

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Public and private keys are components of many cryptographic protocols and applications, for example:

- RSA
- Diffie-Hellman
- Digital signatures
- Key exchanges

The algorithms are well known, but they can generate many keys and can be hard to store in a human-friendly way, especially with multiple users of a single machine. A key pair has a public key that can be used by anyone (including a user) to encrypt a message to the owner of the private key. A private key has its corresponding public counterpart. This is where key signing and signing authentication comes in. A key pair belongs to a particular user. It can be held by a computer and a user can use their private key to sign a message to the computer. And if the owner can access a machine and run a command on it, they can use the machine to query the owner of the private key.

The above is only true when multiple keys are not used by multiple people. This is why they must remain private as that will be how the data is encrypted for the owner. When users store these private and public keys on the computer, they must never be shared.

## Decision

The private and public keys are stored separately in the machine’s storage as files and are both in non-database, non-server location because the keys should always be held by the owner. This can be an error, and I can provide the best practice for users to never leave their keys unsigned (i.e. not run in the case of them not using it) on the computer.

I should provide a utility to do several things related to public and private keys.

## Consequences

To implement the above decision, I will need to implement the following:
- key signing (when a user can sign a message using their private key)
- private signing (when a user can sign a message using their private key)
- key generation (when the owner of the key creates a private and public key and provides the public key to the system)
- decryption (when the owner uses their private key to decrypt a message encrypted with their public key)
- digit signatures (for scenarios when a message owner and receiver need to have multiple parties sign a message in order to validate it)
- key exchanges (when two parties wish to authenticate and exchange a long-lived cryptographic key with each other. Diffie-Hellman is an example of this)

## Context

There are two main categories of CQRS event processing:

- Process events asynchronicly
- Process events synchronously

## Decision

We have adopted the approach of processing events asynchronously.  We use Event Sourcing to track what has been written to the database as a result of processing a particular event.

Using event sourcing means that aggregates can be updated asynchronously.

Queries that need to use events may execute queries on event aggregates which may return many results.

To support asynchronous operation a `read-request` event has been provided which will query the database.  This event may return many results.
### Alternatives

We considered the following alternatives:

- Write-side: Aggregate events may use a `read-request` event to perform read operations in the aggregate.  After executing this query any updates will be performed on the read event.  This approach implies that the `read-request` method is currently not supported by aggregates.
- Process events asynchronously and make queries synchronous
- Process events synchronously and use read-side projections to query event aggregates.
- Use read-side aggregates which query the database and update an event object.

## Context

To manage users traffic to different workloads, Kubespray use one of two
mechanisms in order to create virtual IP addresses:

 1. [Ingress](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/)
 1. [Load Balancer](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/load-balancer/)

Traditionally, Ingress was only supported with Istio; and the Load Balancer
is supported for EKS.

Istio offers a way to manage network policies for Kubernetes clusters. By
installing Istio together with the kubespray, and using Istio's virtual IPs for
ingress to multiple Kubernetes clusters, we get a load balancer fronted by
Istio's ingress gateway and can create a unified load balancer for high availability,
load splitting, etc. The drawback is the extra setup.

Using the Load Balancer requires setting a dedicated NodePort in each
Ingress controller to bind to the port at which a NodePort is exposed (usually
15000:443), and creating a Kubernetes service with the `LoadBalancerServices`
type in the ingress configuration. This is useful for Kubernetes clusters
(e.g. EKS).

If we set a single IP address, i.e. the load balancer's IP (usually in
`alb-ingress-routing.yaml`), for the ingress domain(s), users only ever
interact with a single load balancer.

## Decision

Given the Load Balancer and Istio's easy integration with cloud.gov we will
only use a single Ingress controller for Kubernetes clusters.

## Consequences

If you use Istio (to connect from the ingress controller to another cluster)
and set a Load Balancer Service in the kubespray- ingress.yaml file to bind
the port to which the Ingress controller listens (the `ingress-class` value in
the kubespray-ingress.yaml file should equal the port) and the path to the
entrypoint. The IP address of this Ingress-controller should be set at
`alb-ingress-routing.yaml` and used as the IP of the kubespray-ingress.yaml file.
This can be achieved by creating an ALB ingress-routing.yaml for a load balancer.
The `alb-ingress-routing.yaml` will have an ingress gateway that listens
on 0.0.0.0/0 and sends traffic to the Ingress-controller's IP.

Users will always connect to the same Ingress controller. It will be easy
to manage the single load balancer because we have a single IP for it (from
`alb-ingress-routing.yaml` and `kubespray-ingress.yaml`).

This is useful for a Kubernetes cluster (EKS) but I'm not sure how this will
be managed in other cases (single node Ingress controller as in this current
cluster).

## Notes

- We want users to always be able to access a cluster. We don't care when
  they connect, i.e. whether it's via `kubectl`, `kubectl-proxy` (see
  `alb-ingress-routing/README.md`), `kubectl-auth` or the ALB's load balancer
  management pages in cloud.gov.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Go applications can contain a single binary artifact which combines the application source and all required dependencies. This approach differs from many other languages where separate libraries are loaded at runtime. There are well known advantages to this approach including:

- Simplicity in application packaging and distribution
- A potentially more uniform and predictable application lifecycle
- Improved security as malicious code is less likely to be introduced via dynamically loaded libraries

The approach also has some disadvantages:

- For many years Microsoft's recommended way to handle external dependencies in Go applications is to use 'go get' as a command line tool which pulls in and installs new versions of required libraries. Although this works, it leaves the application at the mercy of the maintainer of the `go get` script and doesn't offer a very clear upgrade path for end users.
- Dependencies and their versions are not portable as part of the Go application binary and require additional management by the application publisher.
- Go applications which depend on a hosted service may not be easily portable to other languages or platforms.

## Decision

The approach that we will take is to develop a set of 'dependency packages' which combine the application source and any required third-party dependencies into a single unit. For example, an application which depends on the `aws/aws-sdk-for-go` library and the `serverless` package will be packaged as a single dependency package. 

## Consequences

Go applications will no longer be composed of multiple, independently deployable components but rather a single, unified artifact.

## Problem

How to represent ndarrays in Python?

## Constraints

The following should be easy to do:

- Support arbitrary array shapes, especially higher-order arrays.
- Support both Python and C APIs for users.
- Be fast enough to not slow down NumPy.

## Assumptions

- That users won't be using very large arrays.
- That most users won't be using higher-order arrays.
- That it will be easy to find someone to review the project.

## Considered Alternatives

- NumPy
- SciPy
- SD array

## Decision

Use Python's array types, specifically `np.ndarray`.

## Rationale

- This makes it easy to work with both Python and C.
- We can get fast enough performance from it using it directly, but slow enough performance that future users can use NumPy and still get similar performance.
- NumPy is already well maintained, and its design makes this type of array native to Pythonic users and NumPy users and it should make any transition between them easier.
- NumPy has nice support for ndarray manipulation.

# 3. Use ports and adapters architecture

Date: 2020-03-05

## Status

Accepted

## Context

In [ADR#2](0002-TCH-RES-overall-technical-approach.md) we decided to use a modular monolith architecture style. Now we're going to dive into the design of ports and adapters for each module.

## Decision

For each module we'll define a port & adapter structure.

*   The port is the interface for other modules to interact with.
*   The adapter is the implementation for a port, allowing other modules to communicate by using the port.
*   The adapters are usually written to enforce a contract and will be easy to replace by other contracts.

For now we're considering two types of ports:

*   The external port is the interface to the outside world.
*   The internal port is the interface between modules inside the same application.

### External Ports

*   The application will have 1-3 external ports.
*   External ports are in the form of an interface with set of methods.
*   Each external port can have its own module, let's call them:
    *   User Access
    *   Application Data
    *   External Services
*   Each external module will have 1-3 ports & adapters.

### Internal Ports

*   An instance of module can have a set of internal ports.
*   Internal ports are the interfaces between modules, for example:
    *   Application context
    *   Application data
*   Ports within the same module will have same name.
*   Application module use cases will have internal ports as parameters.

## Consequences

The internal ports must use keywords like `instanceOf`, `has`, `get`, `set` depending on their use.

-   The internal module's instance can decide which methods to expose as internal ports.
-   The internal module's instance can decide which internal ports to expose as internal ports.

The application will have 3 components:

* A node provider, which provides a device's network information and current

* A decentralized identity provider, which provides a user's public and private

The Tendermint node proxy will provide the following capabilities:

* Get the most recent 500 blocks via P2P
* Get the most recent 500 blocks via RPC

## Context

Many of the components the Digital Business Platform offers need a database for storing information.
Currently Content Services, Process Services and Sync Service do this but there might be more to come in the future. All three are using the same version of the database so the obvious question was raised: Can we just use one database for all our services?

* easier maintenance
* faster failover
* better backup
* economic reasons (licensing)

We also identified some disadvantages:
* a single point of failure
* all components are tied to the same database system
* adding new components requires downtime
* failover is not transparent to the user

## Decision

We will use versioned database services for all our components.

* Adding components becomes less complex
* Components can be deployed without downtime
* A single database restart can bring all components online
* Components are not tied to a specific database
* A single backup can be used to restore all services
* Licensing is simplified
* Reduce the amount of components and configuration

### Disadvantages
* Components will need to connect to different databases
* Failover is no longer transparent to the user
* A database restart will still require some downtime

## Context

In order to act as a central point of data storage and management for the HEE National Website Platform we need to provide a common database system.

There are various different requirements for a database and each has various pros and cons. This ADR outlines how we plan to use each type of database.

## Decision

### Relational Databases

A traditional SQL/RDBMS database. In the context of the HEE National Website Platform we will only be using one type of this - MySQL.

Pros

- The industry standard
- Mature product with excellent tooling
- A single system will act as a central point of data storage and management.

Cons

- Significant work to migrate to a new system
- A new system will require maintenance and evolution over time
- Can be difficult to run in a cloud native environment

### Document Databases

A NoSQL/JSON document database. In the context of the HEE National Website Platform we will be using MongoDB.

Pros

- A single system will act as a central point of data storage and management.
- Significant work to migrate to a new system
- The ability to use MongoDB as an interim system to replace several existing systems will provide a central point of data storage and management.

Cons

- Can have a significant impact on the business as we migrate.
- A new system will require maintenance and evolution over time
- No guarantee that moving to a document store will be easy to do.

## Consequences

We will be moving away from a SQL/RDBMS database and will not be using databases in the future.

All services must use a document database (MongoDB).

for things like user email verification had to pass through to a client (the frontend app in this case).

For all client app uses of the auth-server, the choice to implement their own logic (or trust the

## Status

Accepted

## Context

A naive approach of building an API for a project like cljdoc is to start with the monolith and gradually break it apart into more manageable pieces. Alternatively, one can start with the pieces and build the monolith.

Making monoliths gradually is quite common in practice, but adds extra work when new pieces are ready and have to be extracted. Making everything from scratch or refactoring out the monolith piece-by-piece is quite common as well, but this adds extra work when the new pieces need to be refactored. 

Startups commonly build things fast to learn the problem domain instead of investing heavily into a good, stable design, so a monolithic architecture can have merits for this reason as well, provided adequate time is allocated for research and design iteration in those early stages of development.

There is a spectrum of opinions on the value of starting with a monolith, however it is generally agreed that there should be a priority placed on making the core API as stable and correct as possible before additional work is undertaken on it, and that those additional decisions can be made after the first release is complete.

## Decision

For this project, cljdoc, I have decided to tackle the project as a series of loosely-coupled, self-contained pieces rather than a monolith. These pieces have a clear segregation of concerns and do not violate the DRY principle as I understand it. I will tackle core concerns in the order:

1. Reading Clojure code
1. Reading Clojure metadata
1. Computing and indexing data
1. Serving the web API

## Consequences

This decision makes it easier to take the project in the direction it needs to go, but I will need to revise the approach later if it's clear that all of these pieces are too big. This also gives me opportunity to experiment with making breaking changes in the direction I choose for each piece if and when I take on those responsibilities. 

My plan is not to try to do this as quickly as possible and as monolithic as possible, however there is value to getting a basic set of features working quickly to learn about cljdoc's problem domain and how best to approach using API and other designs, so I will attempt to do that via an iterative approach: this will be a collection of pieces, each piece building off the last completed, and all pieces updated at once into the current iteration's release.

## Context

The Temporary Identifiers (TID) that are currently used in the
registry are being deprecated.

## Decision

TIDs will no longer be used in the registry. Instead a permanent identifier
(PID) will be used.

All existing registries which use TIDs will need to be upgraded to use
PIDs.

## Consequences

### Advantages

* TIDs do not allow for uniqueness, which is required for a registry.
* Uniqueness is required for the REST API to function correctly.
* PIDs allow for the possibility of renaming (in the future) in the
  registry. This is not something that is possible with TIDs.
* Rename requests would need to go via the API, and then be
  propagated into the registry (and the REST API) as new PIDs are
  reserved.

### Disadvantages

* PIDs are currently generated by the API. In the future, we may consider
  allowing users to reserve a PID before it is generated, to make sure that
  the user gets the desired PID.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Certain engine implementations, particularly [SQLx](0004-sqlx-based-engine.md)
(see ADR 0004) and [pg-engine](0006-add-pg-engine.md) (see ADR 0006)), store both
aggregate and process instances in a Postgres database.

The existence of an aggregate and process instance is something that must be
checked as part of a process before executing a process, or it will be
impossible to determine if that process is still valid for execution.

### Decision Drivers

* Should be efficient, as it is part of the normal execution flow after
  an aggregation command has completed.
* Should be minimal in the amount of code it contains, even if it duplicates
  past values.

## Decision

After much research, including reviewing some
[ideas for state management](https://github.com/Dogma/dogma/issues/1097),
"Existence" is an efficient solution to provide a fast way to detect if an
aggregate or process instance exists via some fast queries:

```go
func (e *sqlxEngine) Exists(c, s string) bool {
  if !e.sqlx.Exists(fmt.Sprintf(`SELECT 1
    WHERE c.name = ? AND s.type = ?`, c, s),
  ) {
    return false
  }
  return true
}
```

**Usage**

Existance checks are integrated into `AggregateCommand.Execute()`
(after `ExecuteCommand()`) by calling `e.Exists(a, s)`, where `e` is the
AggregateEngine. `a` is the Aggregate and `s` is the Session.

### Consequence

There might be some duplication of data in the domain model and engine
implementation. This is okay, as we think that by keeping the logic for
interacting with the engine the same, the API will be easier to use in the
future, and any necessary "existence checks" will be part of the engine
implementation itself.

## Context

In order to allow for arbitrarily nested fragment groups, and to keep `mergeFragment` from being a tangled mess, we introduced the concept of a fragment containing its own merge tree.  This was partly motivated by the desire to allow for arbitrarily nested fragment groups, but also by the need to keep `mergeFragment` from being a tangled mess.  

The current approach for handling missing fragments is to ignore them.  We do this by simply skipping over them in `mergeFragment`.  This is easy to reason about, but it's also not ideal:  The fragment is not present in the final result.  

## Decision

We will now provide an option to allow users to specify a fragment template to be inserted when missing fragments are encountered.  The template will be applied to the original fragment group, and the fragment will be inserted in the same position as the original.

### Handling of missing fragments in `mergeFragment`

If a missing fragment is encountered in `mergeFragment`, the current approach will be changed from ignoring the fragment to skipping it.  We will continue to skip over any nested fragments that are also missing.  This is because we do not expect users to nest fragments arbitrarily deeply.  If we did nest fragments arbitrarily deeply, we would need to introduce an additional `isMissing` flag that we'd have to traverse through each fragment to check.

## Consequences

In order to implement the proposed change, we will need to add a new method to `FragmentGroup`:

```java
default FragmentGroup mergeFragment(FragmentGroup fragmentGroup, boolean preserveFragmentOrder) {
    mergeFragment(fragmentGroup, new ArrayList<>(fragmentGroup.getFragments()), preserveFragmentOrder);
}
```

and an `Optional.empty()` as the return value when called with `false`.  To preserve fragment order, `mergeFragment` will be invoked on `new ArrayList<>(fragmentGroup.getFragments())`, and the original list will not be changed in place.

## Context

If a piece of software needs to communicate new information to a user, or the software needs to be communicated to a user, then a software developer needs to handle the communication of messages and display information as a service, the software should be able to raise an event.
If a piece of software handles external interactions with other software, or communication between components within the software, it should be able to register and trigger an event.
If the handling of communication from external sources is triggered by the software, then the software should be able to communicate the message that was received to a consumer.

Software could be configured such that a message that was received is handled by a user, or by a piece of software. The software could be configured such that handling a message is the function of a piece of software and no user is necessary.

## Decision

Software should allow the handling of several types of event, and should allow the registration of several receivers (consumers).

## Consequences

If software has a single point of failure for the handling of an event, then a consumer needs to be registered for the event to be handled.

If software receives an event, but the software is configured such that the event is handled by a user, then the software should provide some mechanism to indicate to the user that an event has been handled.

## Context

Maintaining a database in sync with fast-changing data structures is not an easy task. Data structures change as new data is added and as the existing data needs modification. It would be best to isolate the database to a set of modules that are only concerned with the creation and modification of data. These modules may want to act as a single unit and take care of most of the business logic rather than expose a lot of functionality to the outside.

This set of modules is referred to as the "database" module for clarity. This module is a subset of the overall application module set.

### Architectural Styles

The question is, how should the database module be structured to isolate it from the rest of the application?

#### Clean Architecture

One simple and yet effective way to achieve this is to employ a clean architecture style, where all incoming requests are handled by a dedicated service layer, and all outgoing requests are directed to a data model layer to interact with the database. This kind of separation is often used for other resources, such as data validation, and is well suited for handling asynchronous tasks and cron jobs that are common in Django.

#### Ingest SQL files

Another common pattern in Django is using an "Ingest SQL file" service, where an endpoint is defined that accepts an SQL file and executes it against a database. The end point does not return any information about the success or failure of the query, but the database module would be able to tell via other means if the operation was successful.

## Decision

In order to isolate the database from the rest of the application, we will use a combination of both Clean Architecture and Ingest SQL file. The database module will have two endpoints:

* An endpoint to accept SQL files for ingestion
* An endpoint to run an SQL query and return the results 

## Consequences

* The Ingest SQL endpoint is useful for an administrator to be able to reset data, create data for testing, and/or seed the database with data from an import file. 
* These endpoints should be protected via authentication middleware in order to ensure only authorized users can run ingestion and querying operations on the database.

## Context and Problem Statement

Many complex and abstract EAI patterns can be implemented using FaaS as the backend (compute) component and other standard AWS components (e.g., SQS, S3, SES, SNS, IAM, etc.).

The backend logic of a few such patterns could also be implemented using the function's in-memory state. This would remove the need to persist state in external AWS components, which is often the case for existing EAI patterns.

The logic to implement complex EAI patterns may get quite complicated. It is therefore required to provide a good and easy way for implementing patterns as functions.

## Decision Drivers <!-- optional -->

* Clean way of implementing complex EAI patterns
* User does not care to know whether SQS is used as in-memory state, or if an external SQS is used

## Considered Options <!-- optional -->

* 2 options have been considered in this ADR:
  * Option 1: Functions are implemented as standard AWS functions (e.g., SQS)
  * Option 2: A combination of functions and in-memory state

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: [option 2], because users should not care about all AWS services and logic that is used internally. It is the responsibility of the function developers to make functions re-readable and as simple as possible. There are already some in-memory patterns implemented (e.g., request-reply).

The patterns which are most likely to be implemented via this mechanism are the advanced EAI patterns as defined by [Gautam Karthamurthi](https://github.com/gkp/messaging-patterns).

### Consequences <!-- optional -->

* When we implement complex EAI patterns using the backend logic, and we implement them as FaaS functions, then we have to implement them as user-oriented components.
* Developers would need to implement their own implementation for patterns, which already is a lot. Therefor it is important to review and reuse existing patterns as they will evolve and become cleaner over time.
* For some cases, patterns may be implemented via functions by only implementing the implementation for in-memory patterns.

## Pros and Cons of the Options <!-- optional -->

### *[Option 1: AWS-Functions]*

* Good, because it's standard and known architecture for AWS users.
* Good, because it's easy for users to understand how it works (with a quick glance at the schema)
* Good, because there is a lot of patterns that are available as AWS-FaaS implementation already (e.g., for request-reply)
* Bad, because every service will be used, where an internal service may be needed in some cases
* Bad, because the user will get some services, but needs to implement the code to implement them.

### *[Option 2: Function + State]*

* Good, because it's known architecture for AWS users.
* Good, because it's easy to understand the user and the logic
* Good, because it's easy for the user to implement
* Bad, because it's not so easy to implement every known EAI pattern in this way

## Context

### Why eslint?

ESLint is an incredibly useful linter with support for SASS. It can automatically fix linting errors as we write code, and automatically format code as it is saved.

It has great integration with well known editors like VSCode.

As of writing, over 12 million repositories use ESLint.

## Context

The Tendermint documentation has a number of outstanding issues, specifically around documentation for developers. The site is unwieldy, with content in various states of disrepair. Parts of the site are also inconsistent with each other, specifically around the [SDK](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/blob/main/docs/reference/all.md) and [Specs](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/blob/main/docs/reference/specs.md) sections. The information on how to build and contribute to Tendermint has previously been scattered and the community is in need of an updated resource.

This ADR seeks to provide an overview of how the documentation will be handled for the Tendermint Alpha and Beta releases, and beyond.

## Decision

### Resources

A number of subdomains are reserved for the Tendermint documentation:

- [docs.tendermint.org]
- [alpha.docs.tendermint.org]
- [beta.docs.tendermint.org]

For simplicity, these will be hosted under `docs.tendermint.org`, with additional subpaths for distinguishing between resources, which will be split into their own repositories. For example, `tendermint.org/sdk` will be a Tendermint SDK repository, and `tendermint.org/specs` will be a Tendermint Specs repository.

### Status section

Rather than maintain multiple versions of the SDK, API changes and breaking changes will be handled by versioning in the `sdk` section. Prior to Alpha, `main` will be at Beta 2; once Alpha is released, `master` will be moved to a `stable` branch, and `sdk` will point to this branch, while `alpha` will also point to `master` and be used to publish Alpha releases. After Alpha, Beta and tendermint.org/beta will remain valid.

### Components

In addition to the SDK, the documentation will also need to cover the following components:

- CLI
- Query language
- Consensus
- Indexing
- RPC

These will be included in the SDK resource, and additional subdomains will be reserved for their documentation in Alpha, Beta, and the maintainer's convenience. For example, `query.tendermint.org` will be a Tendermint Query Language resource, with the following mapping to sections in the SDK:

- Query Language is a subset of the SDK
- RPC is included in `components/rpl/index.md` of the SDK

## Status

Accepted

## Consequences

### Positive

- Content can no longer be broken by misnamed sections
- Updates to the SDK can be published continuously, without requiring the maintenance of multiple versions of the SDK
- Community contributions can be incorporated easily
- The [SDK API spec] can finally be updated in one place
- `spec/` can remain a development-oriented section
- `examples/` can finally cover all of the SDK
- Docs for non-SDK topics can be included in the appropriate section
- `DOCS_README.md` no longer needs to include instructions to read the `README.md`

### Negative

- All outstanding issues with the current Tendermint documentation are carried over to the new documentation

[SDK API spec]: https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/blob/main/docs/reference/all.md#sdk-api-specification

## Context

When getting ready to deploy code in the staging environment, our current procedure has these steps:
1. Create several branches, deploying the applications in the master of each branch
2. Create a new deployment cycle for each application with any changes from master to staging
3. Keep each deployment in the master of its branch until an application has been accepted into the staging environment

## Decision

We propose adding a staging app as a deployment option for an application when you are getting ready to deploy your code to the application. This will:
1. Simplify our current deployment cycles for applications, which may or may not cause a lot of work
2. Have the ability for a deploy to change which branch it's coming from and add applications as a feature from another branch that is ready to be deployed
3. Provide an incremental environment where each release to staging is an app-by-app change, but is easily scalable to all applications without requiring creating a branch of your applications in your application environment

### Staging Workflow
1. Login to your Application and select a project
2. Select Create deployment and select a staging environment
3. A box will appear to enter the details of the deployment, including a branch or branch url where the deployment would come from. If you have already selected a branch in step 2, this step will not be required and you will need to create your deployment from your branch.
4. If you have more than one application connected, a menu will appear asking you to prioritize which application would like to be deployed
5. Select and Create the deployment.

### Creating a deployment
1. A new box will appear to determine which branch and applications to create a deployment for
2. Enter the name of the branch that you want to select as the source for the deployment
3. If you want to deploy a branch as a feature from an existing project, this will allow you to add the applications in this branch as a feature application for a given project
4. Once the branch is selected (or a new branch is created), a list of available applications will appear. You will need to select and enable the applications for a feature deployment to be deployed from this branch
5. Once all applications for the deployment are selected, select Create Branch and the deployment will begin to apply changes to your site.

## Status

Proposed

## Consequences

- A branch will need to maintain feature applications and feature deployments
- A branch will still be the preferred way to make and manage the entire application
- Deploying a branch will only require a few clicks
- This solution will now have the ability to deploy a branch of applications from a project to a single environment, for the use of creating a deployment to your branch

- Adding a deployment in your branch will still be the preferred option and can be more easily managed

Technical Story:

Given the importance of defining an anti-affinity in inbound traffic across namespaces between the Gateway and Translator services, why is this not a default behavior?

## Context

Given the following scenario:
The Gateway and Translator services sit within a given namespace. The user in namespace1 creates an instance of the Gateway, called `foo` in namespace2. The Gateway service is bound to the user. The user changes the type of the translator service in namespace1 to `echo`, and creates a new instance of the Translator service called `bar` in namespace2. The user wants to send a message from a pod in namespace1 to `echo` so that the message is redirected to the Translator. Why can the user not filter their gateway and translator to just have the pods in namespace1 be visible for the translator?

## Decision

1. Gateway and Translator instances must always be colocated in a namespace. It is easy to allow users to use the `anti-affiinity-selector` for a placement pattern for the Gateway. This may need to be enhanced and/or removed for the Translator, depending on future design. 
2. All gateway services must have `anti-affinities` specified for all other namespaces in which the gateway is attached to.
3. Use custom resource definitions as the mechanism of setting an anti-affinity. The custom resource specification should be a custom resource kind in a `gateway` namespace and this kind should be removed from namespaces other than the `gateway` namespace for each of the translated services.

## Consequences

If `anti-affinities` were not part of a custom resource, and if custom resource placement patterns are not removed from the namespace and only a generic `all` rule is left, this will make it so that any user can make any translator bind to the gateway. We believe this is the easiest solution to the problem.

For a long time, we have been using the [dcl/ui](https://github.com/dcl/ui) library as the front-end CSS framework for cljdoc. This library has been an excellent choice, allowing us to achieve a lot with its components and utilities. 

Recently, the library has fallen behind, lacking major features and the community is getting harder to find. As we are preparing to go fully remote, we must consider adopting a new library, one that can replace `dcl/ui` but still offer a similar experience for the user.

## Decision

After reviewing several options, we have decided that the [Reakit UI](https://reakit.io/) library is the best choice for the following reasons:

- It has a modern and clean design, drawing inspiration from Material UI and Tailwind CSS.
- It features a wide range of components, from basic ones to advanced, such as data visualization capabilities.

- It has a good community, although not as big as `dcl/ui`.
- The library is well maintained, with frequent releases and a mailing list for community feedback.
- Reakit UI uses [Theme UI](https://theme-ui.com/), which is an excellent library for building design systems in React. It comes with a bunch of pre-defined themes, that will allow us to iterate fast on the design of cljdoc.
- Reakit UI is a single-maintainer project, but the author is very active and open to community feedback. The library is published under the MIT license, so there is little risk in forking it.

## Status

Approved.

## Consequences

We will be replacing the `dcl/ui` library with the `Reakit UI` library in the next major release (1.3).

There are currently two types of messaging API exposed by Dapr:

* **Push API:** Send command messages from the Actor API to the Event API for the Actor System. This is done synchronously and by request.
* **Query API:** Ingests the `GetEvents` request from the Actor API and pushes command messages to the Event API for the Actor System. This is done asynchronously and by request.

The Actor API uses `Push API` to interact with the Event API. The Query API uses the `Query API` to interact with the Event API.

As the actor system is part of Dapr, we are expecting the two APIs to become less important as the actor system is refactored. So the two APIs will eventually be removed and the actor system will directly call the event system.

## Decision

We keep `Push API` but make it more obvious that it's used by the Actor API. We will use `Push API` for the actor system to deliver command messages to the event system, which pushes the events to the event store.

The `Push API` will handle the push of commands from the Actor API to the Event API. The `Query API` will handle the push of command messages from the Actor API to the Event API.

## Consequences

Query API will no longer be needed. We will change the Actor API to use `Push API` instead of the `Query API` to deliver command messages to the Event API. This change will allow the Actor API to deliver command messages to the Event API when executing command messages. The `Query API` will be removed with the next major release of Dapr.
