## Context

The current process for downloading and indexing attachments from the DPD requires the extraction of information
from 25 or more external services. These external services will need to evolve over time in terms of API and
information provided. The current process for handling these external attachments is unsustainable in the long
term. 

In order to gain a better understanding of how the external services are changing, a different approach to storing
incoming attachments will be employed where the attachment data is extracted from external resources and a local
copy is maintained.

Due to the need to interact with the same external services, the local attachment copies will need to be updated
as external resources are modified or consolidated.

## Decision

The approach adopted for handling external attachments will be to maintain a local copy of the attachment held within
a GitHub Actions secret. The secret will be the same in terms of content as the external attachment but will
be updated periodically and, in cases where the external resource is modified, to replace the old attachment data
with the new version.

The GitHub Actions integration will be leveraged to ensure the attachment data is updated in the data store when
external attachments are updated. The GitHub Actions build will be run on acceptance of the pull request made to
update the local attachment data. This ensures that the attachment data in GitHub Actions is always up to date.

## Consequences

The process for storing and updating external attachment data will be more straightforward to maintain than the
current process.

The risk of encountering application errors in the future will be reduced by moving the management of external
attachment data to a GitHub Actions secret.

The use of the GitHub Actions build to maintain the attachment data will ensure it remains up to date with changes
made to external resources.

The move to GitHub Actions to maintain the attachment data will require the attachment data to be moved from the
application into a GitHub Actions secret.

## Status

Accepted.

## Context

Part of @energyweb/frontend requires to test code against an external
API, the Authentication API. This requires mocking of Auth requests in
some test cases.

Before we mock Auth, it is a good idea to have a fallback where no
Auth request is made.

This means that a mock server will need to be set up which runs the mocks.
If a mock server is not set up, requests to a service not under test would
be blocked (because the `Host` header with the required Auth token will
be missing). The mock server may optionally handle other endpoints as
well.

## Decision

We will use the MockServer to provide a single place that can set
request callbacks to mock HTTP requests.

## Consequences

### Ease of testing

Testing is significantly easier. There is no `expect` to pass, no mock
server to set up, the test can just make a call and pass the response.

### More clean tests

Test cases in `utils/mockServer.js` are far less verbose.

### Clean separation between tests and service requirements

In `@energyweb/ui`, there are several sections that use mock requests, and
there are three separate tests that make mock requests. In this style, the
mock requests are tested with `expect`, then mocking the requests in the
`mockServer.js`. This would just be different in `@energyweb/frontend`.
As a consequence, the tests with `expect` may be removed and the mock
server logic split into its own tests.

## Status

## Context

The identity management system which will be developed will use Shibboleth as an identity provider.

### Research

Our research indicated that in order to be able to use Shibboleth for an OAuth2 service we have to implement it as a SAML2 service. 

We identified a few main reasons why we decided to implement Shibboleth as a service as opposed to an application.

We felt that the development of a standalone application would be more complex.

As Shibboleth is configured via properties rather than programming the application provides less opportunity for reusable components which are already written and documented elsewhere.  (An example of this was LDAP auth which needs to be setup differently depending on the expected authentication provider)

The use of properties within the configuration and deployment of the application can also allow for easy integration of other services such as metrics.

## Decision

To implement Shibboleth as a SAML2 service which will be configured using properties.

## Consequences

This decision may make the initial application more complex to build but this will be offset by the use of well known and well supported open source components such as [mod_saml](https://github.com/dkrs/mod_saml).

Ultimately the SAML to OAuth2 mapping is handled by an intermediate proxy such as [auth-server](https://github.com/OWASP/CheatSheetSeries/blob/master/cheatsheets/Implementing-an-OAuth2-Authentication-Server.md) so the SAML implementation will not be required but we have implemented it in order to [meet the OAuth Core 1.0 SAML profile](https://tools.ietf.org/html/oauth-core-1.0#section-4.1.1.1).

## Status

Superseded by [ADR021](ADR021-namespaces.md)

## Context

Dapr offers several namespaces to cater to different needs. For instance, a namespace can be a logical separation between apps targeting different environments, or a mechanism to isolate apps with differing security or resource constraints.

In the past, we have had requirements for both logical separation and security isolation between apps in different environments, and Dapr has not been able to provide this. Logical separation is easy to achieve using standard Kubernetes features such as namespaces and RBAC. However, true security isolation between environments is more difficult to achieve as it requires preventing cross-environment access to production secrets and other sensitive information.

For this reason, we have introduced the concept of dev namespaces.

## Decision

Dev namespaces are isolated namespaces which do not have access to production. In order to make dev namespaces as secure as possible, they will be isolated on a dedicated GSP cluster. This will prevent dev namespaces from ever having access to production, even accidentally.

## Consequences

- As with all other aspects of Dapr, dev namespaces will be isolated and accessible only via the GSP API.
- The introduction of dev namespaces will not change the current isolation between production and other namespaces.

## Context

For us to dynamically load and evaluate Python expressions we need an
interpreter. This is something Python has been built around for many years now
and there are a lot of choices in terms of writing styles and general
approaches. The current approach in clojure/tools is to rely on the
[pyit](http://pyit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) library. This has several
advantages:

1. Initial development of pyit has already dealt with a lot of boilerplate
   code
2. It relies on [ast](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ast.html) the core
   Python language
3. It adds minimal logic and is otherwise transparent.

The main issue with this is that there are other libraries that can
complement it and it's also the approach the clojure/tools team has
decided to go with.

A different approach would be to try and implement a Python interpreter
ourselves. I don't think we are capable of doing this from scratch. It's
more likely that the result would have some issues. This approach may
make sense though if we were to try and implement some functionality
which requires more context information. A couple of things to note
before going any further however:

- Clojure/tools also uses [gargoyle](https://gargoyle-lts.herokuapp.com/)
- This project also plans to be used by multiple users so we would have to
  think about security. This has already been done, in that the
  built-in Python functions are only available in the standard library
  and not by way of a dependency.

A quick way of looking at the differences between the two approaches is to
compare how we handle division. We would not want to expose this as part
of the public API but division is actually an important operator. For
Pyit, you might want to do
`(pyit.eval_file 'x / y')` but this would mean exposing the value of x
and y, which I don't think we would want to do. We might decide to simply
use `(/ x y)`. This is a simplistic example but it touches on the main
point. This is of course a decision to make anyway and the way to go is
to use a built-in operator.

## Decision

We decided we will use pyit and adapt it as we make additional
interpretations, so that we can build upon the existing code.

Date: 2018-04-12

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The various terraform files in this module have slightly different structures, mostly because they are based on the different requirements of the consumers. These include:

- a basic set of resources related to the cluster
- terraform files for automatically provisioning a kops cluster
- terraform files for provisioning a managed set of nodes for kops
- terraform files for automatically provisioning a cluster using gcp
- terraform files for provisioning a managed set of nodes for gcp

### general structure of the terraform files

the files can be divided into two types, those which use a high level declarative language and those which use a lower level imperative language. The imperative language files contain more detailed steps for how a resource is configured, while the declarative files describe the end state of the resources after applying a series of actions. These two types of file can be distinguished by the fact that the imperative files are usually found inside a directory of lower level resources, while the declarative files are in the top level directory. 

Imperative files can be created in two different styles:

- files which use a pattern which applies to multiple resources. This is often used to ensure that a required set of resources exist in a cluster. For example, all kops clusters require a dns zone to automatically provision when it is set up, and so all kops clusters should include logic which ensures that a dns zone is present.
- files which provision a single resource and are not found in a subdirectory. These are typically used to install tools into a cluster, or to configure an integration like the automatic provisioning of nodes when kops is installed.

### problems with different styles of file

imperative files created with a style that applies to multiple resources are harder to reason about as part of a terraform unit. This leads to them behaving as both logic that should apply to all resources and logic that should only apply to a particular configuration. This is a non-trivial problem as sometimes the logic should apply to the entire cluster, but is called in a way that implies a more limited set of resources. It is for this reason that logic in imperative files should typically only be included when absolutely necessary, and should be accompanied by a declarative resource that consumes that logic as part of its provisioning.

[see this thought experiment](https://github.com/kops-lab/kops/blob/3914/core/scripts/ensure-zone.sh#L23-L63)

## Decision

- we will only create files in the top level directory of the terraform module
- we will avoid creating logic in imperative terraform files
- we will avoid using imperative terraform files where it is possible to use a declarative one
- we will provide logic in a centralized location in the terraform module: core/logic/
- we will call the logic from imperative files and declarative resources that consume the logic
- we will use a centralized concept of an integration

### integrations

an integration is a specific set of imperative files that, when executed in sequence, install a given piece of software into a cluster. An integration is not a resource and has no state, but it does have configuration. When a new integration is added, it should be accompanied by an additional set of declarative files that provide an interface for provisioning an integration. This would allow users to utilize the logic in the integration files without burdening them with the imperative files themselves.

#### example

a common set of files for a given integration might include the following, but not necessarily in this order:

- `common.tfvars` - common variables used by imperative files in this integration
- `integration_manifests.yaml` - high level declarative resource that describes an integration and provides values for variables used in imperative files
- `integration.tf` - imperative file that installs a given piece of software into a cluster using logic from an integration. This file may be called `init.tf`, `upgrade.tf`, etc. depending on the integration

#### considerations

- imperative files in an integration may still be useful in situations where a declarative interface to an integration does not make sense, such as immediately before or after a new cluster is created, or when certain resources need to be configured before an integration is ready to be installed.

# Test Framework

## Context

There are many testing frameworks for Python.  These include:

- [pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/)
- [unittest](https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html)
- [nosetests](https://nose.readthedocs.io/)
- [xunit](https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html)

All of these frameworks assert that the code under test is Python and can be used with other languages.

## Decision

Use pytest.

## Consequences

- If another framework is better for the way Python is written for, there is no hard restriction using pytest.
- Easy to integrate in build processes.
- Very common practice for Pytest.
- Has plugins for all major build tools.
- Not a great deal of boilerplate.
- 5 minutes to write a suite of tests.
- 30 minutes to run the suite of tests with all plugins.

accepted

jar for deploying the application.

### **Status:** ACCEPTED

## **Context**

[CCS-ADR-0004][ccs-adr-0004] states that all new digital services should use common components and services where possible.

[CCS-ADR-0009][ccs-adr-0009] states that all new digital services should use Infrastructure as Code to manage their infrastructure.

This ADR should explain how Infrastructure as Code will be used on CCS digital services.

## **Decision**

**What is Infrastructure as Code?**

Infrastructure as code (IaC) is the practice of managing and automating the provisioning of resources in AWS.

[CCS-ADR-0009][ccs-adr-0009] defines "digital services" as:

> all services which make use of AWS resources, either directly or indirectly.

For the purpose of this ADR, we will take the stance that all AWS resources used by a digital service will be created using Infrastructure as Code. 

We will leave open the question of whether the service team, or a central team, will create the IaC that is used to instantiate a service.

## **Further information**

[ccs-adr-0004] CCS Architectural Decision Record: Use common components and services
[ccs-adr-0009] CCS Architectural Decision Record: Use Infrastructure as Code

## Context

In order to reduce the network load from IoT devices, a UUID with 16 bytes of data needs to be compressed into 8 bytes. 
Additionally, it needs to be sent as a binary value. This means that parsing and generating a UUID requires knowledge of both 
IEEE 1642 and the Java UUID API.

### Alternatives

After reviewing the alternatives, I think that using random GUIDs is the best solution for this problem.

The reason why is that it is easy to parse and generate.

Another alternative would be to use human-readable GUIDs, which uses a checksum.

These are the two alternatives I found.

## Decision

Use random GUIDs and not human-readable GUIDs

## Consequences

We will use two different UUID types in the codebase.

## Status

## Context

The entity type `Item` has projection, because for a given item you can have one data structure called `Item` with multiple `Value`s associated.  
However, to make the system more simpler, projections which are not data-structures on their own (like Value, Set, List, Dictionary) will be directly returned using a `Projection` object, not exposing the inner data-structure.

## Decision

The system will only expose a `Projection` object, no nested data-structures will be exposed.  
Inner data-structures will be resolved using projections with `DataStructure.prototype` extension.
Projection will return data as an `Array`, the user can decide what data structure is used internally (or if it's even needed), but projections won't expose their internals.

## Consequences

- It's not possible to return an empty data-structure. A projection will always have some data (from the original item or from the original data-structure).
- We can't use empty collections as arguments to a projection (will cause it to return the empty collection).

# 11. Extract text from documents

Date: 2020-Apr-01

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Researchers may want to extract text from PDFs and images and other file types.

### Current extraction methods

Several Python packages exist for doing OCR. Some notable ones are:

- pytesseract
- image-to-pdf
- pdf-images

Additionally, [https://ocr.space](ocr.space) and [https://eastview.com/ocr](eastview.com/ocr) will allow extraction from URLs.

### General OCR limitations

Despite all this, there are several limitations to using OCR on PDFs in particular (see the last section of this ADR for general information on OCR).

The process of extracting text to a pdf will still be required in several cases, i.e. with an OCR service or through python's Tesseract command.

### Current extraction workflow

Normally, one would extract text to a pdf using a 3rd party service, or run a python script with the Tesseract command and then call a python script that can be called via the API with the pdf (as an AWS S3 object).

This has several shortcomings:

- running commands via the API
- creating and destroying an S3 object in the process of extracting text from the PDF
- multiple calls from multiple sources with different credentials will add more overhead than is needed

#### An alternative extraction workflow

One proposed workflow would allow for extraction from a url to a temp pdf, via the AWS API gateway. This would allow the creation and use of a temporary S3 bucket for placing the temp pdf and then using the AWS API gateway to run it as a command via the Tesseract command.

We could still return the extracted text as a json object via the API gateway.

One advantage of this is that it reduces the number of separate calls and the associated overhead of credentials.

### OCR in document upload

We may want to perform OCR on the uploaded document to preserve the original formatting, and make it easier to read, without having to change how it is stored

### Other concerns around OCR

- PDF security (the need to keep it encrypted, i.e. so it is not tampered with)
- language(s) supported (we may want to support a variety of languages)
- how to handle the text extracted (e.g. include the pdf and OCR text side-by-side)

## Decision

Extract text from uploaded images, converting them to pdfs, into a document, before extraction
to reduce the amount of processing required in the endpoint for reading the document.

If the uploaded document's content can be easily read, render it alongside the original document's pdf.

We will not attempt to extract text to a pdf from images on the frontend.

#### Specifics

We could start with an AWS API gateway API that could do this via the AWS command line tools. This could be a command that extracts text from the uploaded pdf, converts it to a pdf and then runs that text into a db via command line tools. 

#### Why this approach (instead of flask?):

Using python flask would cause us to run the Tesseract command on the endpoint as the flask server would require the file to be stored locally (in memory). However, as the endpoint is already going to run with Python's command line tools and then use the AWS API gateway, running Tesseract via the CLI seems like an appropriate way to continue.

## Consequences

- extracting text to a pdf becomes even less of a necessity
- using OCR text as a temporary replacement for the original pdf (or to extract text from PDF images)
- removal of existing extraction (extract-text) endpoint
- endpoint for conversion to pdf
- text extraction logic moved from endpoint to aws API gateway via command line tools

## Status

## Context

The current revisioning strategy is based on the [semantic versioning](https://semver.org) (in which increments are made to the major version number). Release cycles for Helm chart updates and the binary package updates (fargate) are not aligned and currently run at different times. Release cycles for the binary package include testing procedures which require changes to the Helm chart which is also not aligned. This results in maintaining and deploying several versions of the Helm chart and/or binary package. 

Currently there is no automated deployment of the Helm chart or binary package. These have to be updated asynchronously after the chart and binary package have been updated.

There is sometimes confusion regarding what is the current release of the Helm chart or binary package and when/where to look for the updated release.

We would like to:
- Have confidence that the Helm chart and binary package are both deployed using the latest revision
- Have confidence that the binary package and Helm chart are using the latest binary.
- Have confidence that the current release of the binary package is the latest available in the Helm chart. 

## Decision

Introduce a new release cycle where the binary package and Helm chart will be released simultaneously. 

The binary package will update automatically on Helm Chart update, assuming the Helm chart is updating the binary package (as per current conventions). 

## Consequences
- Binary package will no longer be updated asynchronously
- There will be no delay between updating the Helm Chart and deploying the binary package

## Status

Draft

## Context

Although CloudHSM is the default root authentication system for HSMs in AWS, it is important to restrict the access HSM is able to receive to a particular namespace. In AWS this is normally done by setting a security group on the HSM VPC, but this allows machines with non-HSCP approved architecture to have access to your private IP address. 

## Decision

Access to the HSM namespace should be restricted to a single EKS cluster, and not routed directly to individual VPCs, via the following:

1. **Use AWS' internal network feature** to restrict inbound network access to a single `10.0.0.0/16` CIDR
1. **Set up VPC security groups** to prevent egress outside the above CIDR and prevent ingress from non-HSCP namespaces.
1. **Set up EKS node groups** to use the `10.0.0.0/16` CIDR network.

## Consequences

Any VPCs created by the EKS cluster will have their own security groups, and so need to restrict egress to the `10.0.0.0/16` CIDR only.

Any non-HSCP VPCs which have already been created and provisioned will need their internal IP addresses added to the `10.0.0.0/16` CIDR or removed.

We cannot guarantee that this decision will hold true in the future, but by using the AWS internal network now we ensure we're setting up our HSMs using the same network space as all other services. This will maintain our ability to deploy VPC-less EKS clusters.

## Status

## Context

In commercetools we use the "adyen_notification_url" to call adyen-notification endpoint and retrieve information on new payments which have succesfully occurred, but haven't been linked with commerce.

This endpoint is a custom endpoint, therefore the url has to be provided via commercetools.

### Why 2 urls and not 1 url for notifications

Adyen support 1 url for subscription notifications and 1 url for payment notifications, this allows the user to keep them separate.

If we would have to use same url for both types of notification, then 1 url for payment notification would have to take care of 2 types of notifications.

The complexity involved in retrieving 2 types of notifications from 1 url is high, and has the risk of being complex to manage over time for various reasons. This is the main reason for why 2 urls are used in the solution.


### 2 ways to manage payments (via commercetools or 3rd party)

We have two options on how to handle the merchant-api-endpoint on commercetools;

1.  Create an integration using commercetools integration capability
2.  Create a custom endpoint, then use it directly in the commercetools integration.

## Decision

Option 1: We will create integration for commercetools using commercetools integration capability.

### 1. Create 2 endpoint for AdyenNotificationUrl

Generate 2 endpoint on commercetools integration, 1 for adyen-notification-url (for linking to commercetools), and another for payment-notification-url (for linking to adyen);

```yaml
components:
  - endpoints:
      paths:
        /api/v1/payments/notify-adyen:  // adyen-notification-url - POST endpoint, example above
        /api/v1/payments/notify-commercetools: // payment-notification-url - POST endpoint, example below
    description: >-
      The Api Endpoint that will handle the payment notification from 3rd party (commercetools or adyen).
    requestBody:  // @query-all-items
    responses:
      "payment-notification-url":
        content:
          application/json:
            summary: Returns the linked payment status on commercetools
        description: >-
          Endpoint that will handle commercetools notification, will call adyen-notification-url (Post endpoint) with payment notification data.
        status:  // @success
      'payment-error':
        content:
          application/json:
            summary: Returns the linked payment status on commercetools with error
        description: >-
          Endpoint that will handle commercetools notification, will call adyen-notification-url (Post endpoint) with payment error.

      'missing-fields':
        content:
          application/json:
            summary: Returns the error if fields are missing on commercetools
        description: >-
          Endpoint that will handle commercetools notification, will call adyen-notification-url (Post endpoint) with payment notification data.
```

### 2. Return url on commercetools notification

Upon sucessfully receive payment notification via endpoint on commercetools (adyen-notification-url), the response will return `merchantApiNotificationUrl` to the user which will handle linking to commercetools;

```yaml
components:
  - endpoints:
      paths:
        /api/v1/payments/get-payment-notification-url:  // POST endpoint
    description: >-
      Endpoint to send the link for payment to commercetools
    requestBody:  // @query-all-items
    responses:
      "payment-notification-url":
        content:
          application/json:
            summary: Returns the link to commercetools when payment notification received.
        description: >-
          Endpoint that will handle commercetools notification, will call adyen-notification-url (POST endpoint) and return the merchantApiNotificationUrl
```

### 4. Use Merchant Notification Url to call Commercetools NotifyPaymentEndpoint

Use merchantNotificationUrl to call commercetools NotifyPaymentEndpoint, and finally update commercetools order status accordingly.

### 5. Add missing fields to 3rd party payment endpoint when posting payment data to commercetools
The url on 3rd party payment endpoint (adyen or commercetools) is to be sent in the headers with `paymentData`, in commercetools the `paymentData` will be sent via the POST endpoint

## Context

The current approach of AMI Lookups has a few problems:

- If a lookup doesn't return an exact match, it returns all
  related AMIs. If the lookup returns multiple records, it
  requires the application to choose which record is the
  one they want.
- There's no concept of related records which may or may not
  be an AMI, so the lookup may return a lot of unrelated
  records. If those records contain related objects (like
  users), then this requires the application to loop over
  those records and make sure the user is in their selection.
- The database lookup uses multiple-value fields to perform
  the lookup, which requires writing code to turn values from
  multiple-value fields into a single value.
- Many lookups return the first result, but the
  `count(:lookup_count)` option to the lookup indicates how
  many records are returned. It doesn't work in multiple
  levels.
- The database lookup in multiple fields makes it hard to
  use a range of values instead of an exact value.

## Decision

This version introduces a new model and several small
changes to existing ones to address the problems.

The key structure is the `lookup_result` model and this has
been extended to `database_lookup_result`, which is the
model returned by the database. It is an `object` with a
`record` model in its JSON structure, with the same
`fields`:string-value relationships as the original record.
Lookup-based searches may now return multiple records.

The database-level API still supports looking up a single
record and is implemented using multiple-value fields. The
database-level API only now returns the
`first_result_count` option if a lookup has multiple records,
but the API for performing a lookup is unchanged, so the
application can still use multiple fields for the search
expression.

## Consequences

The application doesn't always have to choose the record
when multiple records are returned and is instead can
return the `database_lookup_result` object. The use of `count`
in the database level API still provides an option for
limiting the number of records in the results.
`database_lookup_result` uses multiple-value fields to
implement the database lookup.

The SQL in the API is still written using multiple-value fields
to achieve the search. The domain layer may convert
multiple-value fields into an array (for a field that
was looking for a single value) and `array-merge` function
to find multiple records.

If this approach is more verbose, we'll choose which pieces
it's verbose in when adding a `use` tag. For example, if
`create_user_lookup` is always a verbose API, then it may
receive some improvements without making the rest of the
package more verbose.

## Context

There is a large amount of text data in the original source documents from which the `searchengine` application was derived.

## Decision

We have added an SQLite database in which to store this text data.

## Consequences

A large amount of text cannot be inserted into RAM in Java without excessive use of paging libraries. The usage of a database on disk reduces this requirement and it becomes possible to store more text. ## Context

UEFI requires a partition to be mounted as `/boot/efi` during startup. This partition contains an EFI application, known as the EFI shell, and data used by UEFI's secure boot feature.

In some instances the drive used for `/boot/efi` has a single FAT partition which does not support dual-root. The native way to handle this issue is to create a new NTFS partition and move the current EFI configuration into this partition. This configuration will generally remain on the original drive, but with the benefit of requiring less secure boot data on the original disk. This allows you to, for example, test or rebuild a system after a format without discarding your current configuration, but this method is easily reversible. If something goes wrong during the process, I can assure you it will be an interesting debugging process.

## Decision

Instead of moving around disks and partitions on an existing drive, I am proposing to create a second disk for the system and place it as `/`. This allows for easier rebuilding/restarting from scratch with the added ability to also include a dual-root environment with a re-useable partition to start with if you are trying to migrate off an old disk due to bad sectors or anything of the sort. 

I'll be adding a `reboot-into-dual-root` option to GRUB and have this ask for the old drive as an old-root disk before allowing you to choose which drive would be your new root disk.

## Consequences

* Dual root is the native way of doing this on UEFI systems now and will make migration easier, and also rebuilds and resets simpler, and it is also how OpenMTA does it now. 
* Creating a new disk before hand is a nice easy way to migrate disks as well as re-using an old disk with bad sectors and this will allow for an easy transition when attempting to use the disk again
* It also is the only way to now dual-boot with Windows, but this is an additional layer above the configuration steps, which I will cover in a following ADR

# Context

Blockchain and in fact Bitcoin itself is a large number of different data types assembled together.

This is true for most if not all blockchains and thus there is not a lot of point in reinventing the
wheel when it comes to how to handle data in such a system.

In this case the data types become somewhat complicated by Bitcoin's requirement that most data
be in the form of *sequences of bytes*. This means that we must decide on how to handle
various non-byte data types such as fixed-length integers, fixed-length byte arrays, and
boolean flags.

This ADR is concerned primarily with data types which can be assembled together to form the
content of a transaction and the associated block. That is, it is concerned with the "core"
data types of a blockchain.

# Decision

The types of data which will be supported are:

* Boolean: A simple on/off switch which can be included in transactions and blocks
as a field of bytes with a defined meaning.

* Fixed-length integer: An integer which is encoded using a fixed number of bytes.
Examples include variable-length integer encoding in Bitcoin (uint256) and fixed-length
integers used for indexing.

* Variable-length integer: An integer which can be encoded using a variable number of bytes.
Examples include variable-length transaction IDs, output amounts, and Timestamps.

* Fixed-length byte array: A sequence of bytes where the length is fixed. Examples include
Merkle proofs and Sigs.

* Random data: Data where the contents are truly random and not encoded in any way. Examples
include non-deterministic proofs and some cryptographic operations.

# Status

Proposed

# Consequences

1. All the data types supported by this ADR can be assembled together to form the content of a
transaction and the associated block.

2. It will be possible to include non-byte data types in transactions and blocks.

## Context and Problem Statement

A [framework](https://docs.spring.io/spring-introduction/html/) reduces the amount of boilerplate code that needs to be written for common tasks in a given application. Frameworks promote reusable components, and often include design principles and guidelines for usage. Choosing a proper framework can significantly ease development effort and promote a more maintainable codebase.

## Considered Options

* [Spring](https://spring.io/)
* [Vert.x](https://vertx.io/)
* [Akka](https://doc.akka.io/)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Spring", because it is a robust framework that is well suited for the application in question.

### Positive Consequences <!-- optional -->

* Use of the [spring-actuator](https://spring.io/projects/spring-actuator) for implementation of health checks.
* Use of the [spring-data](https://spring.io/projects/spring-data) for implementation of database functionality.
* Use of the [spring-kafka](https://spring.io/projects/spring-kafka) for integration with Apache Kafka.

## Alternatives

### Vert.x

A modern framework supporting the most current programming concepts.

Vert.x can be a good option for prototyping, but the application framework's main focus seems to be clustered, microservice architecture. The documentation is quite sparse in places, and the framework uses a considerable amount of in-house libraries, including asynchronous event-bus-style in-proc/in-memory.
While Vert.x does support HTTP, there is an impression of putting HTTP first rather than building HTTP on top of reactive networking primitives. This leads to many small components which require configuration that is often quite verbose. 
There does not appear to be a strong ORM in Vert.x and the reactive-first approach also does not lend itself to straightforward design patterns like REST and JSON. 
Vert.x is designed for use cases where asynchronous is the rule, rather than the exception, and where the network is a resource to be consumed, rather than a system to build upon. 
Because of Vert.x's reactive-first design it might be challenging to implement HTTP interaction using the same principles that drive most Vert.x-centric code, e.g., http calls are not performed on the JVM. 
Vert.x includes a reactive HTTP client but as an option, and this in turn utilizes the asynchronous capabilities of the underlying web framework.

### Akka

A general-purpose framework facilitating the building of distributed, message-oriented applications. 

Akka is a good fit for use cases where a distributed application model is required, where asynchronous is a norm, rather than the exception, and where resilience to error is paramount. 
Akka provides a lot of building blocks for constructing distributed applications, including an API for distributed publish/subscribe messaging, a master-worker architecture, and tools for secure cluster configuration. 
It is also very strongly idiomatic and appropriate for use with _akka-http._
However, Akka has a steep learning curve, and is probably better suited for distributed application developers, rather than typical web application developers. 
It is also idiomatic to implement HTTP functionality using akka-http rather than akka-jms.

## Further Reading

* [http://martinfowler.com/bliki/Spring.html](0)
* [http://martinfowler.com/bliki/Vert.x.html](1)
* [http://martinfowler.com/bliki/Akka.html](2)
* [http://theburningmonk.blogspot.de/2010/11/comparing-nodejs-flask-django-spring-akka.html](3)

# 6. Users will be able to relay state in headers

### Status: Decided

## Context
On submission success users can receive one email per `site-content-item` after a delay. Right now there are two options:
- site content item has the setting `enable_delayed_email`, and defaults to `true`.
- the submission page can show the item immediately after a success. This is implemented, `for example`, via `SubmissionController#success`.

So, in theory, this would become less-useful and be moved into a private beta or deleted, at:
- [submission_controller#success](https://github.com/gardener/community/blob/main/app/controllers/submissions_controller.rb)

## Decision
In theory it would be easier to only use submissions for which `enable_delayed_email` is on, but, as of writing, the options of using the normal, now-redirected submissions, and the non-normal that have delay settings are not separate. So, a decision was made to:
1. use `delay_email` for site content items, that send emails,
2. use `submission_controller#success` or a similar, for each, site content item submission that has an email-enabled option, so that one submission has two submissions (site-content-item, submit-submission).
1. use the normal submit-submission functionality (now with a choice of sending the submission immediately, or delayed).
1. use the non-submitting option for site-content-items that send emails.

The above allows:
- we could use the `submith-submission` behaviour as an implementation option for the submissions (with no delay) with the new `submission_controller#success`
- we may be able to move `site-content-item` emails into a private beta, with its delayed email functionality in `SubmitionController#success`, so that we can experiment with delays.
- we are setting the correct API (which will be future-able) for site content items that send emails in some way.

## Consequences
The submission `success` will be able to function as a regular submission page that sends the submission to the normal route.
In the future the `site-content-item` emails can move into a `BetaSiteContentItemController#submit`.

# Background

The Tendermint repository contains numerous outstanding issues which address
architecture concerns that exist within the current codebase.  These issues
address a wide variety of concerns from different sources:

1. Code quality issues discovered by static and dynamic code analysis
2. Extensibility issues identified by reviewing pull requests and code
   contributions
3. Performance issues reported by the Tendermint mailing list
4. Security issues identified by code audits

The Tendermint Community has an architecture discussion on #359947689


# Complication

In order to holistically address the concerns that have been brought forward
in #359947689, a decision must be made on how these issues will be addressed.

There are currently 33 active forks of the Tendermint repository.

There are a number of repositories which fork Tendermint as a base to build
other software.

The Tendermint Core team has the ability to either:

1. Merge the `tendermint` repository with the master
2. Create and maintain a `tendermint-core` repository containing only the
   `tendermint` repository's history
3. Do nothing, and allow forks to continue as they exist today


# Options

The Tendermint Community has put forward 2 options regarding how outstanding
architecture issues can be addressed:

1. Forking the Tendermint repository
2. Copying the `tendermint` repository's history into a new repository

### Forking the Tendermint repository

1. Copy the `tendermint` repository into a new directory
2. Rename the directory to `tendermint-new`
3. Add a new commit to this `tendermint-new` directory containing all
   the outstanding architecture issues and their proposed solutions,
   correcting the history of the `tendermint` repository to remove these
   issues (using the `--no-history` command in the `git filter-repo` tool)

### Copying the `tendermint` repository's history

1. Clone the `tendermint` repository into a new directory
2. Rename the directory to `tendermint-new`
3. Add a new commit to this `tendermint-new` directory containing all
   the outstanding architecture issues and their proposed solutions,
   correcting the history of the original `tendermint` repository as
   described in 3.  Optionally merge in the `master` branch of the
   `tendermint` repository to bring in the updated version of `tendermint`


# Decision

The Tendermint Community has decided to implement Option 1, described above.

The rationale for this decision is that:

1. Allow forks of the repository to continue being created to implement
   customizations to Tendermint Core
2. Maintain an accurate history of the `tendermint` repository, including
   the history of the architectural decisions made on the Tendermint
   Community as described in #359947689
3. Provide an incentive for forks of the repository to not address
   architectural issues that are discovered in the `tendermint` repository
4. Allow the Tendermint Core team to make architectural changes to the
   current `tendermint` repository without the need to branch and merge
   countless forks

## Status

Proposed

## Context

See [RFC for JSON-LD (Draft)](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc0149)

### Choice for parsing

[Mark Logic](https://github.com/LogicML/marklogic/tree/master/marklogic-json-ld) uses the standard, recursive JSON-LD
notation to parse JSON data to create an RDF graph.

### Choice for emitting

[Apache lucene](https://lucene.apache.org/java/6_0_0/) includes a fluent API for generating JSON documents,
which can be used for emitting JSON-LD as a textual data format.

These libraries support a subset of RDF standard. They do not provide an API for emitting RDF, nor do they 
support the JSON-LD API. 

### Limitations of lucene-based emitting

Generating RDF documents from an existing graph is the simplest approach and may make sense for the initial
version, but it is very unlikely that this approach will scale to the size required for production applications.
Also this approach does not allow us to reuse the SDBM's own terminology in JSON-LD form. 

### Limitations of marklogic-based parsing

This library does not provide an API for emitting RDF.

### Context
Current search is on the website, it can be easy to use for some people but as it is now some searches need to be done by using many filters. Searching on GOV.UK can be a simple thing for some users (it's only a click or two from the site home page), but for others it may be a difficult, time consuming process involving multiple pages, lots of clicks and inputs (especially if they're using a mobile device or a screen reader).

Our users are using lots of different browsers and devices to access GOV.UK, and we should make sure our search is accessible from all of them.

People search in different ways - for example they may make a spelling error, or use a phrase rather than the precise word. They may also use filters to narrow down the search results without using the search bar at all.

This work aims to improve the basic search so it's more user-friendly - especially for new users or those with disabilities. It should also make it easier for power users to find exactly what they're looking for.

### Decision
We're improving the current search so that:
- the search bar uses auto-suggest to give users better options as they type.
- filtering options are grouped sensibly and can be applied to multiple criteria at once.
- the results are displayed more clearly, with the most relevant results highlighted.
- users with disabilities can search the site as easily as anyone else can.
- pages with high search traffic but that currently have no search bar (like the Help section) should also have one.
- existing searches should be analysed to see how users are using them now, so that we can understand what improvements would be most beneficial to them.
- a new `govuk` site should search both sites seamlessly.

### Consequences
We will do usability testing on every stage of the rebuild.

We will use analytics to measure the impact of the changes we make on our users.

We will eventually remove the existing site-specific filters and rely solely on the unified GOV.UK filters.

## Context

* The application logs into a MySQL database to access to user data.

## Decision

The schema for the database is currently:

```
CREATE TABLE user
(
    id        bigint       not null auto_increment,
    username   varchar    not null unique,
    password   varchar    not null,
    email       varchar    not null unique,
    created_at timestamp not null default 'now'
);

CREATE TABLE organization
(
    id            bigint       not null auto_increment,
    name           varchar    not null unique,
    description    text(64)    not null,
    created_at      timestamp not null default 'now',
    updated_at      timestamp not null default 'now'
);

CREATE TABLE membership
(
    id              bigint       not null auto_increment,
    user_id        bigint       not null,
    organization_id bigint       not null,
    created_at        timestamp not null default 'now',
    updated_at        timestamp not null default 'now',
    role            varchar(20) not null,
    UNIQUE (user_id, organization_id)
);
```

The organization database is not an instance of the organization. It is an instance of the `user` table.

## Consequences

A better design would use a simple two tables solution, where the organization id and the role in the membership table would be foreign keys to the user table. This would make querying simpler and more efficient.

## Problem

Currently there are two possible locations where API help messages are displayed:

1. The endpoint metadata in the Swagger UI.
2. A separate "Help" endpoint, which displays a static page with the same content.

In practice, the "Help" endpoint is rarely updated, and so it is not clear
when it is last updated. Moreover, the API description for an endpoint can
be obtained from the YAML definition, which is more precise and automatically
generated from the code.

## Constraints

- We should avoid maintaining two different versions of an API description.

## Assumptions

- Most users will rarely if ever use the endpoint directly.
- Most users will rely on the Swagger UI for finding out about the API.
- The effort required to generate an API description from the YAML is worth the benefit.

## Considered Alternatives

- Generate an API description from the YAML and display it in the Swagger UI.
  If there is no help message, do nothing.
- Generate an API description from the YAML and display it on a separate "Help" endpoint.

## Decision

Generate an API description from the YAML and display it in the Swagger UI.
If there is no help message, do nothing.

## Rationale

Maintaining an endpoint just for displaying an API description makes no
business sense. It is a static piece of content, and so is better suited
to the YAML definitions, which are also the source of the content. The
YAML API description can be made to serve this purpose by leveraging the
existing `yaml_content` field, which is already generated from the YAML. This
description will be generated for any endpoint that has an entry in `api_helper.jsonc`.

## Related Decisions

- [Low-level API - YAML structure](#low-level-api-yaml-structure)

- Problems moving to the next application step

User actions and views will need to be modified for undone steps to use the new column.

## Status

Proposed

## Context

Unique reference identifiers (URIs) will be generated to track access to public datasets as well as manage schema evolution.

Currently, a `dataUri` is generated for a dataset. This is a universally unique identifier (UUID) which includes a checksum of the dataset title.

A `dataUri` provides a unique but not evolvable identifier.

The need to both track access and allow for schema evolution requires a different strategy.

## Decision

This decision is to replace `dataUri` with a `dataRef`.

A `dataRef` will be generated using a [Hash-based algorithm and checksum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptographic_hash-based_message_authentication_algorithm). This will be done using the following steps:

1. A UUID is generated (using a standard random process).
2. A cryptographic hash of the UUID is calculated (using SHA-256 with an initial seed value of 0).
3. The result is a 256-bit (32-byte) string.
4. The first 64 bits (8-bytes) of this string is the hash of the seed value.
5. The remaining 192 bits (24-bytes) is the hash of the UUID.

The `dataRef` has three roles:

1. Unique identifier of the dataset in a particular schema version.
2. Unique identifier of the dataset in its own schema.
3. Allows for access to a particular snapshot of the dataset at a specific point in time.

## Consequences

- Access URIs will be updated to use `dataRef`s instead of `dataUri`s.
- When datasets are updated in place, the access URI should be updated accordingly.
- When datasets are removed, their access URIs should remain valid for historical purposes.

## Context

As described in [ADR-0001](0001-record-architecture-decisions.md) and
[ADR-0002](0002-version-software.md) this project uses an MySQL database to store
data on open repositories for GitHub.  A primary reason for this is that is
allows us to use optimistic locking to avoid data corruption that can result
from parallel transactions.

The general idea is that a transaction attempts to update a database record but
only commits to the transaction once it knows that the update has been applied
successfully.

If optimistic locking isn't used, there is an alternative to use
[MySQL`s p`soft-version](https://mysql.com/de/support/cheatsheets/read-vs-write-multiple-rows-in-a-transaction/)
method, which is to first read the data out of MySQL and then retry the
transaction using an if/else block to implement retry logic.  I will use
`psoft-version` in an [example of this](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/127404211/best-practice-for-optimistic-concurrency-in-mysql-async-example-including-pyhon-and-mysqlpython-libraries).
The obvious disadvantage of this approach is that it means the application
has to keep the read and then the written transaction in memory and if the
transaction commits multiple times, due to failure to apply the new values,
then it will have to do the logic again.

A question raised about is the trade off of readability vs the other
consequences of using `psoft-version` in an [example of this](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/127404211/best-practice-for-optimistic-concurrency-in-mysql-async-example-including-pyhon-and-mysqlpython-libraries)

## Decision

I am going to use optimistic concurrency.  

I will use `psoft-version` on transactions that write to the database and
then use a python library to automatically retry the transaction if the query
fails.  I will refer to the first one that is used in the [pyhon tutorial](https://sql.confetti.org/python/sql/opt-concurrency/).

There are other uses of this kind of logic in the system which rely on the
[MySQL`s p`soft-version](https://mysql.com/de/support/cheatsheets/read-vs-write-multiple-rows-in-a-transaction/).
There aren't any plans to use this approach with other code.

## Consequences

- My queries should be simpler and more readable than if I use the read
  and then retry logic as
- I will be ready to transition to another algorithm if the use case calls
  for it.
- MySQL does have an algorithm of optimistic concurrency
  (https://mariadb.com/kb/articles/277819/how-it-works-optimistic-locking.html)
  but I have read that it's not easy to write the query logic to implement
  the logic of this algorithm for which `psoft-version` is a workaround.

## Use Cases

This would be useful in any situation where several updates may need to be
read and then written to the database and then a transaction should be
conditionally applied to the changes in data. I think this is most useful in
cases where there are multiple inserts or where a high number of rows may be
updated. I believe even simple updates could still benefit from using this
method to prevent code that implements `psoft-version` from being written.
[This article](https://webdev4cats.com/blog/2020/03/27/mysql-optimistic-locking.html)

## Alternatives

My solution is far from great.

## Further Reading

- https://mariadb.com/kb/articles/277819/how-it-works-optimistic-locking
- [MySQL`s p`soft-version](https://mysql.com/de/support/cheatsheets/read-vs-write-multiple-rows-in-a-transaction/)

  It's a bit more involved and seems to have more requirements for using,

There are a couple of good reasons to implement the REST architectural style and the Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State (HATEOAS) constraint.

The first is that the [Open Lobby Server project](https://github.com/openlobby/openlobby) was originally envisioned as an API-based system. While this is no longer the case, the architecture and APIs designed to be consumed by external systems are still in the codebase.

The second reason is that by using RESTful APIs, the system will encourage adoption by frontend applications, whether they be in the form of GUIs, mobile applications, or other similar types of applications.

These reasons are not mutually exclusive and likely many other benefits will be realized as a result of making the system more RESTful.

## Decision

All new functionality will be built to be RESTful and HATEOAS-compliant, and there are no exceptions to this decision. This means that the application will allow consumers to build whatever frontend application they choose without requiring any work to be done in the frontend application.

The application will only consume GUIs running in the browser.

## Consequences

We will implement APIs and endpoints that are compliant with the HTTP protocol and HATEOAS.

We will remove any non-RESTful endpoints. This may require substantial investment as many non-RESTful endpoints already exist.

There will likely be many endpoints that allow us to combine functionality. This will require us to invest in logic that distributes requests appropriately among these endpoints.

This application's work delivers a single, outcome-oriented product for 2 users. It is an [MVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_viable_product) that prioritizes learning about users and the problem space, rather than rapidly validating a solution.

We want to understand whether or not the benefits of using a tech radar justify the cost of developing and maintaining a new one.

# Decision

We will use a hybrid tech radar in [application monitoring](https://github.com/last.fm/learning-platform).

We will keep the current priorities of technology at GDS Tech separate.

For the purposes of developing a minimum viable product, we will create a tech radar that communicates:

- what type of technology [LPA] engineers, developers and other stakeholders are working with in their daily tasks. This will be gathered via interviews, [job profiling](https://wiki.gds.gov.uk/5508) and [surrogate profiling](https://wiki.gds.gov.uk/5509).
- what future technology we need to be aware of in a project for which [LPA] is responsible, regardless of whether we plan to use them.

The tech radar will be a living document that evolves as [LPA] grows and matures.

# Status

Accepted.

# Consequences

We will use the current GDS Tech technology radar as [GDS] understands it.

The tech radar will remain a single page, with future versions of the product as [LPA]'s needs become more complex.

We will consider other options for [LPA] communication as we have data about [MVP] users and an understanding of their needs.

We will expect the [MVP] to [be useful] as it solves a well-defined, albeit simple, use case, for a clear and defined [user] group.

We will expect people to contribute to the radar as we gather information about the [MVP].

We will review as part of our [continuous delivery] process whether new technology should be highlighted on the radar.

We will expect the [MVP] to change quickly with new [users] and new [needs], which will help us understand whether the [radar] continues to be useful to [LPA].

We will consider whether and how we can differentiate between [past, present and future] [radar] releases in [LPA] communication.
[LPA] communication will be provided by the delivery team when people use [LPA] the most.

We will review after 50 [user] [iterations], taking into account the [cost] of running an [LPA] in a hosted environment. [Costs] will also [include] [external cost] of operating [LPA] for 35 [people] from [GDS].

We will consider whether [LPA] hosts will [be needed] beyond the [MVP].

We will make a decision on whether any future [LPA] needs and [use] of the [radar] [will be made] [explicit].

# Deprecate and replace MessageFactory with MutableMessage

## Status

Draft

## Context

We introduce a requirement for a `MessageFactory` in [#85](https://github.com/OpenMessaging/specification/issues/85).  This leads to two implementations, an interface `MessageFactory` and a concrete implementation, `MessageHandler`.

The use of an interface, with a single method to create a `Message`, seems to violate the principle of least surprise, as well as being semantically backwards incompatible with `MessageHandler`, where `newMessage(..)`, `getMessage(..)`, etc.

Additionally, the interface `MessageFactory` requires a stateful counterpart `MessageState` ([#89](https://github.com/OpenMessaging/specification/issues/89)), which is a common design pattern.

## Decision

* Deprecate `MessageFactory`
* Merge functionality into `MessageHandler`
* Add a `MessageState` property to `MessageHandler` ([#89](https://github.com/OpenMessaging/specification/issues/89))

## Consequences

`MessageState` and `MessageHandler` become the new main component for handling synchronous messaging.

Interfaces for asynchronous messaging ([#130](https://github.com/OpenMessaging/specification/issues/130)) will be based on `MessageState`, and `MessageHandler`.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

A person in the system can be a primary contact or a secondary contact for a citizen or organization. A primary person is usually the main point of contact for an organization or a single individual who is a citizen. They should therefore be the first point of contact for the portal.

The primary person may share their Identity with other users like a partner, family member, carer or friend. In an ideal world, adding an additional person should be as simple as selecting the correct field on a user form. 

But for some people, adding their partner as a user on a platform like GOV.UK would involve filling in a lot of additional information and multiple forms before they have their own account. This is sometimes also the case for other caregivers, friends and family.

## Decision

These users will be treated as a "primary person". The login user has the option to add a primary person. This is distinct from their own account, but as an alternative. The term 'primary person' is meant to be inclusive of caregiver, partner, friend or family member.

## Consequences

When logging in, users will have the option to enter their user ID OR the ID of their primary person. Users will enter their password when they log in, and will be taken to a different page to enter their primary user ID. This may involve selecting one of their carers or family members from a list of suggested users, if they're currently registered.

### First login
```
[user] = {
  ...,
  primary_person_id: 'some-user-id'
}

```
The ID to enter will be in the form:
```
someone-you-know-12345
```

This will be presented to GOV.UK users to enter their password.

### Registering a new person
As a registered user, if you're using their primary person to login, they will automatically load their own personal page when they have a valid user ID. The user will be redirected to their own space, which has its own form for adding another person to their account later.
#### Updating the primary person
The user will see some 'how to register your own account' page before they have their own account. This page will be updated to say 'how to register YOURSELF', with a button to switch the login option to your own user ID.

## User Stories

1. As a user, if I register another person to login to GOV.UK on my behalf I know that they are their primary contact person.
2. As a user, I know that my partner (or friend) will be treated as my primary contact person for GOV.UK.
3. As an admin, I have the ability to reset the primary person status on a user's account.

**Date:** 2021-02-12

**Status:** Accepted

## Context

In GKE, the default way to expose services is via an Istio-managed load
balancer. This is very easy to set up, and the Istio load balancer has the
standard load-balancer features:

- Static IP address
- TLS termination
- Stickiness

However, this kind of load balancer creates an internal IP address and does
not make it accessible to the public Internet. This means that if the services
need to be exposed to the Internet, an additional ingress controller needs to
be set up to forward traffic to the internal IP. An example of this is [sookocheff/s3-ingress](https://github.com/sookocheff/s3-ingress).

There's also a [solution for using Google's Network Load Balancer](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/containers/ingress-control-and-network-load-balancer-strategy)
which uses an external GNLB in front of an Istio-managed internal load balancer.

The main problems with the load-balancer ingress controller are:

1. **Stickiness**. TL;DR: Google's Network Load Balancer does not support sticky
   requests based on X-Forwarded-For. Istio-managed load balancers do.
2. **TLS termination**. Google's Network Load Balancer does not support TLS
   termination. If there's no TLS available at the ELB, it will return HTTP.
   Istio-managed load balancers support TLS termination and can automatically
   issue and manage TLS certificates.
3. **Custom domains**. Since the ingress controller is using an external
   load balancer, the provisioned IP addresses will always be public, but the
   custom domains provided to the user will not be.
4. **Custom domains**. We want to provision/manage custom domains for ingress,
   which is easy with an ingress controller, but not with the GNLB.
5. **Logging**. It's difficult to know who is behind the ELB, and it's hard
   to use VPC-level logs for applications on the ELB. The ingress controller
   does log access to the X-Forwarded-Proto header to the ELB's log stream.
   We may be able to use GCP's Cloud Platform Logs to access and query the
   user traffic data using the ELB IP addresses.

The host network option ([see RFC 7430](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7430))
has a number of problems:

1. It's not useful for applications that do HTTP because they will
   never use the server's IP address.
2. It's only suitable for HTTP/S applications.
3. It might not solve the stickiness problem for TCP applications.

## Decision

We will provide the option to use either an Istio-managed load balancer or
the Google Network Load Balancer as the ingress solution for applications in
all namespaces.

## Consequences

- The X-Forwarded-Proto header will be automatically added to the traffic
  sent to the ingress controller so that the backend can make a TCP/UDP
  connection to the user IP without having to request the frontend URL.
- Access to the X-Forwarded-Proto header in the ELB logs might be done via
  [C3 log queries](https://cloud.google.com/app-logs/c3-api).
- If the custom domains we provide to our users are not in the ELB's logs,
  we will not be able to see their traffic. However, users cannot control
  their access to custom domains.
- We will have access to ELB logs for HTTP traffic coming from the user
  IP addresses.

As a part of the latest improvements, we implemented a self-hosted CI/CD platform. This approach gives us a lot of flexibility, as well as the ability to have full control over the infrastructure. We've set the self-hosted CI/CD platform as the default option for all new projects. The self-hosted CI/CD platform can be either:

* A Single server: [CircleCI](https://circleci.com)
* Distributed: [TeamCity](https://teamcity.jetbrains.com)

## Decision

To implement the *runner proxy*, we can use a single or distributed self-hosted CI/CD platform. We have decided to implement the runner proxy using a single server, as there are no apparent issues with it.

Regarding the following use cases:

* _Running: 'group', 'app', 'bot'_, _etc_ self-hosted CI/CD platforms:
  * The self-hosted CI/CD platform *can* run multiple projects at the same time
  * The self-hosted CI/CD platform *can* run multiple projects in parallel
  * The self-hosted CI/CD platform *can* be configured to run the projects in "pipeline", e.g. the same project can run multiple times for other developers, etc.
  * Use of self-hosted CI/CD platform can limit the number of projects that can run in parallel; in case of a failure, some projects in a pipeline may be canceled (see ["Dealing with project concurrency", support.atlassian.com](https://support.atlassian.com/jira/docs/dealing-with-project-concurrency/))

## Status

Accepted

## Consequences

* The number of self-hosted CI/CD platforms is increased as more and more projects are going to be migrated
* We can't say we have a single platform that can run all kinds of self-hosted CI/CD platforms
* Using the self-hosted CI/CD platform may require some effort depending on your needs

## Context

Providing rich and granular observability will be a basic requirement for a PCEP implementation. In this context, "observability" refers to a set of capabilities that allow a user to assess and understand the behavior of their system using their metrics, logs, and traces. A system is considered to be "observable" if this data is available for all components used. In addition, this data may be analyzed using an observability tool or dashboard to give the user additional context as they analyze the data.

### Use cases

Observability will allow users to:

* **Monitor:** Track KPIs (Key Performance Indicators) of their system, so that they can monitor the health of their service and system. Examples include: latency, error rate, availability, and throughput.

* **Analyze:** Users will be able to debug issues and root causes of problems by using a combination of logs, metrics and traces.

* **Understand:** Users will be able to understand:

  * The current state of the service and system
  * Historical changes to the service and system (i.e. degradation of performance)
  * What happened in a particular incident (i.e. root cause and contributing factors)
  * An incident as it happened with rich, granular details

* **Discover:** As users analyze their system, they may discover:

  * New system metrics and values (i.e. unexpected spike in latency)
  * Previously undocumented system behaviors (i.e. correlation of latency with network traffic)
  * New root causes of past issues (i.e. discovering that a DDoS attack was the root cause of a strange set of symptoms)

* **Forecast:** Using their knowledge of the current state of the service and system, users may be able to:

  * Anticipate future health of the service and system
  * Plan for capacity and budget

## Decision

We will provide the following core observability capabilities:

* Time-series metrics, derived from _all_ logging events, including kubernetes, distributed system, database, and application.

* Availability and performance analysis, including latency, error, recovery, and throughput, at all levels, including system and application.

* Dependency graphs, showing relationships between components used.

* Querying metrics and logs, with support for the most common use cases, including but not limited to:
  * Average, minimum, maximum, and standard deviation over time
  * Percentiles over time
  * Down-to-earth statistics
  * Event correlation
  * Causal discovery

## Status

Approved

### Context

We currently expect our observability to come from:

* Kubernetes
* Log streaming system (e.g. Fluentd)
* Application logs (e.g. lambda x-ray)
* Request/service/queue/database metrics (e.g. k8s' metrics server)

## Consequences

* Collecting and aggregating metrics from the service and system will increase the load on the logging service.

* Some users will automatically be able to access a subset of their data as a default.

* Observability will be an area for infrastructure monitoring in future deployments.

## More reading

* [Fluentd's operators](https://docs.fluentd.org/fluentd/4.x/operators/index.html)

## Updates

### Update 1

After a disagreement between teams, we've decided to use a single log stream for a single observability endpoint and not provide options for writing logs and metrics into separate streams.

We still maintain our commitment to providing a full endpoint for all events as a default and to maintain an abstraction around this in our SDKs, but we're choosing to build towards this in one endpoint. This should decrease the complexity burden of writing and maintaining two endpoints in the early stages of our architecture.

An alternative in the future could be to allow a user to have a single endpoint for metrics, and another endpoint for logs. This will allow a user to implement their own aggregation endpoint for their log or metric data if this is a concern for their use case.

## Status

## Context

We're able to offer a project license via our [licensed-components](0003-licensed-components.md) ADR.

Currently our license register is just a hardcoded set of mappings from package `@nrwl/` to `MIT`, `Apache-2.0`, `GPL-3.0`, and `CC-0`.

In future we'll want to add custom license types and we don't expect these to all be `MIT` or `Apache-2.0`, so we may add licenses from the [Creative Commons family](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/ic/license.en.html) and the [EU-UN license](https://opensource.org/licenses/eu-un-license.en.html).

Adding custom license types would also let us differentiate between licenses that permit commercial use and those that don't, and to add licenses that are specific to the EU or the UK.

## Decision

We've decided to implement a [Semantic Version Scheme](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html) for our project licenses, that encodes the following information:

* The license family (e.g. MIT, Apache, GPL, EU-UN)
* Whether commercial use is allowed

There was a prior discussion about how best to plot data in Kibana for the Elasticsearch pipeline. It was decided that we would leverage commercial software to do so. After some research, it is clear that the best option is [X-Charts](https://xcharts.com/).

X-Charts will allow us to parse JSON, do some minor customisation to format the data for display, and then render the resulting visualization into a Kibana dashboard.

# Status

Superseded by [ADR-0010]

# Consequences

We can provide a single point of integration to Kibana with Elasticsearch (as well as other data sources via the `_source` field). This means that the majority of our dashboard logic is rendered outside the Kibana console, which reduces maintenance concerns to that of building and consuming a [Kibana console][kibana-console]. The [Kibana console][kibana-console] would be used for tasks such as creating a `index alias` to reduce the amount of data we receive back from Elasticsearch.

## Alternatives considered

### [Using `if_*` expressions in the ElasticDSL pipeline][ELSDXLTS]

We know we have to use `if_*` expressions in our pipelines to make use of a metric DSL in order to reduce the amount of `toY` metrics we receive back from Elasticsearch. These expressions would have to be constructed such that they parse into `if_*` expressions in Kibana, making them difficult to comprehend.

### Using `n-gram` aggregations to parse JSON][N-gram]

This involves parsing the JSON data to extract key-value pairs. We then aggregate values by a `n-gram`, which is then compared to a list of `n-grams` in the pipeline data to produce a `if_*` expression for each of the parsed values. This is very easy to understand. An n-gram can be `default` if the field is not present.

We have done some prototyping with this approach and there is an [n-gram aggregations pipeline][n-gram] which provides a template for it.

Pros:

* We already have a pipeline to template this approach, `n-gram`

Cons:

* The `n-gram aggregations pipeline` contains the entire ETL logic of extracting key-value pairs, parsing them into n-grams, aggregating the data and generating `if_*` expressions - quite some lines of code, but [quite easy to understand][N-gram-pros]


### [Using custom aggregation fields][Custom Agg]

Previously we were happy to provide a `terms` aggregation field in the ElasticDSL pipeline to return a list of `n-grams`. This has been taken up by the [Standard & Analytical Defaults][StdAndAnalytic] and we have the option of including a `terms` field in the `n-gram` pipeline, returning an aggregation with that field and then parsing the `n-gram`s from `terms` in the `Kibana` pipeline. This makes it very easy to integrate - just a flag in the JSON query `terms` which is parsed by the `n-gram` pipeline and then parsed into an `if_*` expression in `Kibana`.

Technical Story: [#134](https://github.com/property-server/property-server-server/issues/134)

## Context and Problem Statement

* Key-value pairs are a data structure often encountered in JSON messages.
* These pairs are usually not well structured and can appear arbitrarily nested.
* This poses some challenges for parsing and validation.
* As a result, to support arbitrary JSON messages, the `PropertyValue` object needs to be made more flexible.
* This is done by introducing the concept of custom properties which can be specified by the user.

## Considered Options

* `PropertyValue` remains a simple immutable struct
  * arbitrarily nested properties are supported by recursively using `PropertyValue`
  * adding custom properties is not supported
* `PropertyValue` becomes an interface
  * arbitrarily nested properties are supported by recursively using `PropertyValue`
  * adding custom properties is supported

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: the second option, because it seems to be the most flexible and correct approach.
