## Context

In an epoch, any Validator or Light Client can produce a "double signature".

A double signature occurs when a Validator produces two signatures on the same block header, for example to make it appear as if two different people (i.e. two validators) signed the block header.

Double signatures reduce the amount of trusted validators as any single node can produce multiple signatures at an epoch.

To reduce the introduction of double signatures, this ADR proposes a number of changes to the Light Client and an Endpoint to prevent double signatures.

## Status

Under review

## Decision

The double signing issue is introduced using the [Endpoint](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/blob/develop/proto/tmdbm.proto#L125) where a validator produces the signatures of their peers for the next epoch at the Light Client.

This endpoint is modified to require validators to produce the signatures of their peers, as well as their own.

The endpoint is then moved under the `/authn` path and renamed to `GetSignaturesForNextEpoch`.

## Consequences

* Any client making multiple simultaneous epoch activations will now be prevented from creating double signatures.
* Using the `GetSignaturesForNextEpoch` endpoint will ensure that no double signatures will be introduced into the Cosmos-SDK.

## Context and Goals

Currently, we are using the common conventions of `git flow` that has us creating feature branches off master and dealing with the messy process of choosing and collapsing feature branches back to master when they have been completed. As well as this, we would like to have an easy way to test that we can recreate the changes of a particular commit.

## Decision drivers

- Easy to understand
- No conflicting choices between tools like pre-push and post-push are common.
- Ideally, have easy access to branches at all times (though not necessarily one at the global level)
- Able to have `dev` branch for quick iterations
- Able to isolate branches from main.
- Easy to delete and recreate branches as needed.

## Considered options

- [Standard git flow]
  - The industry standard.
  - We add an additional naming convention to deal with releasing under a conventional semantic version bump (`<patch>.<major>.<minor>`)
  - The process has a number of common pitfalls:
    - It forces us to deal with 3 different sets of commit author: `commit author[|commit author|commit author|commit author]`, which is confusing to the human.
    - We must make the confusing choice between `master` and `main` on development and production environments, respectively.
    - In practice, the master/main dichotomy does not exist for most teams
- [GitHub's gitflow]
  - GitHub's implementation of a gitflow: [https://help.github.com/articles/splitting-and-merging-branches/
  - Uses `feature/*` branches for each feature, then `develop` to keep all feature branches to the same branch.
  - Have no specific rules regarding the `main` and `master` branches.
- [GitHub's Flow]
  - GitHub's gitflow: [https://help.github.com/articles/splitting-and-merging-branches/
  - Uses `feat/*` branches for each feature, then `develop` to keep all feature branches to the same branch.
  - The branch pattern uses `[issue #](#issue-number)` so that an issue can be linked directly to a commit that addresses it.
  - GitHub recommends the flow as a "good default" for new projects.
  - I'm not sure why but I really like this one.

## Decision outcome

GitHub's Flow: 
- A gitflow based on github's recommendation would force us to add `main` and `master` and I think that is a decision most people will never make when they start a project.
- In practice, every branch pattern we have now is just a different iteration of `feature/*` so the onus is really on the branch names rather than a complex `master/*` dance.

We adopt the GitHub's flow.

## Decision

There are numerous benefits to using ECS as a hosting platform, and some
easy to understand examples include:

* **Universal resource management**. All of the application's configuration and
resources can be managed centrally in code.
* **Scaling**. The ability to scale applications up and down with cloud native
reliability and availability.
* **Resource isolation**. Application components can be isolated from each

different environment's resources (e.g. RDS instance).

maintenance as AWS takes care of that.
* **The easiest way to build container orchestration solutions**. If you use
other cloud hosting platforms, you'll probably know how complex it is to use
their container runtime platforms as a host. ECS eases you into this world
with a minimal set of configuration.
* **ECS Fargate** is an excellent starting point for many users moving into
containers, as it provides the ability to have the tools and the container
runtime (and the management of that runtime) managed by AWS.

## Consequences

We will move to an ECS-based hosting platform.

## Context

All living things need to keep track of the time as do humans.
Time is always going to be a consideration as a framework designer in order to make a program's response time predictable.
Some things to consider as to what 'time' is.

* Calendar time is commonly known and should be a first consideration when dealing with time.
    * This would be the time of a day, week, or year, and could be tracked as a continuous system
    * As time is a fundamental concept of mathematics, treating it as a variable and using tools like iteration is appropriate
    * The number of iterations through each range should be documented, i.e. `days in week 1 = 28`, `days in week 2 = 31`, `days in week 3 = 28`, `days in week 4 = 30`
* Project time and time of events is commonly known.
    * There will be a primary type to track time, and secondary types to track time intervals/events.
* Time of event is relative to a given start time.
    * This would be commonly used to track the history of a project and record when certain tasks are done in relation to each other
* Time of event is a point in time and may be used to record durations
    * This would commonly be used to measure the amount of time between two project milestones

## Decision

Record project milestones, task start and end times as the 'time' type for a project.

* Milestone times should be recorded as a single date.
* Task start and end times should be recorded as two separate dates, with the end date being on a later date in the future.
    * This allows for measuring the time between start and end and also distinguishing when a project moves from 'in progress' to 'completed'.
    * The start date is an optional type and can be recorded as such to track when project starts.

## Consequences

* If the project is a collection of tasks in which the start and end times are important, a good primary data type for these times should be chosen and used.
    * `System.DateTime` is an appropriate type in the .NET ecosystem
* As `System.DateTime` is used for the 'time' type, the method `AddDays` should be used for calculating the end date of a project on the following day of the last completed task.
* If a time interval between project start and project end is useful to track, use the `TimeSpan` type to store the duration of the project in days.

Technical Story: [EASI 3337](https://dsdmoj.atlassian.net/browse/EASI-3337)

## Context and Problem Statement

Currently in EASi 2.4 we continue to live by the 4 freedoms. This means that with each patch we do add more and more non-transferable changes to the program, that are required for the maintainability of EASi as a whole.
 
* EASi needs to support older systems, for instance the EASi used in Leeds is currently based on the 1.7 release.
* The majority of EASi users are not aware of, or care about, the changes that are made in EASi before it's formally released.
* EASi users can never actually use the features of the EASi they can get their hands on - they must always upgrade to the latest features.

There are two options available to support this series of releases:

* Using feature prefixes (like `2.4.3-beta1`) and release notes to describe changes that are backwards compatible, and are kept within the EASi release series, and can be uploaded by EASi users.
* Feature prefixes (like `2.4.3-beta1`) and release notes to describe changes that are backwards compatible, and are kept within the EASi release series, and are handled by EASi developers.

There are advantages and disadvantages to both of these options.

## Decision Drivers

* Backwards compatibility
* Security
* Maintaining the integrity of the EASi codebase
* The user experience

## Considered Options

* Use feature prefixes for backwards compatible feature
* Use feature prefixes for backwards compatible feature but require code review, and require documentation of feature addition in EASi Releases 

* Feature prefixes for backwards compatible feature but require code review, and require documentation of feature addition in EASi Releases

## Decision Outcome

We will use feature prefixes in EASi 2.4 to denote changes that are backwards compatible and are kept within the EASi release series, and handled by EASi developers. 

Changes that are backwards compatible and are kept within the EASi release series, but which are not handled by EASi developers are handled by EASi users, and are supported by EASi 2.4's build-in release notes feature. Users can upload release notes in an EASi-release-specific folder on Github.

Any change that is not backwards compatible will not be compatible with EASi 2.4 and will not be uploaded as an EASi-release-specific folder to Github. Any such changes will be handled as part of the EASi-next release, when EASi's release series will be reset to 3.0.0, and EASi 2.4 will be deprecated.

### Context and Problem Statement

As described in [ADR027](adr027-argocd-apps-of-apps-structure.md) ArgoCD support is available for Kubernetes.

GoG Galaxy 2.0 includes a number of ArgoCD applications:

- ArgoCD
- Jupyterhub
- VS Code
- Credhub
- Argo Workloads (ArgoCD-workflows)

Some of the ArgoCD applications:

- Jupyterhub
- VS Code
- Credhub
- Argo Workloads (ArgoCD-workflows)

are applications on top of ArgoCD which we call for now "Apps of Apps".

These Apps of Apps are not integrated into the ArgoCD deployment but into the ArgoCD application where they run.

In a traditional ArgoCD deployment the ArgoCD application may grow in size rather quickly and may get very difficult to reason about.

### Context and Problem Statement

Since ArgoCD support is available for Kubernetes, and the ArgoCD applications are not integrated into the ArgoCD deployment, what would be the best way to approach this use case?

### Considered Options

#### A. ArgoCD as a control plane

Use ArgoCD as the control plane of ArgoCD applications and move there all the ArgoCD applications:

- ArgoCD
- Jupyterhub
- VS Code
- Credhub
- Argo Workloads (ArgoCD-workflows)

#### B. ArgoCD as an autopilot

Use ArgoCD only as an autopilot for ArgoCD applications and use the following approache for the remaining apps:

- Jupyterhub
- VS Code
- Credhub
- Argo Workloads (ArgoCD-workflows)

#### C. ArgoCD as a control plane and other technologies as apps of apps

Use ArgoCD as the control plane of ArgoCD applications and use other technologies for the remaining apps.

- Jupyterhub
- VS Code
- Credhub
- Argo Workloads (ArgoCD-workflows)

### Decision Outcome

Option C. It does not restrict the control plane to just ArgoCD but also gives the option to use other technologies and it makes the ArgoCD application as a control plane that deals with ArgoCD applications.

### Negative Consequences

All ArgoCD applications can be on top of ArgoCD and are not integrated into the ArgoCD application. This might make the ArgoCD application big to reason about and maintain.

### Positive Consequences

- We can use other technologies for ArgoCD applications without needing to integrate them into the ArgoCD application.
- We can keep ArgoCD as a control plane of ArgoCD applications.

## Context and Problem Statement

In the HTTP request/response cycle, the headers are sent via a request and are parsed by the server to find any kind of information about the request or information about the user.

## Decision Drivers

- should be able to add headers for a request, such as adding a custom header `X-My-Key` for the current user. The user can set it to any value. This header is parsed by a middleware to run some extra logic.

## Considered Options

- `X-My-Key` was added to `request`
- `X-My-Key` was added to `response`
- `X-My-Key` was added to `headers` (optional property, so has to be parsed by a middleware)
- `X-My-Key` was added to `session`
- `X-My-Key` was sent with `context`
- `X-My-Key` was added to `user`
- `X-My-Key` was added to `metadata`
- `X-My-Key` was sent via header parameters
- `X-My-Key` was sent via JSON body (usually in `data`)
- `X-My-Key` was set via a cookie

## Decision Outcome

- `X-My-Key` was added to `request`
- `X-My-Key` was added to `response`
- `X-My-Key` was added to `headers` (optional property)
- `X-My-Key` was added to `session`
- `X-My-Key` was added to `user`

### Positive Consequences

- easier to send the request
- the same logic is used when parsing from headers and body, e. g. for an optional body, we can add a custom header and it has the same purpose.
- it's easy to validate the request, e. g. if the user must set the value to a mandatory key, then the middleware can immediately do so, and the optional request or headers don't make the code more complex.

### Negative Consequences

- there are many `addHeader` statements in `request`
- there are many `addHeader` statements in `response`
- `addHeader` is also used in `session` (and `metadata`), so we need to be sure `X-My-Key` is parsed in session as well.

## Context
There is a handler `BaseHandler` and several specific handlers inheriting from it, for example `AuthHandler`. The current `BaseHandler` has a lot of methods marked as final and inaccessible. There is also not a single handler that can create a handler. We have many problems with maintaining handler hierarchy like:
* How do we make a decorator for handler `H1`?
* How do we add additional functionality to handler `H2`?
* How do we make a handler accept multiple parameters?

## Decision
After much consideration, we have decided that our handler hierarchy will no longer be inheritance based, but on composition. To achieve this, we created an interface named `Handler`:

```typescript
interface Handler<T extends HandlerInput = HandlerInput> {
  apply(): T;
}
```

This interface can be implemented by handlers and decorators. Each handler adds an implementation to create something more complex, such as combining all sub-handlers. Each decorator adds a method to apply a simpler version of the handler. 

Handlers implement the `Handler` interface and can extend `HandlerInput` (which we'll cover in next section). 

## Consequences
* We can no longer extend `BaseHandler` because there is no context to add functionality, but we can compose other handlers as the body of `apply()`, so `@BaseHandler` is now an interface. 
* We use inheritance to extend the functionality of `Handler` for each handler like `AuthHandler` or `DataValidator`.
* There is no more `HandlerDecorator` class and decorators simply return the result of calling the handler.

## Context

Previously, as part of the development process, I was using the [docker-client](https://www.npmjs.com/package/docker-client) package to interact with the Docker API. At the time I felt it's not in the best way possible for me.

Since then I've had an idea of how this library could be improved upon to make it better for both new and current users.

## Decision

I am going to start developing an application based on docker-client that communicates with a Docker API running as a daemon in Docker environment.

### Use Cases

#### Launching an Image

Launching an image is the most basic use-case for this library, but also the one with the most options to play around with.

* `docker.run('latest')` - runs the latest image
* `docker.run('classic')` - runs an instance of the classic image
* `docker.run('v1.0.0-rc.5', { container: 'mycontainer', command: ['ls', '-l'] })` - a more complex use-case using a specific version of an image and running it with a custom command.

#### Listing Images

This library should be able to tell us which images are available to run. This could return a basic text listing, or a more advanced output that shows information about each image as well as their status. This is a lot of work, though, and can be neglected if its not in the time frame of this project.

### Future Considerations

This is a lot of work, and as such this project will not be able to be truly separated from docker-client. 

#### Command Execution

Rather than exposing a `command` option to `docker.run`, it would be better to create a new function that allows you to run an arbitrary command on an image, and then specify the output from that command as the return value.

#### Updating Images

A common use-case is to want to automatically update an image. This could be implemented as a function that takes a 'last-known-good-version' and 'current-version' and will automatically update an image to the latest one if the current version is less than the last-known-good-version. 

#### Destroying Images and Environments

Given that Docker itself is still in beta, it's reasonable to expect docker-client to be as well. There may be some functions, like `destroy`, that are used to delete an image or environment.

### Issues in Docker-Client to Address

Docker-Client was originally designed around a Docker implementation that was built into it's API. These functions are not defined in a way that is based on current CLI's and API's of Docker-Engine, leaving it a bit broken in terms of functionality.

* [issue 1](https://github.com/mranney/docker-client/issues/240)

## Consequences

* A lot of effort will be required to parse the outputs from various Docker commands and make those outputs useful for an API user.

## Links

* docker-client [Github](https://github.com/mranney/docker-client)

There are a number of different sources of truth regarding location and
condition of tide stations around the world.

[National Oceanographic Data Center](https://www.nodc.gov/stations)
[ESSC](https://www.essc.noaa.gov/stations/ML_0006)
[IFRS](https://www.ifrs.eu/geohub.html)
[Tide Data](http://www.tide-data.org/locations)

These lists may change over time, and conditions of tide stations (particularly
the equipment on site) changes over time.  

## Decision

A single `Stations` table will store location and status of tide stations.

Each `Station` record will have one or more `Conditions` records.

The `Stations` table will have the following columns:

| Column           | Type                | Notes                                                          |
|-----------------|--------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| stn_no          | VARCHAR(10)          | unique identifier of the station                         |
| name           | VARCHAR(100)          | name of the station                                          |
| domain         | VARCHAR(100)          | IO, EC, AO, MS or combination                            |
| long_desc      | TEXT               | general description of the station                     |
| end_datetime   | DATETIME(3)            | the last date the station was in use                  |
| latitude       | FLOAT(10,4)         | decimal degrees                                            |
| longitude      | FLOAT(10,4)         | decimal degrees                                            |
| altitude       | INT               | in meters                                                    |
| is_active      | BOOLEAN            | TRUE if the station is currently collecting data, FALSE otherwise|
| status         | VARCHAR(50)          | eg. IN_COMMISSION, DISMANTLED, _RETIRED_                |

The `Conditions` table will have the following columns:

| Column        | Type                | Notes                                                          |
|-----------------|--------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| condn_id        | VARCHAR(10)          | unique identifier of the condition                      |
| stn_no         | VARCHAR(10)          | foreign key linking to `Stations` table               |
| condn_description | VARCHAR(100)          | description of the condition                             |
| start_datetime   | DATETIME(3)            | the date the condition started                          |
| end_datetime     | DATETIME(3)            | the date the condition ended                           |
| lat_diff        | FLOAT(10,4)         | decimal degrees                                            |
| lons_diff        | FLOAT(10,4)         | decimal degrees                                            |
| alt_diff        | INT               | in meters                                                    |

## Consequences

* Updating the `Stations` table requires code and manual process to load data
* Updating the `Conditions` table requires the above work in addition to
 code to convert list format of data provided by some sources (such as FRS) into the format of `Conditions` table
* An `end_date` date will be required to allow for the transition period where a station may not be closed after a data dump date

The EASi Server supports the use of individual user ssh keys rather than using a single admin key. There are a few reasons why we adopted this approach:

- Multi-site environments: The EASi platform is deployed on more than one machine in several datacenters. The admin key approach requires that the administrator log in locally on each machine in order to add authorized keys for the admin user. If the administrator loses the admin key, then he/she will be locked out of all EASi servers.

- Rotation of admin keys: Ideally, every admin user will regularly change the admin password/key pair. This allows for an extra layer of security and/or to recover from lost keys.

## Implementation

This method is the most simple and easy to implement method that accomplishes the above goals. 

- Users with admin privileges gain the ability to add authorized ssh keys to the admin user in the configuration management system (Ansible in EASi's case).

## Detailed instructions

In EASi, the user that logs into the administrative server via rsync is prompted to set an admin password. Then when the admin user logs on via rsync, they should be asked to change the admin password/key pair.  These two passwords/key pairs should be stored in separate files in the home directory.  The keys should be added in alphabetical order.

# Context

We have users with hundreds of repositories requiring access to the GSP.

Having individual accounts for all users is impractical.

A single account with multiple repositories would be cumbersome to administer.

A single account with a single repository (defaulting to users') would still retain the ability to administer access at a higher level and would be more scalable as a result.

# Decision

We will use a single account with a default repository with the following structure:

 - applications/: all gsp applications in a single directory, each application will have its own local gsp.
 - my-awesome-application/: one repository per application.

All users will retain the ability to grant permission to other users at a higher level by virtue of their administrative permissions on repositories.

# Status

Superseded by [ADR019](ADR019.md)

# Consequences

- It is easy to migrate from a non-local development environment to a local development environment, as long as the user has permissions to the default gsp.
- It is easy to build and deploy to the gsp, as long as the user is a maintainer of the gsp.
- All users will still have a sense of ownership over their repositories.
- All users can still grant access to others at a higher level.
- Future permissions will have to be updated on a per-application basis to grant/revoke permissions to a user.
- If an application is removed or moved, the commands for exporting/opening the application will still need to be executed for each application.

## Context

### JSON object

This project was originally designed around the delivery of JSON objects, and there are multiple existing clients who depend on a particular JSON structure for the data returned from this project (such as the [EIM JSON](https://github.com/emory-libraries/emory-data-interchange/tree/master/xsd/emoryData#emory%20data%20interchange%20format)). While we support, and will continue to support, providing JSON as the response type, this project is expanding to include other possible response types. 

### JSON structure

As a consequence of supporting a variety of response types, this project will begin to experiment with different ways of structuring JSON documents. While JSON is a relatively new technology, there has been quite a lot of discussion already over the best and most appropriate ways to use it. We plan to experiment with different models, including but not limited to:

* The [JSON object](https://tools.ietf.org/html/json-object)
    * Pros: easy to understand the basic structure, supports simple data types
    * Cons: a single key value can only be used once
* The [JSON array](https://tools.ietf.org/html/json-array)
    * Pros: an item can appear once or multiple times, which is useful for handling collections
    * Cons: the presence of multiple items may not always be clear
* The [JSON blob](https://tools.ietf.org/html/json-blob)
    * Pros: allows for arbitrarily nested objects
    * Cons: a JSON blob object can be difficult to understand


## Decision

This project will begin to experiment with different ways of structuring JSON documents, as described above.

For non-embedded applications (i.e. those using a J2EE web server) the appropriate OpenJDK is easy to determine - the user will have to manually adjust it.

For embedded applications (i.e. those not using a J2EE web server) OpenJDK is much more difficult to determine, and the user probably does not want to know the exact version.

In the past I have used `jdeps` to query the required OpenJDK version and have been able to patch a new version by using a script with the `--force` option.

This is manual, and I don't have a way to automate it beyond writing a batch script.

## Decision

I will start by using `jdeps` in `main.sh`.  This may not be in the `homebrew-library` prefix, but it will be in the standard `brew-install` locations.

## Status

PROPOSED

## Addendum

I was able to patch `jdeps` as part of the same script that makes the decision to build OpenJDK 11.

It turns out that the patch is actually less invasive: instead of finding and replacing `(eu.siis.dk)` (the old prefix) with `(java.se.gui)`, it simply replaces the old prefix with an empty string, effectively removing it.

The script is just:

```sh
(rm -rf /usr/local/bin/jdeps*)
(cd /usr/local/src/*)
(patch -p0 OpenJDK-JDeps.patch)
(rm -rf OpenJDK-JDeps.patch)
```

## Status

Accepted

## Context

MongoDB has a concept of 'streams' to track an operation happening in MongoDB. This is to achieve the goal of an atomic transaction (A transaction
that either fails and rolls back any changes made upon it or succeeds and commits all changes).

Streams are not part of MongoDB 2.4 and are only available in MongoDB 3.0 and later. In the past there was a separate feature for this called
`changeStream` which was not part of the public API. This allowed the database to emit `MongoChangeDocument`s which contained changed documents in a MongoDB
database using the public API. It is noted that not all streams of MongoDB 2.4 may not be available in 3.0 onwards.

## Decision

The change that has been made is that `getStreamId` and `getStreamNextBatch` have been implemented so that `streams` can be tracked and iterated
over in `MongoDB` (Streams are not implemented for `MongoDBServer`).

These methods emit `MongoChangeDocument`s which contains an `id`, `changeTime`, `operationType`, and `document` in the MongoDB database using the
public API.

## Consequences

A `MongoChangeDocument` has been added. This is part of the `mongo-change-streams` module which has changed in version 1.0.0.

This module is added when you use a MongoDB server in `MongoServer` (e.g. `changeStream(MongoServer, { ... })`) because it requires `Streams`
to be enabled, which the implementation understands is part of `streams`.

This module adds the following `functions` to the `MongoServer`:
- `getStreamNextBatch(this, operationType)`: returns the next batch of changed documents
- `getStreamId(this, operationType)`: returns the ID of the stream (empty string if there is no stream active for the operationType).

The `operationType` argument should be one of:
- `"create" | "update" | "delete" | "unknown"`.

This allows you to filter which types of document changes you are interested in.

Note that if the change operation fails, the `document` field will be `null`.

This module will continue to emit `MongoChangeDocument`s even if the change operation is not successful.

MongoChangeDocument is a `subclass` of `DocumentType`.

## Context

Both SDKs must be able to preserve semantic versionness for end users in a more complete and easier way than what is currently feasible in Javascript. The most important two use cases are applications that are building for multiple platforms and applications that are deployed to multiple environments. 

### SDK1: SDK for Javascript

There are two basic approaches to versioning that are pursued by our Javascript SDK:

1. By versioning the SDK, regardless of the project structure, the compiler builds a single bundled file that only has one version identifier (a global object that is built into a JS object). In order to support multiple applications for the SDK in a project, this approach depends on using a `package-lock.json` or equivalent to maintain version control of the bundled JavaScript.
2. By versioning the project, regardless of the SDK's architecture, the compiler builds a directory of code that contains multiple bundled artifacts, one for each application.

### SDK2: SDK for Python

Similar to the Javascript SDK, this SDK also offers two basic approaches:

1. By versioning the SDK, regardless of the project structure, the compiler builds a single bundled file that only has one version identifier (a global object that is built into a Python object). In order to support multiple applications for the SDK in a project, this approach depends on using a `setup.py` file (or similar) to maintain version control of the bundled Python.
2. By versioning the project, regardless of the SDK's architecture, the compiler builds a directory of code that contains multiple bundled artifacts, one for each application.

## Decision

We decided to:

- continue to only offer one bundle per SDK in both Javascript and Python
- require projects that use the SDK to release under a semantic versioning scheme (major.minor.patch)
- require projects that use the SDK to include the SDK version as part of the `package-lock.json` or equivalent in Javascript, and the `setup.py` file in Python
- require projects that use the SDK to release in the major.minor.patch format (e.g., 1.2.3)
- require projects that use the SDK to also include the `package-lock.json` or equivalent in the `npm run build` command in Javascript, and the `setup.py` file in the `pip install` command in Python
- make the SDKs only compatible with the major.minor.patch versioning scheme by versioning the SDK as a whole

### Future Considerations

In the future, we may offer mechanism for projects to extend beyond major.minor.patch versioning such that application developers can make choices that extend to the patch level as they continue to add features to their application.

# Proposed changes for managing resource lifetime

*Status: proposed*

## Context

The existing Lifetime resource [includes only a simple registry](https://github.com/eclipse/les-discovery/blob/master/services/lifetime.md)
and as such does not provide a central management point for all persistent resources.

In order to have a complete overview over persistent resources (i.e. those that are stored on a database or filesystem)
a mapping from resource GUID to persistent resource must be kept as well as the ability to trigger deletion of all
resources registered with RESSource.

The existing [Resource registry](https://github.com/eclipse/les-discovery/blob/master/services/resource.md)
is not appropriate since 

1. It does not provide an interface to the registry
2. It manages deletion of resources and thus should provide an interface to that

## Decision

We will provide a Java API to manage persistent resources attached to RESSource (see [ResourceRegistry.java](https://github.com/eclipse/les-discovery/blob/master/services/resource/ResourceRegistry.java)).

The [Resource Registry](https://github.com/eclipse/les-discovery/blob/master/services/resource/ResourceRegistry.java)
will act as a central mapping from resource GUID to persistent resource.

We will add a registry to allow for persistent resource management within RESSource.

## Consequences

Adding a registry to manage persistent resources will make interopability easier. 
It would be possible to combine different registry implementations in order to use resource from different 
environments (i.e. a Docker registry and a S3 registry).

## Context and Problem Statement

A Microfrontend architecture is a single product that is decomposed into multiple frontend applications, called microfrontends, that when integrated provide a unified user experience.

Dotcom rendering is currently a monolith. There for the following questions arise:

* How should we decompose the monolith into frontend applications?
  * Should each business module (Candidate, Provider, Vendor API) have their own application?
  * How many applications should be created?
    * Should there be an MVP with few applications that can be iterated upon?
    * Should the number of applications be increased with each iteration?
    * Is there a way to create a single application that can be iterated upon?
* Where should the application boundaries be drawn?
  * Along with the module boundaries?
  * Across modules?
* How should the applications be laid out on the page?
  * In one column?
  * In a grid?
  * Using a masonry layout?
* How can we ensure the UX is consistent across applications?
  * Branding
  * Forms
  * Navigation
* How can we ensure the UX is *perceived* consistent across applications?
  * Loading animations
  * Transitions
  * Accessibility
* How can we mitigate the risks of microfrontends?
  * Maintaining state across applications
  * Communication between applications
  * Overall system complexity

## Decision Drivers

* Ease of integration
* Consistency of design
* Separation of concerns
* Mitigation of risks

## Considered Options

1. Single application monolith
2. Decompose monolith into microfrontends

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: Option 2, because:
* The maintainability of monoliths decreases with size and complexity over time.
* A monoliths scope eventually exceeds its domain.
* When a monolith is decomposed, it is easier for teams to own separate pieces.
* Separate pieces can move more independently from each other and from the monolith.
* Separate pieces are easier to replace in isolation.
* When combined the independent pieces form a whole that is greater than the sum of their parts.

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Single application monolith

* `+`
  * There is no code to maintain but the monolith as a whole.
  * No endpoints to manage.
  * Entire application state is contained within a single application.
* `+`
  * Single application is in control of UX and branding.
* `+`
  * Fast time to market (no endpoints to develop, less UX work)
* `+`
  * Can scale with serverless computing.
* `+`
  * Easy to reason about dependencies (because there are none)
* `-`
  * Fast time to market (likely to have bugs/security issues)
* `-`
  * UX is constrained by server-side rendering.
* `-`
  * Maintenance will require increased effort over time.
* `-`
  * Tightly couples domain and infrastructure logic.
* `-`
  * When the monolith *does* scale, the work is increased.
* `-`
  * When an application needs to change, a monolithic approach to code requires that the entire application be considered.
* `-`
  * Testing and quality metrics are difficult to gather at the application level.
* `-`
  * Does not encourage reuse (internal and external)
* `-`
  * When the monolith *does* scale, the work is increased.
* `-`
  * Increases coupling to monolithic system.
* `-`
  * Makes iteration more complex and slower.

### Decompose monolith into microfrontends

* `+`
  * Allows for iterative, parallel production development.
  * Teams can own separate pieces (domain, UX, infrastructure) of the application.
  * Removes coupling of domain and infrastructure logic from the UX.
* `+`
  * Removes need to consider the "big picture" of the application.
  * Testing and quality metrics can be gathered at the application level.
* `+`
  * Domain applications can be developed and iterated upon at an increased pace.
* `+`
  * Improved UX will lead to faster iteration on the application as a whole.
* `+`
  * The application will be easier to reason about as a whole (domain pieces are decoupled)
* `-`
  * Code is distributed among multiple

Date: 2020-04-14

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Deployment can happen to every part of the application - API, frontend, auxiliary services, data fixtures. There can be multiple ways to do deployment, in a monolithic application or microservices architecture. Choosing the right deployment pattern and provider could make or break the application.

### Docker

We use [Docker](https://docker.com/) to build the application into a container. Choosing the right container runtime can be a decision point - for deployment, we will use [Gunicorn](https://gunicorn.org/) which supports the Python deployment method and uses AWS' Lambda functions as its deployment mechanism.

### Architecture

When selecting a deployment provider, there are several constraints:

- Should be Python or Ruby agnostic
- Support Linux execution environment
- Support Docker distribution and deployment
- Should support and/or provide custom Docker commands
- Should be relatively fast and cheap
- Should scale easily

Since choosing AWS' Elastic Container Service has the possibility for Docker support in the future, it makes sense to use AWS services for initial development. 

### Architecture

Here's a simple Docker-based deployment architecture:

![Architecture](images/architecture.jpg)

The architecture currently only considers Lambda functions, but it can be extended to include Docker containers for APIs, workers and other elements of the system.

### Static assets

Static assets will be served by S3 via the Django static file server, the easiest solution at this moment.

### Auxiliary services

[Docker-base](https://hub.docker.com/_/docker/) will be a useful utility to build all auxiliary service containers.

## Decision

- Use [Docker](https://docker.com/) to build application containers
- Use [Gunicorn](https://gunicorn.org/) to run application
- Use AWS Lambda for API containers (API and worker containers)
- Use [Docker-base](https://hub.docker.com/_/docker/) to build auxiliary service containers
- Use S3 for static assets


## Consequences

- A non-Docker-based deployment architecture would have to consider [Bash](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/) and [Awilix](https://github.com/awilix/awilix)
- The choice of Python distribution is a decision point - see this article [Python versions and requirements](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/28729444/python-versions-and-requirements)
- There's some idea about creating a Docker image of each environment for custom applications - to provide a Docker-based solution, it would be useful to separate applications that would be deployed using Docker containers.

## Context

The core runtime is the part of the software that provides the basic services required for other systems to run. For an OS, this is traditionally the kernel. However, in the 21st century the term "kernel" is less common, especially outside of embedded systems. These days, the core system software is better referred to as a runtime, and it encompasses much more than just the kernel. This includes basic user mode utilities, system services, and sometimes system libraries.

For an OS, all of these should fulfill two roles:

1. They should provide services that can be invoked by any user of the OS. These are often called "system services" or "built-in programs". Examples of these are `ls`, `grep`, `awk`, `sed`, `ps`, `kill`, and many more.
2. They should provide tools and libraries that can be invoked by any program written for the OS. These are often called "system libraries" or "system headers". Examples of these are `gcc`, `make`, `glibc`, `systemd`, and many more.

In addition, in modern operating systems there are often important "infrastructure" programs that are not intended for general use, but are critical to the correct functioning of the system. Examples of these are `cron` and `syslogd`. These programs often interact with other system services, but they are not intended for general use and shouldn't be invoked directly by user programs.

## Decision

The following is a list of important system components of the Core Runtime.

### System Services

These programs are intended to be invoked by any user of the OS. They are often called "built-in programs" because they are part of the operating system itself. These programs are often grouped by their function, with one "super-program" that invokes them in turn.

- init (or startup)
- shutdown
- logging
- systemd (or openrc)
- cron (or periodic tasks)
- ssh
- rsync

### System Libraries

These programs (and their headers) are intended to be invoked by any program written for the OS. They are often called "system libraries" or "system headers" because they are part of the operating system itself. These programs are often grouped by their function, with one "super-program" that invokes them in turn.

- gcc
- make
- gdb
- perf
- syslogd
- cron
- tar
- gzip
- pgrep
- sed
- awk
- git
- wget
- curl
- vim
- emacs

## Status

Accepted.

### System Context

A system will normally be given a single "Core Runtime" package, in addition to a number of optional "Core Runtime Extensions" packages that can add new system services and/or libraries. The default set of Core Runtime Extensions is designed to provide a "minimal but useful" set of additional features, and can be expanded upon by the system architect to provide additional features useful for the system as a whole.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We have several hundred species in common use in MOC, including algae, fungi, and plants. These organisms live in a huge variety of habitats. Many parts of those habitats are very hostile (e.g. the deep sea), and present unique challenges for analysis. They are also very different from one another. They vary enormously in size, and the physical properties of their bodies. Many of them also vary enormously in their physiological requirements.

There are several limitations to the kinds of measurements we can make about an organism, or habitat. One obvious limitation is that we can only measure fluxes (inputs and outputs) that can be detected in the lab, or with remote sensing from above. Another limitation is that we can only measure the physical properties of organisms, but we can't measure what's going on inside (e.g. an enzyme reaction or a gene expression profile). Lastly, measurements of fluxes or physical properties can only be made in situ, on a single point in time, or across a very short interval of time.

These limitations don't invalidate the importance of flux measurements, but they do complicate it. They force us to recognize that any given measurement is an instance of a more general class of measurements. We should keep that in mind when deciding what measurements are appropriate for a given task.

## Decision

We should take great care when deciding what measurements are appropriate for a given organism or habitat. We should decide each instance on its own merits.

## Consequences

We will continue to develop new methods for measuring a wider range of properties.

### Status

### Context
 
### Background

Te Reitiriti o Aotearoa has a vision to provide the option for 
users to subscribe to a set of related content items stored within 
a 'subscription store'. In the initial iteration of the business
model, this subscription store will be provided by Media
Ransom, thus the term 'subscription service' is being used here to
refer to subscription services hosted by Media Ransom or
similarly-structured SaaS providers. 

### Complication

The definition of 'subscription service' is ambiguous. In the context
of subscription services, 'service' implies a system providing
functions that can be used by client users over a network. The notion of
"function" is vague.

### Issue

We need to define what is meant by 'subscription service' to reduce
ambiguity.

### Decision
 
We define a 'subscription service' as a hosted service that provides
the ability for users to combine a number of 'consumption items' into
a single 'subscription'.

We define 'consumption items' as the building blocks of subscriptions.
Specifically, a 'consumption item' can be:

* A 'product service': For example, Netflix, Spotify, etc.
* A 'content service': For example, RSS feeds, mail digests, etc.
* A 'data service': For example, daily newspaper, sports scores, etc.

The 'subscription' is the combination of all 'consumption items'
included in a single subscription service. 

### Consequences
 
#### Easier
* This definition is more explicit than simply "service" and should
	reduce the issue of ambiguity.
* It may still prove difficult to build a business model around
	such a broad range of services, but building the service
	itself should be relatively straightforward.

#### More Difficult
* Creating a mechanism for combining items from very different
	'service types' into a single subscription will be non-trivial.
	(e.g. Combining a RSS feed subscription with a Netflix subscription)
* Once this 'combination' is built, expanding the system to provide
	users with a single subscription service to manage the combination
	of subscriptions will be non-trivial.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Previously in SAM we've found that specificity of type definitions was a
problem.

We have two ways of defining types currently:

1) Type aliases, e.g. `type MyType = int | string`
2) Type classes, e.g. `class MyType(x: int)`

As type aliases do not provide any additional information, we can safely
ignore them when checking for type consistency. However, type classes
provide additional information and we cannot ignore them.

## Decision

We will add the following two properties to the `Type` type:

1) `additionalInfo` - a `map[string]string` - any additional information
   that the type provides.
2) `isSpecific` - a `bool` - whether the type is specific or not.

## Consequences

### Pros

1) Any additional property that the type provides can be captured, e.g. for
   use in type checking
2) We can now formally capture the concept of a "specific" type, which is useful
   when discussing the semantics of the system

### Cons

1) `isSpecific` - a `bool` - a `MyType` may or may not be specific. We may
   never have a good reason to believe it is specific, but we would have to
   make the decision for each type whether it is specific or not

## Context and Problem Statement

Deploying GDS (aka Ministry of Justice Digital & Technology) Supported Platform (aka MISO) support node on a standalone node is a fairly straight forward process, which is captured over at https://cloud.gov/docs/deploying-an-miso-platform-with-kops/.

However to deploy it on GOV.UK PaaS you must take into account a number of security/compliance requirements, which have some technical impact.

You'll need an SSL certificate (let's encrypt is the easiest option). This must be signed and provisioned on the GOV.UK PaaS.

If we were deploying an Apache or NGINX reverse proxy to an instance of mapex, we would need to keep in mind that the end-user's requests pass through a very high level SSL, and then another high level SSL at the endpoint of the backend.

## Decision Drivers

* Security, as described in GOV.UK PaaS SSL cert migration guide.
* Compliance, as described in GOV.UK PaaS SSL cert migration guide.
* Desire to keep the number of proxy nodes as low as possible.

## Considered Options

There are 2 options that support SSL on GOV.UK PaaS:

1. S3 Classic Cloudfront
2. S3 Cloudfront + ELB (or ALB)
3. S3 Custom ELB (https://github.com/hhatto/s3-cloudfront-kops)

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "S3 Cloudfront + ALB", because

* Better integration with S3 for storage of the SSL certificate.
* ELB (or ALB) adds few lines of code.
* ALB adds support for X-Forwarded-For, if required.
* ELB/ALB is fairly universal in AWS architecture.

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### S3 Classic Cloudfront

We can load an SSL cert via an S3 bucket, directly into an unencrypted apache httpd server, and redirect via internal DNS to the S3 url

* Good, can support HTTPS directly, 
* Bad, because the request will pass through two HTTPS connections.
* Bad, because SSL sessions can't be cached, will require keep alive and/or session caching.
* Bad, in my opinion they need to be the same url.
* Bad, needs 3 ports. 
* Bad, DNS complexity - 2 zones.
* Bad, when I use GDS as server, the URL that is exposed should be from my local url. 
* Bad, URL will have domain from S3 and url of the server. 
* Bad, no support for X-Forwarded-For 
* Bad, I think in 2018 is deprecated. 
* Bad, needs 3 IP addresses. 
* Bad, SSL certs must be provisioned on the S3 bucket (or the SSL won't be able to be created)

### S3 Cloudfront + ALB

We could provision SSL and HA on ELB/ALB, and then use CloudFront to request the URL via a standard httpd or nginx server and forward the original URL

* Good, SSL is more secure, and can be placed across the internal IP to S3 URLs
* Good, this is the approach I know, and can be easier to execute. 
* Good, the URL I will use, will have the correct url - either: (1) the original IP address / domain mapped to the ALB and ELB or (2) the original IP address / domain mapped to an nginx/httpd server. 
* Good, ALBs support custom X-Forwarded-For, so forward headers should map correctly
* Good, less DNS configuration - use a `CNAME` to map to the ELB or ALB to the nginx/httpd or nginx. 
* Good, the SSL cert and DNS are in a single domain and ALB/ELB handles the SSL connections
* Bad, because it will require integration with the S3. 

### S3 Custom ELB

As an additional option for deploying the mapex node directly from the domain, you could provisioning a custom ELB that provides SSL (and potentially HA) capabilities directly over the S3 connection, which is a fairly well described process as well, but I have not done it

# Use double array in memory for pixel data

* Status: Accepted
* Deciders: Lewin Chan, Aaron Collier, Paul Dubs
* Date: 2020-04-16

## Context and Problem Statement

Pixel data often varies in dimensions in an image. Previously, we took the approach of creating a fixed-size array and padding it with zeros to the desired size. This resulted in an array that had rows with potentially different numbers of pixels.

In some cases, like working with pixel data, it is more performant to use a 2-row array where the first row contains pixel data and the second row contains the pixel data for the next row. This is because accessing pixel data by row minimizes the number of memory accesses.

This approach is already used in `Image` and `Pixel` classes.

## Considered Options

* Use double array
* Use single array padded with zeros

## Decision Outcome

Use double array for pixel data

## Context

To deliver a great user experience, many applications need to offer some kind of
"hot reloading", where changes are applied to the app as soon as they are made,
without requiring the user to close and re-enter the app. This is commonly found
in single-page applications.

A good way to achieve this is to add a post-mortem handler to every request to
allow the system to detect when the request failed along with a user that failed
with that error. From here we can roll-out an automated troubleshooting strategy
to detect and diagnose problems in a fast-moving system.

Some apps will naturally fall into this category, like an IDE, but some
interopable parts of a system require the user to give an explicit signal of
failure. Examples of these include long-running queries to a disk, or sending
emails to a workflow system.

Apps that have this kind of architecture have to make a choice: allow requests to
run inside threads or to explicitly request that they be placed on a thread.
These choices need to be communicated to the end user in the app.

While threads are generally good for short-running parts of a system, placing
queries or calls that return information in them seems to break that pattern.

## Decision

We will offer an API/database mapping object in the user system that indicates
how the user's actions map to threads.

The user system will return this mapping along with any action to a user of
the app when the app can provide an explicit action to execute inside a thread.
The mapping's data is an object that contains two pieces of information:

* A string key that describes the action.
* A string key that points to the SQL query to run that fulfills the action.

The SQL statement returned by this mapping object is the actual query to run in
a thread.

## Status

Proposed

## Consequences

This API might be redundant:

* If the user requests that a query run inside a thread, the user system will
  automatically place that query on a thread.
* If a user cancels an action, the user system will add this to the back of
  the queue of threads.
* If a user gives a thread another action to run, the user system will add this
  and the rest of the user's actions into the back of the thread.

We will need to add an API that can be called for the user system to place a
query onto a thread for this.

If the SQL query is not correct, or a thread is interrupted, the error may be
ignored:

* All threads are expected to be a short-running task and the API will be
  created to handle exceptions thrown by a thread.
* This may result in no errors being displayed for the app user.
* While this may be considered a failure mode, it is easy to think of a
  follow-up action to notify the administrator that a thread has failed and
  why.

The use of SQL in this mapping object is appropriate because we do not
understand the app or user system architecture; neither do we know if the
queries will be parameterized (which is best) or hard-coded (which is more
complex).

# Channel Lifecycle

### Context

The current lifecycle of the Channel instance is as follows:

- The `Lifecycle` command is invoked to trigger the lifecycle.
- For Channels created via API, the `create()` operation is invoked. This operation contains all the steps as described in [ADR 0002](adr-0002-channel-lifecycle.md)
- For Channels migrated via the command line tool, the `migrate()` operation is invoked. This operation contains all the steps as described in [ADR 0003](adr-0003-channel-lifecycle.md)
- Once the migration is finished, it is reported via the current monitoring plugin as `SUCCESS`
- Once all Channels are considered as migrated, the end-to-end migration is considered as SUCCESS

### Decision

- The `migrate()` operation should be refactored to call the appropriate `create()` operation for migration.
- This decision implies that Channel lifecycle cannot be managed via command line tool anymore.
- The `migrate()` operation will be renamed `create()`
- The migration section will be refactored and the following operation will be invoked:
  - `migrateChannelMigration()`
  - This operation will call the `create()` operation and report the status of the channel.
  - As part of the same operation, a callback will be given to handle the notification of success or failure.
- For Migration initiated via command line tool, a new operation will be introduced:
  - `initiateChannelMigration()`
  - This operation will call the appropriate migration plugin to handle the migration initiated via command line tool.
- A new endpoint will be added via the admin API to report the status of end-to-end migration.
  - `POST /api/1/channels/migration`
  - Request body: JSON representing channels that will be migrated.
  - Each channel JSON includes the current status of the channel and an additional `state` field which can be `PENDING_INITIATION`, `PENDING_MIGRATION`, `MIGRATION_IN_PROGRESS`, `SUCCESS`, `FAILED`.

### Status

Superseded

## Status

## Context

The current content structure and identifiers are tightly coupled. Changing the content structure may break existing identifiers. URLs do not provide a way to identify content. The current domain is not flexible enough to support changes to the URL without changes to the content. The current way of generating URLs is difficult to change.

## Decision

Use the path for an identifier. The path must be a url-safe string, i.e. no slashes or reserved characters. The url-safe string must map to a content item identifier. A content item identifier is the primary key of the content item and must be used as the identifier. This way, a content item identifier is used to generate the path and to query for that content item.

Example:

Given the following content items:

`http://example.com/topics/1/articles/12` -> topic 1, article 12
`http://example.com/topics/1/articles/13` -> topic 1, article 13

Given the above, the identifier for topic 1, article 12 is 1.

Given the above, the identifier for topic 1, article 13 is 2.

So, for topic 1, articles 12 and 13 can be accessed via the following URLs:

`/topics/1/articles/12`
`/topics/1/articles/13`

## Consequences

All content must be accessible via a URL. All URLs must be changed to use the path identifier. All queries must use the identifier instead of the URL as an argument. URLs may change in the future, but this shouldn't matter as long as the URL is changed before the associated content.
The URL should be optional. Content may be added to the domain directly, but this is discouraged.

There are a number of reasons why Smartdown will not work.

First, Smartdown builds on top of the YAML specification, which is not a specification of a data model.

Second, it does not appear that Smartdown has been through the same rigors as the YAML specification or Bidi YAML (which Smartdown is a drop in replacement for).

Third, as YAML is a human-readable serialization of a JSON-like data model, there is no reason to believe that Smartdown, which is designed to be read by machines, would necessarily be human-readable.

Lastly, Smartdown has a number of features which appear to be ad-hoc and unnecessary.

For example, Smartdown allows a `domain` tag to be applied to a YAML element, so that the YAML element can be interpreted as a Datomic-style data model in which the element is a type of `rdfs:domain`.

The only reason for allowing this is that Smartdown provides a printing function that can interpret YAML with Smartdown tags as Datomic (so that the element can be printed as the domain of a graph property).

This allows us to construct the YAML for a graph as Datomic, which is then serialized to JSON, which then becomes YAML.

## Decision

Remove Smartdown.

## Consequences

If Smartdown has been adopted in a context where it is not easy to remove Smartdown, it may be possible to remove Smartdown without backward-incompatible changes.

## Context

When building and deploying a Svelte application, you may consider the testing and validation process to be a step-by-step process.
Building a testing framework or suite of tests for your Svelte application can be time consuming and there are many options to choose from.

There are two main strategies I am aware of for testing Svelte applications:

### 1. Testing libraries

There are testing libraries that wrap around DOM-like functions and allow you to write tests that ultimately render the application.
These libraries vary widely in their functionality and may require additional knowledge to understand what is required or expected.

One of the main benefits of testing libraries is that you can start writing tests without having to build and maintain your own fixtures or mock functions.
These testing libraries are sometimes building blocks for a larger testing framework, but are generally standalone.

Some popular options include:

* [Testing Library](https://testing-library.com/)
* [Intern](https://github.com/intern-js/intern)
* [SvelteKit's `test` command](https://github.com/sveltekit/svelte#testing) (Intern package)

### 2. Testing framework and mock functions

There are testing frameworks which operate outside of the application code.
These frameworks typically require you to build mock functions in a separate function and call these in your tests.
This approach requires you to write more code yourself, but may offer more fine-grained control over the process.
You have full control over what is mocked out and what is tested.
You also maintain complete control of how the application is tested.

Some popular options include:

* [Jest](https://jestjs.io/)
* [Jasmine](https://jasmine.github.io/)
* [TestCafe](https://testcafe.org/)
* [Intern](https://github.com/intern-js/intern) (can be used standalone)

## Decision

We will use the testing library `Intern` with the testing framework `Jest`.

Intern provides a layer over the DOM which makes writing tests slightly less verbose, but doesn't require you to know or use DOM-like functions to understand the code.
It offers a blend of convenience and accessibility.

Adding a testing library to the application and calling the native `test` command in `svelte.conf.js` makes the developer experience very low-lift.

`Jest` is a fast and well-known framework.
Because testing libraries build on top of `Jest`, getting started with `Jest` should be straightforward when using a library like `Intern`.
The maintainance cost of writing tests is relatively low.

## Consequences

- There are no immediate consequences to the build and deployment process.
- Using both `Jest` and `Intern` can sometimes require additional care when linking or introducing new code.

Technical Story: https://dsdmoj.atlassian.net/browse/DS-1717

## Context and Problem Statement

This ADR is concerned with two use-cases involving smart contract wallets and meta-transactions:

1. Sending payments using smart contract wallets which can be used by anyone (including DSD) to generate a unique 32-byte SHA-512 hash of the smart contract address. This can then be used by any user in `ClaimFlow` to claim their token.

2. Generating the correct (unique) 32-byte SHA-512 hash of the smart contract address for use in `ClaimFlow`.

In use-case 1, this would need to work in a two-step process. First, a user will be given the option of generating a 32-byte SHA-512 hash of the smart contract address and associating that 32-byte hash with their DSD token ID. Second, the user can then use the 32-byte SHA-512 hash (in addition to their DSD token ID) to claim their token when they complete a purchase. This might be used to enable users to claim when sending money to generate the SHA-512 hash.

For use-case 2, this is a single step process but the code will need to generate the 32-byte SHA-512 hash once the smart contract address is known. Once the 32-byte SHA-512 hash is generated, it would then be stored by DSD alongside the user's DSD token ID (using the same mechanism as use-case 1).

### Issues

* [DS-1717](https://dsdmoj.atlassian.net/browse/DS-1717) - Generate a unique SHA-512 hash of the smart contract address for use in ClaimFlow
* [DS-1719](https://dsdmoj.atlassian.net/browse/DS-1719) - Smart contract wallets and meta-transactions

### Decisions

- The issue [DS-1717](https://dsdmoj.atlassian.net/browse/DS-1717) will be addressed using a unique 32-byte SHA-512 hash of the smart contract address for use in `ClaimFlow`.

- The issue [DS-1719](https://dsdmoj.atlassian.net/browse/DS-1719) will address two use-cases:

  - When a user enters their payment (or beneficiary) smart contract address in `SmartContractWallet` they select a 32-byte SHA-512 hash of that address (generated using `Solc.compileAndRun`) as the recipient of the funds. This would be part of a two-step process. First, a user will be given the option of generating a 32-byte SHA-512 hash of the beneficiary smart contract address and associating that 32-byte hash with their DSD token ID, using the mechanism established in [DS-1717](https://dsdmoj.atlassian.net/browse/DS-1717). Secondly, the user can then use the 32-byte SHA-512 hash (in addition to their DSD token ID) to claim their token when they complete the purchase.

  - When a user enters the smart contract address of their wallet directly (omitting the SHA-512 hash) in `SmartContractWallet` they use it to generate a unique 32-byte SHA-512 hash that is saved by DSD, using the same mechanism as described in [DS-1717](https://dsdmoj.atlassian.net/browse/DS-1717). This hash is then used by users in `ClaimFlow` with their DSD token ID to claim the appropriate token.

## Consequences

- This will result in a shorter public-facing User Interface.

- This is a top priority for the team (ROley and ml019) and the issue is tagged as `critical`.

### Consequences - Risks

- As this relates directly to money entering and leaving the wallet, and potentially the exchange, security is a top priority.

## Context

[Event sourcing] is a pattern that enables applications to store a sequence of changes to business entities, making it possible to query and view the history of those changes. [Implementing event sourcing] for simple use cases like displaying recent activity might be quite easy, but for complex use cases it can be a challenging problem to grasp the best way of handling events in the application. One significant issue is [handling event consistency], e.g., ensuring that the event log returned to the client reflects the current state of the application.

The [Knative API] defines [Eventing], an interface for sending and receiving messages. There are many potential message brokers which implement the Eventing API or [it's equivalent] for specific use cases. Examples include Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS or AWS Kinesis.

### DR 013 - Use the GraphQL Gateway for interacting with Kyma

For all Kyma specific usecases there is a Kyma GraphQL API. Using this API means that the choice of the message broker is not limited to those who are Eventing API compliant. However there is no officially accepted standardized way to use the GraphQL API for returning messages and there are no drivers for this purpose. Using the Eventing API message broker makes the solution independent from it's underlying message broker in the future.

### Kyma Eventing as a Dapr Feature

There are a number of reasons why Kyma's Eventing system might be an interesting choice for implementing event sourcing:

* Kyma Eventing is a part of the Kubernetes, as such is well-known for the Kubernetes ecosystem
* It might use the Kubernetes Event system, making use of existing knowledge to use and understand this feature
* Kyma Eventing's event format might be integrated with Kubernetes resource structure (e.g., using kubernetes resources such as Service Accounts, Policies and Roles to grant event permissions)

## Decision

* We are going to implement Kyma's Eventing in dapr
* We will reuse Kyma's Eventing with any Eventing message broker
* We will not expose an Eventing Event Interface for Dapr application users (see decision DR 021)
* We will use Dapr's GraphQL Gateway to receive the messages
* Dapr GraphQL Gateway will be returned as a part of the GraphQL Query Response for the `/event` endpoint
* There is no Eventing System that will be used other than the Eventing implemented in Kyma

## Status

Implemented on 2018-12-17.

## Consequences

* We will use Kyma's Eventing in the dapr event sourcing implementation
* The GraphQL Gateway will be returned as a part of the GraphQL Query Response for the `/event` endpoint
* We will use Kyma's Eventing in the GraphQL Gateway
* There is no plan to include and use an Eventing message broker like RabbitMQ or NATS in the dapr implementation

## Decision

We have two strategies that we considered as two options in handling synthetic
tenants:
1. allow new users to manage their own synthetic tenants directly via a cloud
provider or VM and using the new tuf-service to make the migration
themselves,
2. have the current system create synthetic tenants for them automatically and
then run a script to migrate them over. This would mean that we would maintain
two sets of scripts, one for the current system (`py-tuf`) and one for the
new tuf (`py_tuf`).
3. introduce another intermediate model where we create synthetic tenants, and
this will be a model from which a separate script will be able to migrate
them over. 

As we are still in the design process for this work, the proposed decisions at
this stage is that we will introduce synthetic tenants in the new `py_tuf`
code. In practice this means that we would need a way for users to manage
them via the cloud provider or VM when they make the migration over.

If the cost of maintenance for synthetic tenants becomes a burden, we can
introduce a separate model to migrate or disable them automatically.

## Status

Draft.

## Consequences

We will need to be able to create synthetic tenants in the new `py_tuf` codebase.

In order for the maintenance of synthetic tenants to be as straightforward as
possible, we will use the same architecture as we used in the `py-tuf` codebase.

# 14 - Use Jenkins for network path storage

Date: 2019-Dec-20

## Status

Accepted

## Context

The PACE project is running on an ARM-based cluster running CentOS 7. 

GridLabD is no longer being updated and institutional support for it is limited. 

The public-facing GridLabD site is no longer accessible as the RDS instance that hosts it has been disconnected from the Internet. 

Access to the project's storage system is currently managed via a samba file share mounted under `/srv/data`. The share is currently on the `filesharing` volume and is only available to users logged into the cluster via bastion. 

In this way, file access and identity are separate things. It is not possible to control access to the share without using group ID. The user could share the drive by setting the appropriate group ID to a dedicated user, then removing this user when they have been removed from the project and a new user with the same ID is loaded by the bastion. 

Alternatives to a samba share are:
- local file system for Data
- a git-based file storage system (`pact-data` currently)
- cloud storage (S3, Azure etc)

The use of a standard grid-based file system would fit well with the current and future development of infrastructure. 

## Decision

The decision is to change the network path storage to the GNU GPL v4 Open Source Panoptes alt-storage implementation. 

In this way:
- we use the correct data management tool for the project's data
- we are able to align identity management in with the infrastructure

## Consequences

The current storage solution and access to it is a mix of custom script-based access control, a custom-built service and a community-supported file system.

There is a path to making file creation, storage and destruction an automated process, with all new users (identified via OAuth2) only able to delete files in the private-facing Alt-Store. 

There is no equivalent to `pact-data` or `grid-storage` in the GNU GPL v4 Open Source Panoptes alt-storage implementation. 

Any additional user-space tools we add in the development pipeline must conform to the GNU GPL v4 Open Source Panoptes alt-storage implementation's use of standard UNIX APIs and command-line interfaces. 

The URL to an instance of the GNU GPL v4 Open Source Panoptes alt-storage implementation currently points to the `k8s-cluster` in the "live" environment.

We will still use an authentication system other than username/password for moving files around the network.

We are no longer required to use `pact-server`'s `file-storage` (now part of the `storage` service) when storing files in the "live" environment (the storage mechanism has no consequence for storing files in Alt-Store). 

### Authentication for moving files around the network

In `file-storage` there is an abstract base class for all storage backends:

```c++
class Backend
{
 public:
  using KeySet = std::unordered_set<std::string>;
  using KeyValue = std::unordered_map<std::string, std::string>;
  using Storage = std::vector<KeyValue>;
  using ObjectStorage = std::unordered_map<std::string, Storage>;

  // returns Storage for objects identified by the Keyset
  virtual Storage* load(const KeySet& keys) = 0;
  // returns Storage for objects identified by the KeySet
  virtual Storage* store(const KeySet& keys) = 0;
  // deletes an ObjectStorage
  virtual ~Backend() {}
};
```

In the current "live" environment, `file-storage` returns only the private facing Alt-Store (`file-storage/private`) as an ObjectStorage in which:
- `key` is a username (actually a GUID)
- `value` is the mount point of the backend on the "live" environment's mount points in `/srv/data/**.mount`
- `value` contains the user's ID and the mount point of their files on the private facing Alt-Store 

In Alt-Store, the mount point is a filesystem key and the user is the authentication mechanism. `Backend` does not require the concept of a mount point or key set (as it only works with a single storage backend).

## **Context**

React can provide components in one of three ways:

1. **js-sdk** - this approach involves generating a javascript file containing all the components in question. This is then imported into an application using `import { Box, Text } from 'my-cool-library';`. A useful example of this is [emotion](https://emotion.sh/), which allows importing styles as well as components.
2. **css-variables** - instead of importing a javascript file, an application using `css-variables` can link to an `index.html` file containing the css variables in question.
3. **direct usage** - a developer can directly include the html and css for a component, for example a button, into an application using the `div` element.

## **Decision**

The developers at FDS have decided to use option 1, generating a js-sdk module for each library they import. There are advantages to this approach. The module can be reused in multiple applications and the code is typically more concise than using option 2 or 3.

## **Consequences**

Generating a js-sdk module for each library import has the following consequences:

- All applications must link to the same version of the package, which may require extra work when updating
- The generated javascript file must be placed in the `src/` directory, which typically requires access to the repository
- Applications that make heavy use of direct usage of elements (a.k.a "custom html") may find it difficult to integrate FDS modules

## Consequences

## Related Decisions

### Error Handling in ABCI

The handling of errors for ABCI messages was first defined in the proto files.  There were two basic strategies.

## Context and Problem Statement

The problem statement is: "Should we use buildpacks to create an application to be deployed to the PaaS (cloud provider) or use containers?".

## Considered Options

### Buildpacks (for example the ones by Google Cloud)

The Buildpacks approach takes all the required components for building a application.  Application dependencies, build context, cloud provider specific configuration and cloud provider runtime, are all packaged together.  An application, or a change on an application's needs, will cause the buildpack to rebuild the entire application in the background (using the Cloud Build steps).

Pros and cons:

- Easy and fast (due to using Cloud Build as part of the solution, leveraging the free tier).
- Does not require container infrastructure.
- Requires manual creation of projects and configuration outside the buildpack (e.g. the bash scripts).
- Requires manual updates of `gcp/cloud` package.
- We can use containers to replace a buildpack.
- **Best if**: The application has few or no external dependencies, is easy to create and build once, and does not change very much.

### Containers (as Docker)

There are two ways to handle the packaging of the application into a container.
We can use the command line or we can use cloud providers specific services, i.e. the GCP Cloud Container Platform called Container Builder (or gcloud builder).  The latter offers the advantages that the buildpacks and the command line:

- Fast and easy to use once `gcp container build-runner` is in the system.
- Very little boilerplate code.
- Allows to package also the application's bash scripts for creating the final image.
- Free.
- **Best if**: The application is complex, or the creation of the final image is done as part of the overall Docker environment.

### **Summary**

|                  | Buildpacks                                          | Containers                                                    |
| ------------------|--------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| Package type      | Cloud-specific Buildpacks, bash scripts, json files | zipfiles, json files                                         |
| Development team    | 1                                                 | 1                                                             |
| **Pros**            | Fast, easy to create and build once, very little boilerplate code    | Integrates with cloud provider's solution for packaging |
| **Cons**            | bash scripts are an overhead, cloud provider specific config needed|                                                              |

## Decision Outcome

The Buildpacks approach seems to be a very fast and easy way to build an application to be deployed.
However, given that we want to have the application's bash scripts included in the container image, we may be forced to use a bash script based buildpack (such as the Google Cloud Buildpacks)
