Technical Story: [Moving frontend into a npm package](https://github.com/hmrc/govuk-react/issues/1391)

## Context and Problem Statement

The modernisation of the frontend for NHS.UK is a strategic priority for NHS.
This is being done in two ways - by building a new frontend in React and by
modernising the existing frontend by extracting it into a new npm package.

This ADR is concerned with the decision around whether to host the NPM package
created in modernising the existing frontend.

## Considered Options

### Hosting the npm package on GitHub pages

The first option would be to leave the package on GitHub pages as before,
never removing it from the monorepo.

The benefits of this are:

- it is easy to do
- the package will never be removed

The downsides are:

- the package will contain code that is not actually in use in NHS.UK,
  resulting in a higher maintenance effort.
- code splitting is harder to do

### Move the npm package into a new repository

The second option would be to move the package into a new repository per
frontend microservice, establishing a pattern for moving frontend code into
their own repository (see ADR 0007).

The benefits of this are:

- no code splitting
- no code that is not actually in use
- the package is more likely to evolve into a single service

The downsides are:

- for each package we move, we're introducing a new frontend microservice,
  requiring frontend and UX co-ordination and possibly data structure
  re-engineering.

## Decision Outcome

We have decided to move the package into a new repository rather than leaving it
in the GitHub pages under the monorepo.

## Links

- [Frontend technology considerations](0007-frontend-tech-considerations.md)
- [Moving frontend into a npm package](https://github.com/hmrc/govuk-react/issues/1391)

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Historically, we have made decisions on the design and refactoring of the
Datomic's API. These decisions have included:

- Choosing a data format for API requests and responses.
- Choosing a data structure for API resources.
- Choosing HTTP verbs for API endpoints.
- Implementing caching behavior.

The rationale for introducing these decisions, along with the options considered
and the context that motivates them, was documented in
[API Playwright](api-playwright.md).

This proposal is a vote to also document decisions that *aren't* made in
Playwright, but which *have* an impact on the endpoint's behavior,
architecture, or implementation - especially decisions that result in:

- Changes to Datomic's behavior or capabilities.
- Changes to the way in which Datomic resources are described.
- Changes to the representation of relationships in Datomic.
- Changes to the authentication, authorization, or auditing systems in use.
- Changes to the way in which Datomic's resources are indexed in S3.

## Consequences

- Users of Datomic's API will be able to understand the choices made on a
  particular question, and the reasoning for those choices.
- Existing users will be able to update their expectations for how Datomic
  interacts with clients.
- New users will be able to make informed decisions on how to use Datomic
  by referring to the API Playwright and making it clear what options are
  off the table.
- Users will be able to understand the history of Datomic's API and how
  decisions have shaped its development and future direction.

## Context

The `migrate-variants-to-new-v2` migration was implemented with a workaround
for the fact that there was no `migration-year` column in the V2.
Instead, a `created-on` column has been added.
When the new migration has been implemented, an `after-migration-year`
has been added, which is set to `NULL`, but we've been hoping to use the
migration as an asynchronous operation.

We have been encountering the problem that a migrate operation may be
attempted on a batch of ids that would be in a state that we want to
migrate to an older migration year.
We have encountered a problem where an `after-migration-year` of `NULL` may
be in a state we want to migrate as opposed to a year that has not had
migration done yet.

## Decision

After having discussed it with @tdecoster, @sdelpino, @jpacx, and @cperry,
we have decided to introduce a new migration year in the migrations
database table.
The only way to make this happen should be via an API, not the
application.
The new migration year will be used solely in a migrate operation.
This is so we can start calling the migrate operation from the API for
batch migrating, then switching to the application for updating of the
individual rows as the update operation should run in an asynchronous,
idempotent operation.
This is an example of what the code for migrating from 56 to 57:
```js
migrateLatestAndCreateNewMigrationYear('https://api.genomics.org/variants?created-on:57');
```

We intend to support the same migrations (the latest one) with an API
migration.
As described above, this is so we can start calling the migration from the
application for batch migrations.
In the future, we may introduce an endpoint that allows a user to turn
this on and migrate all remaining genes.
This migration is a decision of the migration itself, and should be
optional as is.

## Consequences

We will have to make changes to the migration.

The migration itself should remain at 0.  
The migrations table is a temporary table, and this will be handled
when creating migrations in a separate operation.
This may happen asynchronously from the migration itself.

An action has been added to prevent the first migration year (0) from being
added to the migrations table.
In order to add a migration year, the migration must be created
by an API as the first time a new migration year will be added should be
by using the API.
This is so if the migration has been updated, the application will run
the new migration again.
This prevents the first year from being deleted when the application
runs the migration and it finds it in the table.
This does *not* mean that is when the migration will be executed, the first
time a year is added, the migration is created asynchronously.
When it is picked up, a separate operation will run the current migration
for the year.  
A query has been added for showing all migrations in the migrations table
and returning their creation year, for the purpose of the API.

The order of migrations in the migrations table has no meaning other
than for finding migrations via migrations-db package.

To update the created-on year in a migration, there's two options:
1. create a migration with created-on: new-year + 1 (if the year is
   the first year to be added)
2. create the new migration with a created-on of 0 (we don't care what
   the value is, but the year must be a year that has been migrated,
   otherwise we won't call migration-by-batch)
3. create a new migration with created-on: 0
    * use new-year as the new migration year
    * it can make it more obvious which is a new migration year for future
      scenarios, and it also prevents a current year from being added
      again, if there's already a migration for this year
    * when loading all migrations from migrations-db, the `created-on`
      field will be the migration year

These options are not mutually exclusive. 
3. is an option if a user wants to migrate to the new year in a singular
action with the application, and is not a scenario where batch operation
for each set of ids should be loaded from the API.
We may make the API option "async" or "batch" for migrating by year.

## Context

Different applications will need to connect to the API and use the service. Some applications will require the ability to authenticate using usernames and passwords.

## Decision

We allow applications to register themselves, and provide an authentication token, to use the service. This token should be limited in scope and time-bound, but cheap and quick to generate.

The registration should provide the application with an opaque token, which should be retained by the application.

When the application is ready to disconnect from the service, it should submit the token to the service to unregister it.

## Consequences

Any application running a consumer of the API will be able to register itself, using one of the built-in authentication mechanisms in the server. The application can, if it needs, present a username and password to the server to add a new token to its registration. This is useful, as an authentication token stored in the server may be more persistent (to register a token, the application needs to be registered first, for the server to set up a database entry) and more resistant to tampering than user authentication.

As with the user authentication mechanism of registration, a user account (and, in turn, a token) will need to be created by the application in the server before the token can be registered with it. This may be implemented as part of the setup of the user token application.

## Notes

The token should live no longer than the user token, perhaps limited by the user access or session.

## Status

Accepted

Supercedes [13. Lifecycle of the object model](0013-lifecycle-of-the-object-model.md)

## Context

Interlok is a application designed for long-living services. We can draw a useful lifetime for an instance of a Service as Long-Living as a concept:
 1. The service is created.
 2. A set of parameters (the configuration of the service) is provided.
 3. The service is updated while receiving new parameters.
 4. The service stops.
 5. The service is deleted.

Each stage of a useful lifetime could be considered a *lifecycle stage*. The useful lifetime of a Service is the set of all stages, not just one.
 A Service may go through several life cycles, and stages of other services may be intertwined.


## Decision

We will manage the life cycle of services.
The useful lifetime begins with creation and ends with deletion.
Stages of a useful lifetime will be considered *lifecycle stages*.
A lifecycle stage is a step a Service moves through, from one status to another.
A lifecycle is the set of stages a Service goes through.
Creating a service has 3 stages: service is created, initial parameters are set, service is updated.
Receiving parameters and updating the service is done concurrently as a number of parameters can be set at any point of the service lifecycle.
Stopping the service is done once all parameters are set; deleting the service is done once the service is stopped.


## Consequences

Services may have multiple stages, concurrently. This leads to a slightly more complex, yet easier to understand, application of state management.
Services may go through their lifecycle multiple times.

## Context

There is currently a class called `GlobalContext` that is in use in the `grob-common` package.
The value of this class is its `context.Context` which contains a lot of useful information about the current execution environment.
This includes things such as the user who is logged in, the page they are on, the section of the application they are in, and much more.

This class however has a lot of other issues in addition to being a source of confusion due to its name.
For example, the type name clashes with the Go standard library, making it difficult to work with.
It is also missing from the Go standard libraries, which should provide a standard way to handle request and context information in Go.
Finally, the current usage in `grob-common` is confusing, since any module that wants to use the Context has to pass a new instance of the class to every route.

We decided to split the `GlobalContext` class into three separate types:

1. `Context` - a subset of the `GlobalContext` class that contains the value of the `Context.Context` out of that class.
2. `Request` - a subset of the `GlobalContext` class that contains the value of the `Context.Request` out of that class.
3. `Response` - a subset of the `GlobalContext` class that contains the value of the `Context.Response` out of that class.

The `Context` type contains a `Context` type as its value, the `Request` type contains a `http.Request` type as its value, and the `Response` type contains a `http.Response` type as its value.

## Decision

We will use separate types in place of the `GlobalContext` class.
These types will be called `Context`, `Request`, and `Response`.
These types will only have one method in the `GlobalContext` type: `Context.AsContext` which returns the underlying context.
These methods will be in the `grob-common` package.

## Status

Accepted

## Consequences

### Positive

* There is no confusion from the user on how to access the current context.
* It matches the Go standard library, which provides a standard way to handle request and context information.
* The public API is no longer confusing, and any module that wants to use the context can do so by simply passing a `Context` type.

### Negative

* In many places in the codebase the `GlobalContext` class is used.
* `Context` types do not provide a default way to handle the request/response.
* Any application developer will need to add a new dependency to their project that contains the new types.

Date: 2020-Apr-01

## Status

Accepted

## Context

There are currently a lot of unnecessary commits being made on the master branch, the number of commits on master has increased over time and is no longer an easy to reason or intuitive experience for any user, visitor, or maintainer. It is difficult to keep the options for branches and their content clean, comprehensible, and up to date given that there are always several options for branches (feature, hotfix, release, etc) depending on the circumstances.

## Decision

The goal for the next iteration is to reduce the number of long-running branches, and other complicated use-cases. It will feature 1-3 long-lived branches which serve to create and manage the current iteration and long-term development; in addition, we will continue to maintain a `master` branch as a central point for releasing new versions of the application. The `master` branch should only contain the most stable and tested version of the application for the appropiate channel, as well as a commit indicating the current state of development and long-term work on the `master` branch.

## Consequences

- Release planning is more constrained to the master branch, we must plan and design new releases at the beginning of each iteration, and this should be done early enough to include any necessary releases early as a feature in the current iteration
- Release process is simplified, the current release process assumes that a stable version of the app has been merged to the `master` branch, and tagged as such, any stable release can then be more easily released using the current release process
- Commit message format and branch names should be consistent, we will use [conventional commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org) to track the progress of each iteration at the beginning of the current iteration, using a `0.x.y` semantic version, the `y` in `0.x.y` should be tracked throughout the iteration, and used as the minor version within a channel in which a new version is made, and the `y` in `0.x.y` should be increased only when the application is ready for a release
- `x` and `y` in a `0.x.y` semantic version are arbitrary, they are there simply to provide a way to distinguish between major version changes, and for channel grouping and release identification, we use their values at the project's discretion
- We will still actively maintain a `master` branch, but as a staging area for a channel, there will typically be no commits directly to `master` once a new release has been tagged by the team as ready for the current channel, and `master` is not a versionable release branch, and will not be tagged and potentially published to a npm package manager or app store or other software repository
- Major version increases, and major changes to the application require a new semantic version number, the first minor version number will be used to indicate when the application is ready for the current channel, once the application is considered stable, and ready for the next release, the minor version number will be increased by 1, and the next major version increase will be 2, as before

## Context and Problem Statement

When the number of lines of code a class has exceeded 1000 in an object oriented language, should we start to break it up into several classes.
When should we start to build classes?
Does it have something to do with the number of lines of code (1000 as already stated)?
And does the problem deepen depending on the type system of the language?

In the context of the javascript, should we start building classes with a custom object?

### 1. Options to build classes
A class can be build from one of these options:

1. A bunch of constructor-related methods in an object
2. A class body with all its properties and methods

**2** was suggested for the javascript context. The problem with the constructor only approach is that no code actually needs to be put into it, so why waste space with `function Factory()`?. This also doesn't allow for some "magic":
    ```
    class Data {
      *static getData()* {
        // some logic
        return 42;
      }
    }
    Data.getData(); // should be like an interface: () => 42;
    ```

### 2. Should we build classes from objects?
Does it matter, do we actually build classes from objects, and then build new objects that inherit from those classes?
Does this mean we are going to build `Object`s and cast them to `Data`, and then we need another class for `_Data`, and `Object`s are going to be used as constructors for `Data`?
This is not an ideal scenario.

### 3. Why classes are good in an OOP language
Object-oriented languages are not mandatory, but it feels like this is a language feature we cannot ignore.
Object-oriented languages are ideal for:
- encapsulation
- inheritance
- polymorphism
- abstraction
- modeling
- design
- ease of comprehension
- ease of development
- reducing boilerplate code
- reusable code
- maintainable code

They also make sure to:
- hide implementation details and do not expose an interface to the user, so users can focus on the big picture.
- users can use functions and interfaces to interact with objects.
- users should not care about the internal state of objects, just as long as they get the same results (contract between object and user)

## Decision Drivers

- reducing lines of code
- easier comprehension
- easier development
- maintainable code

## Considered Options

- [ ] using objects
- [x] using classes

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: using classes.
When an object has lots of methods or properties, we will start to build a class body and later use constructor logic to put the methods into it.

## **Context

Currently, the [subscription platform](https://github.com/smartforgood/subscription-platform)
has its [back-end architecture][subscription-architecture] split between two cloud
services and an integration in third party service.

### **Architecture Overview
There is a complex database system that has been a source of many error-based
discussions to manage. The decision was made to integrate a single, database-like
firestore service to replace the existing architecture. There were three options available
as the integration type:

-   REST or gRPC
-   GraphQL as external API
-   REST API with GraphQL features in the backend

-   `GraphQL` GraphQL is a language for describing, validating, and executing
    queries and commands for a graph-like data structure, i.e. the data structure
    used in databases. A GraphQL client allows the external service to send a
    simple request via GraphQL to a GraphQL server of GraphQL endpoint in order
    to fetch and mutate data. GraphQL allows both the front-end and back-end to
    make many small queries on the same data without the overhead of the
    back-end pushing their own queries to a server. GraphQL gives the front-end
    the option of switching to more GraphQL without the need to change the back-end.
    GraphQL also allows for modularity in the back-end. There can be multiple
    queries with a single API call.
-   `REST` REST and GraphQL are architectural styles used for developing API
    services. REST implies an HTTP API, i.e. HTTP GET and POST methods in
    HTTP resource requests with REST API. REST is well established and well
    understood. REST resources represent actual data objects and are easily
    identifiable via unique URL in HTTP request. REST API supports the concept of
    resource representation and allow the external service to return and accept
    one or more representations of its resource. HTTP is part of [IETF](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc/rfc7418)
    and [W3.org](https://www.w3.org/TR/webarch/index.html). This makes it a protocol
    that has wide support on most operating systems. REST HTTP protocol is easy to
    understand and simple to implement. HTTP URLs are human-readable, which is
    easy to understand. REST gives the front-end the option of switching to GraphQL
    without the need to change the back-end. REST resource requests accept various
    HTTP request bodies and have many protocols in place to parse them, e.g. JSON
    which is the format of GraphQL.
-   `GraphQL` GraphQL and REST are architectural styles used for developing API
    services. GraphQL API is based on a GraphQL language for describing data
    sources which is an API language similar to SQL with a layer in the GraphQL
    server that maps the data and then selects the requested data at query time.
    GraphQL specification is based on [IETF](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc/rfc7946)
    and [W3.org](https://www.w3.org/TR/graphql/). In GraphQL API, the client
    requests data via HTTP POST to an HTTP endpoint of GraphQL server with a
    GraphQL query describing the data the client wishes to receive. GraphQL API
    does not define how data is returned. GraphQL API is similar to REST, but
    GraphQL API has its distinct architecture that is based around GraphQL API
    language.

## **Decision

Google Cloud Firestore is the selected solution in favour of the alternative options
due to a number of reasons:

-   Google Cloud Firestore and REST both share the notion of a collection and
-   Collection as a REST resource. Firestore’s database, the database-like
    firestore service, is a good choice for managing API to handle GraphQL queries
    from front-end.
-   Document structure in Firestore is not validated like REST resources are to
    make GraphQL. REST resources are validated and are similar to JSON schemas
    or GraphQL types.
-   Firestore has its own query language that has some, but not all, of the
    functionalities of SQL, which is also used by GraphQL.
-   Firestore is a [managed database](https://cloud.google.com/firestore)
    service and back-ups are generated daily (SQL).
-   The API does not define its own query language or syntax that is used to
    handle the query input and output like GraphQL and REST.

Technical Story: [Evaluate the feasibility of using cache aware properties in the application](https://github.com/realshady/clean-architecture-tutorial/issues/13)

## Context and Problem Statement

Cache-aware properties should be easy to use for both admins and front-end developers. They should be simple to understand and straightforward to implement in real-life applications.

Consider the following scenario:

An admin is editing a product on an e-commerce site. They want to change the selling price of that product. If they use a cache-aware property (`SalePrice`), we can store the original price in a cache, so that when they click a button to update the selling price, the old price is rendered for them, then when they confirm, the original price is deleted, and finally the product price is set to the new value. So you need a cache to store the original price to render for the admin, but also need to delete that cached property on confirmation.

### Architectural Context

* Frontend
* Domain
* Users

## Decision Drivers <!-- optional -->

* Ease of understanding
* Ease of implementation

## Considered Options

* Use cache-aware `PropertyInfoStore` implementations provided by Guice.
* Implement custom cache-aware `PropertyInfoStore` implementations using `CachingPropertyStore` interface.
* Use cache-aware `PropertyInfoStore` implementations using [ehcache](https://ehcache.org/eclipse-cache/).

## Decision Outcome

We are going to implement custom cache-aware `PropertyInfoStore` implementations using `CachingPropertyStore` interface.

## Pros and Cons of the Options <!-- optional -->

### Use cache-aware `PropertyInfoStore` implementations provided by Guice.

* `+` Can be implemented simply using reflection
* `+` `PropertyInfoStore` is an interface and does not provide cache-aware implementations. It just requires caching the original value
* `-` Guice packages are hard to understand
* `-` It will not work without a custom implementation for each `PropertyInfoStore` implementation and an additional `GuiceCache`
* `-` Guice packages require some learning and some time
* `-` `PropertyInfoStore` interface may or may not provide the necessary logic in the future
* `-` Guice packages may be hard to understand
* `-` `PropertyInfoStore` interface may or may not provide the necessary logic in the future
* `-` Guice packages may require a more in-depth learning path in future for other `PropertyInfoStore` implementations to be added
* `-` Guice packages may be hard to understand
* `-` `PropertyInfoStore` interface may or may not provide the necessary logic in the future
* `-` Guice packages may require a more in-depth learning path in future for other `PropertyInfoStore` implementations to be added
* `-` `CacheStore` interface not designed with the concept of keys
* `-` `CacheStore` interface not designed with the concept of keys

### Implement custom cache-aware `PropertyInfoStore` implementations using `CachingPropertyStore` interface.

* `+` Gives full flexibility to implement
* `+` `CachingPropertyStore` interface provides minimal requirements for cache-aware
* `-` More work to be done

### Use cache-aware `PropertyInfoStore` implementations using [ehcache](https://ehcache.org/eclipse-cache/)

* `+` Can be implemented using reflection
* `+` `CachingPropertyStore` interface provides minimal requirements for cache-aware
* `+` Can be improved from Guice package if further
* `-` We have to figure out all the logic to be added
* `-` We are adding a cache and an interface
* `-` To be integrated with other stores, we'll need to add Guice packages
* `-` `PropertyInfoStore` interface may or may not provide the necessary logic in the future
* `-` Guice packages may require a more in-depth learning path in future for other `PropertyInfoStore` implementations to be added

# 9. Support links between ADRs inside an ADR

## Context and Problem Statement

Currently the system is supporting external links between the Resource and the ADRs (in the sense of external resources attached to an ADR).
Now the users need the same feature for links between different ADRs (e.g. for linking related decisions).

## Decision Drivers <!-- optional -->

* fast to implement
* the approach should be easy to reason around
* the code should be clean

## Considered Options

* allow for an arbitrary list of resources inside the JSON file
* provide special support for ADRs (internal links). Treat ADRs like resources and have a resource type "ADR"

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: 2. Since there are always special treatment for ADRs (see below).

### Positive Consequences <!-- optional -->

* the approach for external resources and the approach for internal ADR links are similar
* this leads to a minimalistic implementation

### Negative Consequences <!-- optional -->

* n/a

### Links between ADRs <!-- optional -->

When referring to another ADR an optional property `related_adr_id` should be provided.
The optional property `title` can be used to link to an ADR outside the JSON file (e.g. in the jsonld file).
This allows the user to provide a short title of the related ADR to make it easier for the user to navigate between entries.
This property is optional so if omitted the ADR will not be linked.
The linked ADR will not have the `title` property filled, thus the entries can be linked by their IDs.

In addition to writing unit tests, code coverage is a great way to track the progress of adding enough tests to
a module. Sonar has a build plugin to determine code coverage for JS and TS files, which can be used to
track the progress of adding enough tests to cover a module.

There are other plugins for Sonar that can be used for other testing purposes, but this ADR is focusing on
how to use the code coverage plugin to track progress of adding enough tests to cover a module.

## Considered Alternatives

* Use a build and code coverage tool.
* Do not use a build and code coverage tool.

## Decision Outcome

* Chosen Alternative: Use a build and code coverage tool.

## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives

### Use a build and code coverage tool

* `Sonarjs.org` is a great resource for learning how to add a build and code coverage tool to Sonar.
* `Sonarjs.org` mentions add-ons to add other tools to Sonar, such as Jest, which provides an integration to
  run as a build step in CircleCI or GitHub Actions.
  - https://github.com/sonarsorg/sonar-js/blob/master/docs/en/usage/manual.md#jenkins-and-the-maven-plugin
  - https://github.com/sonarsorg/sonar-js/blob/master/docs/en/usage/manual.md#circleci
  - https://github.com/sonarsorg/sonar-js/blob/master/docs/en/usage/manual.md#github-actions
* Example Workflow using CircleCI:
  ```bash
  circleci build
  circleci code-coverage
  ```

### Do not use a build and code coverage tool

* Can be integrated into a `build.js` file of a module, but this would require writing and maintaining two
  separate build steps to actually execute the tests.
  - https://github.com/timarney/eslint-plugin-coverage
  - https://github.com/mrmrs/sonar-js/tree/master/lib/plugins/eslint
* There are benefits to keeping the `build.js` file as a bare build step, as this would not be
  altered by adding additional steps before it.

## Status

## Context

Data storage and management is a key component of the tta smarthub platform. At a fundamental level, a relational as well as NoSQL systems were considered. Because the platform's data is mainly structured  and with a need for frequent updates and queries, a relational database management system was viewed as more suitable. With that in mind we looked at MySQL and PostreSQL (Postgres) both open source and popular choices.

## Decision

While both databases provide adequate storage and management, especially with updates provided by version 8 of MySQL, in the end Postgres was chosen. The main advantages of Postgres are implementations leading to better concurrency, specifically the MVCC (Multiversion Concurrency Control) without the need to use read locks, transactional ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) support making the system less vulnerable to data corruption. Postgres also allows for customisation at build time for various use cases and provides extensibility through modules.

## Consequences

We believe Postgres will provide most if not all that is needed from a database. Couple of minor disadvantages of Postgres include a need to register type extensions for custom data types, however this is a rather minor point.

## Status

## Context

We discussed a number of ways to organise source code classes and files and ultimately settled on the following pattern for classes:

- Models
- Mailers
- Repositories

### Models

These classes will each represent a table within the database.

### Mailers

These classes will be responsible for sending emails. They do not have any dependencies to other classes outside of the Rails package.

### Repositories

These classes will be responsible for storing and retrieving data from the database.

## Decision

We will use the proposed directory structure and class names.

## Consequences

We will follow the same directory structure and class names for all our source code files.

## Background

As the codebase grew over time I noticed that there was a lot of unnecessary
friction with the configuration of Ember itself. For example, when I would
update to a new version of Ember, I would have to manually update the versions
of my dependencies and refactor the way that my plugins and components were
declared. This was due to Ember only supporting a single version of a plugin
unless you explicitly asked it to ignore the version, and also because there
was no clean way to remove a plugin once it was loaded.

[0006](0006-ember-files-tree-structure.md) describes how I was using and
organizing my files in Ember, in a more conventional setup. I am proposing a
different way of doing this which I believe will still be relatively conventional
but will address the issues I've been having with versioning and dependency
management.

## Findings

- Old code in `src/` that isn't in `src/components`. The current directory
  structure has everything related to a component on the same level, making
  it hard to understand where things are in their development lifecycle
  throughout the code base.
- Files required by the `add` command should go into separate subdirectories
  for their module/plugin rather than just being in `src/`
- There are several plugins and modules that extend the base manifest `vendor/`
  file instead of extending or copying the `src/` files over to `vendor/`
  This doesn't make sense because these plugins, when not used in development,
  could just be deleted entirely with the `ehmctl` command, leaving no trace
  behind.
- Files required by the `update` command should be in the `src/` directory and
  should be removed once the component has been updated, rather than being
  directly in `vendor/`
- When the directory structure of your current source directory changes
  everything will need to be moved to follow this new structure. Make sure
  you backup up your current source.

Date: 2021-01-21

## Status

Accepted

## Context

This application deals with several important pieces of information that must
be kept secret:

- the API token used to authenticate requests to the backend API
- the user's email address
- the user's username
- the session ID (in use on the front end as well as backend)

These values are set as cookies. The reason for using cookies instead of
session storage in the backend is primarily to make the application more
secure. Backend storage is vulnerable to XSS attacks, and while XSS is less
of a concern with the API token (since it's only accessible via backend
requests), the other variables are still sensitive.

Cookies can be encrypted with an HMAC algorithm to make reading them
difficult for an attacker on the front end. If encryption isn't used, a
user could access the data via post-processing the response in the browser.
It's also possible the user could intercept the response between the backend
and browser.

In short: encryption isn't technically necessary for security of the application,
but it is a step to further ensure the application's security and privacy.

## Decision

To add encryption functionality to the application.

We will use HMAC encryption with SHA-256. This provides good security against
attacks as long as:

- the key is kept secret
- the implementation is correct
- the cookies are sent via HTTPS

To keep the `backend/utils` directory clean, a new file, `kdb.ts`, has been
added. This contains only the HMAC encryption/decryption methods.

[The rationale for using ES-modules can be found in ADR-0003](0003-es-module-system.md)

## Consequences

Encryption is an additional burden on the front end and back end. It's not
too big of a burden though, since cookies are set by the backend in ES-modules
via `process.env`, which is set on the server via `NODE_ENV`. This is usually
okay for most applications. As it stands, it does not add any major issues
other than needing extra care in the code, e.g. in `server.ts`.

_Important Note_: There is no `public` folder, but in a real application that
would be required. We will use the `kdb.ts` file as the encryption utility,
and it will live outside of the `public` folder (in `backend/utils/kdb.ts`)
and won't be directly referenced from the client. The reason for using the
`public` folder is not specifically for security here, but as well to make it
clear what is and isn't sensitive in the application and as a step to keep
in line with best practices and keep the application as secure as possible.

Date: 2021-02-13

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We need to allow users to send a single command to multiple TaskManager instances.

The single command is a `Job` structure which defines a list of `Tasks`, where each task is executed on a different instance of the TaskManager.

In our distributed `TaskManager` architecture, one instance may not know about the other instances.

## Decision

The `AwaitedJobs` is distributed in the system using the following logic:

1. When a `Job` is created, the system checks for recently `AwaitedJobs` in the distributed registry (`AwaitedJobsRegistry`) in the context of the project which knows the latest instance of the `TaskManager`.
1. When an `AwaitedJobsRegistry` is empty and the instance of the `TaskManager` has its own registry, the instance will be updated as the instance of `AwaitedJobsRegistry` and return a response that all `AwaitedJobs`s have been updated for the instance of the `TaskManager`.
1. When the registry of the `AwaitedJobs` has `AwaitedJobs`s in the `AwaitedJobsRegistry` and it is found that the instance of the `TaskManager` is no longer the one used by the registry, then the registry is updated to update the instance of the `TaskManager` and return a response that all `AwaitedJobs`s have been updated for the instance of the `TaskManager`.
1. Otherwise the response should return all `AwaitedJobs`s for the instance of the `TaskManager`.

## Consequences

The `AwaitedJobs` should be distributed to maintain a consistent registry of `AwaitedJobs`s on the latest instance of the `TaskManager`.

## Context and Problem Statement

Concurrent requests for data, validations and commands are common in most parts of the application.
For instance, in `PatientSearch` endpoint an increasing number of search requests, combined with a large amount of `ConcurrentBag<T>` items in the storage and in `PatientSearch` endpoint itself, will cause `OperationCanceled` exception, especially given that `PatientSearch` should be executed in the context of a single request.

## Decision Drivers <!-- optional -->

* Performance
  * The amount of concurrent requests should be increased
  * Reduce the probability of `OperationCanceled` exception
* Consistency
  * Handle concurrent requests such that we return the same result, if it would be re-executed in the context of a new command.

## Considered Options

* [option 1](#option-1)
* [option 2](#option-2)
* [option 3](#option-3)

## Decision Outcome

No quick fix is currently available to handle concurrent requests for data, validations and commands.
The recommended approach would be to follow the use of `DistributedTask` and move the operations which have a synchronous execution and return a `CommandResult` within `Operation` into a distributed operation which is executed in the context of a `CommandScope`.

Date: 2020-02-05 (Updated 2021-12-27)

## Status

Accepted

## Context

A well defined development workflow helps keep the development cycle on track and as an agreed-upon plan.

There are many different development workflows that can be applied to a project, including Agile, Lean, and Waterfall.

Regardless of the selected methodology, the team will need to define a set of actions to accomplish two main goals:

1.  How to execute the tasks required for development and deliver features?
2.  How to manage conflicts and make and track changes to the codebase?

## Decision

A [modified version of the Agile/Lean] workflow will be used where a development team manages its work, in an iterative manner, using short cycles to maximize learning and quality of code.

Specifically, the workflow will focus on delivering at the end of a development cycle to create a deployable code base. A deployable code base would be one that is tested, and ready for user acceptance testing or production users. A code base contains a deployable code base when it is working and ready for the next step and contains the learnings from the current development cycle.

### Concepts

The following are key concepts that will inform the development workflow:

*   A working environment is available for the team as a whole.
*   A feature is a proposed change to the current status of the codebase that would deliver a benefit to the user.
*   A story is a collection of features that are related and should be treated as a whole.
*   An iteration is a timeframe and contains one or more features and stories that are finished or deployed in their entirety.
*   A deployment is the process of moving a code base from its current environment into a new environment.
*   A deployment may be accomplished via automated or manual processes.
*   A code review is a process of examining a submitted change before it is merged into the main branch and a new iteration begins.
*   A code review will be accomplished via tool.
*   A code review is the responsibility of the entire team, but especially the Principal Developers and Technical Architect, when necessary.
*   Retrospective is a meeting and period of time set aside to examine the previous iteration in detail.

### Development Tasks

Use Story Cards to track progress of development on individual features and stories. Stories are tracked from a story's creation until it is deployed to production.

Each feature or story contains one or more tasks that are needed to accomplish it. Tasks should be simple and free of complex decisions, leaving plenty of time for team members to review the proposed solution.

Stories progress through a number of states:

1.  To Do

    *   The story is a description of work to be done but hasn't been started yet.
1.  Doing

    *   The story is currently in progress and may be worked on by one or more team members.
1.  Delayed

    *   The story hasn't been started because it was blocked, or the right time or because we've prioritized other work.
1.  Resolved

    *   The story is finished and a new iteration begins here.

### Code Review

The code review process:

*   Use GitHub to track the acceptance and merging of proposals to a feature or story
*   Discuss changes using the [GitHub] proposal feature.
*   Implement automated testing and integrate into the CI pipeline to fail builds that fail to address reviewer comments.

### Continuous Integration and Deployment

Combine the output of the code review process with a continuous integration tool to build and deploy the proposed changes into a development or staging environment. [CircleCI] is one option for a CICD tool.

### Retrospective

At the end of each iteration, the team will conduct a short retrospective meeting to:

*   Review past iteration: Discuss history of iteration and what was accomplished
*   Identify good and bad: Identify a few facts and discussion points surrounding the iteration, looking at facts not opinions.
*   Inspect and adapt: Develop two or three concrete proposals that address the team's behavior and process and increase the iteration's effectiveness.

## Consequences

Conducting a Sprint retrospective should be handled by a highly motivated and trusted member of the team, and each member of the team is expected to participate. Retrospective results should be held as confidential to the team, but may be shared with management as desired.

Sprint planning and the current status of each Story should be updated in our epic.

## Status

Approved

## Context

A Search instance has been provided that supporting querying a dataset. A language has been chosen as part of a design process to make this easy and intuitive for new users to make a start with, while also providing the option to more advanced users to take over as required.

The language used allows for searches based on two types of comparison, with a value and a field;
These are not mutually exclusive and are used in conjunction to make complex searches and queries.

## Decision

Searching is done using a query `field` string to be able to search the content of the fields. In addition, a value may be searched for, in which case the string value must be escaped so it is sent to the database. This means that searches are limited to searching by name only (e.g. if the given field in searching for is a text field), but other fields are not constrained.

As most searching is driven by filtering from the SQL side, the filter section will use a standard string `WHERE` clause in SQL to combine fields and values in a search expression.

## Consequences

Searching by text strings requires the value to be escaped so that the database supports searching, but also allows SQL searches to be more flexible and complex, allowing the field name to be searched for in combination with text strings. This means SQL and JSON search text should provide the same capabilities from the querying perspective.

## Considered Alternatives

* Extend the [Validate CSV](https://dp3.atlassian.net/browse/MB-354) endpoint to handle CSV requests
* Provide a new endpoint specifically for CSV validation

## Decision Outcome

* Chosen Alternative: *Provide a new endpoint specifically for CSV validation*

Since the initial CSV validation endpoint was part of the broader schema validation feature,
the logic to support it felt rather buried in the schema validation codebase. When the
CSV validation logic was moved to this API endpoint, it was still under the original
assumption that it's validating against the full schema. When used with the CSV
validator, we've discovered that the CSV validator has to handle many exceptions
[for the original CSV schema design](https://github.com/buildit/buildit-server/pull/1960/files)
which was not part of the original plan. These exceptions often have to deal with
invalid CSV strings in which case some error message is still required.


## Pros and Cons of the Alternatives

### CSV validation as an endpoint of the Validate CSV API

* `+` The JSON schema validator could still be called from this endpoint
* `+` Less boilerplate to maintain
* `-` Validation messages and custom validator implementations will now be scattered between two endpoints


### A new CSV endpoint (CSVValidator)

* `+` We'll need to make fewer assumptions about how custom validators might be implemented or the types of exceptions they'd deal with (eg: error messages are now expected only for CSV files)
* `+` Moving the CSV validation logic here will help provide clarity on what this endpoint is responsible for (CSV validation only)
* `+` This endpoint can call the existing JSON schema validator if needed for extra logic (eg: validating against an alternate schema)
* `-` We will now need to write validation code for each CSV validator in two locations (CSVValidator and the original CSV validation endpoint)

## Dependencies

* [MB-354](https://dp3.atlassian.net/browse/MB-354) # Extend Validate CSV to support CSV validation
* [MB-373](https://dp3.atlassian.net/browse/MB-373) # New API endpoint for CSV validation

# Status

Accepted

# Context

The Publishing API only requires an API token in a request body, where
`content-type` is set to JSON.

# Decision

We've decided to use an ID token signed by a R500-signed SAML2 endpoint as
identity and pass this via the client-side SDK `x_auth_token` header to
request the Publishing API.

# Consequences

## Pros

* `x_auth_token` is a known, well-tested and maintained header to use in
  requests.
* We can utilise other features in the [node-r500 package](https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/node-r500)
  (e.g. signing SAML2 attributes).
* By returning an `HTTPStatus.UNAUTHORIZED` in `auth` endpoints, we leave
  open the path to allow tokens to be issued and validated by a SAML2
  service, where `content-type` is set to SAML2 signed JWT.

## Cons

* Adding additional security measures for token validation and checking
  it's not in a public place (e.g. as a configuration value in the case
  of node-r500), may have the effect of slowing the API.

Technical Story: [Evaluate the use of an interim metric when parsing the Fridge data](https://github.com/planet4r/planet4/issues/21)

## Context

While the team is optimistic about the value of the existing `fridge-intakes` table, there is a good possibility that that is the wrong data structure to make use of. It would be easier to add an interim table when a more robust parsing strategy is in place to address a variety of issues that have been discovered in testing. In this interim phase, that table will be a temporary place to hold data before it is re-parsed.

## Decision

A new interim table has been proposed: `stale-data-from-fridges`

This table will be inserted into when the following conditions are met:
- The `fridge-intakes` table has been successfully parsed
- No purchases have been made on items in that `fridge-intakes` table
- Items in the `fridge-intakes` table have no corresponding purchases
- The `stale-data-from-fridges` table is not immediately updated for a fridge location when a purchase is made
- Item's are added to the interim table only when they meet two criteria:
  - There have been no purchases of that item in the current `fridge-intakes` table
  - There has never been an ingestion event from a `fridge-intakes` table for that item. (Ingestion Event data will be available from a `fridge-intakes` table.)

## Consequences

When `stale-data-from-fridges` is not updated on a given ingestion, for a given set of items and given fridges, that data will not be migrated to an existing `fridge-intakes` table during that ingestion and will not migrate on a subsequent ingestion.

If a location can have multiple ingested items, and those items will be added to `stale-data-from-fridges`, then a purchase on one of those items will trigger the migration of all other items from `stale-data-from-fridges` in that location.

For the past two years, we've used Coveralls as our test coverage tool of choice. However, during that time, I've come across references to CodeClimate that I'd like to explore.

CodeClimate seems to offer a lot of the same features as Coveralls, plus a few more, such as integrating with CircleCI directly (we already have the pipeline configured via CircleCI).

## Decision

We will use CodeClimate to track and improve our test coverage.

## Consequences

* The free plan will work perfectly for our use case, allowing us to understand the product and provide feedback on the product, but not allowing us to extend the product through automation.
* Future, more expensive plans allow for the use of CodeClimate as a plugin for popular CI tools and test runners, like CircleCI, Travis, CircleCI, and more.

### Context
 
At the time of writing the `Model` class in `skypy` is in a somewhat embarassing state. It is an
instance of `dataclasses.dataclass` and this causes a lot of problems, especially when trying
to use standard data science libraries such as NumPy and TensorFlow. 

The `Model` class also has a lot of static methods, making it difficult to instantiate and use in
typical workflows. For example, setting up an MCTS tree requires multiple nested function calls,
making it hard to reason about.

### Decision
We are proposing two alternative implementations for the `Model` class:
 
1. A plain old Python class (no `dataclasses` involved) with static methods (rather than making them
   instance methods). This would probably require us to implement a `monad` type in order to
   model things like default values, but it's a small price to pay for getting rid of the
   `dataclass` inheritance chain.
 
2. A `dataclasses.dataclass` but heavily customised version of the `Model` class. This would
   involve customising the `__init__` method to take a `**kwargs` argument (to allow for setting
   extra keyword arguments to static methods) and probably also add some magic methods to make
   using the `Model` class less painful. 
 
### Status

Provisional
 
### Consequences
 
If we choose option 1, the `Model` class will become more difficult to use. In particular, it will
be harder to allow users to provide their own subclass of the `Model` with their own `__init__`
method.

## Problem

Validation plugins operate as independent blackboxes.
For every backend each mounted validation plugin iterates
over the whole keyset, checks every key for its trigger metakey,
and validates the key.

Currently all needed validation plugins need to be specified at
mount-time - if additional validation is required, the backend
has to be remounted with the required plugins and plugin
configuration.

If validation of a key fails, each plugin decides on its own
how to handle the issue and proceed in ways that might be
different from what is expected or desired.

## Constraints

## Assumptions

While plugins should always fail and return an error if validation
fails on kdbSet, there are several different requirements
for what should happen on kdbGet and handle problems e.g.

- only issue warnings

  we want to read the whole configuration, but issue warnings
  if keys fail to validate instead

  problems are handled external by an application, a user, ...

- remove invalid keys

  we want to read the whole configuration, but drop invalid keys

  invalid keys might be replaced by default values, requested
  from the user, ...

- fail with error

  we only want to read valid configurations, and fail with
  an error if the configuration is invalid

## Considered Alternatives

- Extend validation plugins to allow us to specify what should happen
  if a key fails to validate
- Export a validation function that allows us to use an additional plugin
  to decide what should be done

## Decision

Use a wrapper plugin to iterate over the keyset and delegate the validation
of each key to the corresponding validation plugin.

## Rationale

- Validation plugins don't need to know what should be done if the validation fails
- We can run multiple validations on every key and improve error messages
- Different ways of handling errors only need to be implemented once

## Implications

validation plugins have to export their validation routine

`static int validateKey(const Key * key, const Key * errorKey)`

returning 1 if validation succeeded, 0 on failure

## Context

There are currently two possible ways to specify the ORID of an individual, (1) through the individual's `family_id` and `name` fields, and (2) directly via an `orcid_id` field on the `Individual` model. 

The current approach of using `family_id` and `name` creates the issue that more than one individual can share a name and family_id (siblings, parent-child, etc.). This approach also assumes that the database is the source of truth for family relationships and that merging families will be handled outside of the application through an external tool or wizard. 

Adding a `orcid_id` field is more time consuming but is also more direct. A `orcid_id` would not solve the issue of how to handle multiple family relationships, but it would handle the issue of how to handle individuals who have an ORID from a different database. 

## Decision

The `family_id` and `name` fields should be removed. If the database is the source of truth for family relationships, the application should be built to merge families automatically upon request or upon importing. 


## Consequences

A `name` should be mandatory when creating a new `Individual` in `family_id` for the sake of forward compatibility in the event that this is now the only way to identify an individual.

Technical Story: The domain layer should be decoupled from the rest of the application.

## Context and Problem Statement

In a previous project we found that there is a tight coupling between the domain layer and the UI.

As a result of this tight coupling:
* The UI was depending on the domain model
* This allowed the UI to receive the message without having to send an event
* Then, after the UI action was committed, a domain event was raised
* The event was triggered, sending the message back to the UI and to the rest of the system

For that project this propagation of messages was done in synchronous way, step-by-step.

Later in the project we went through a process of refactoring the domain layer and eventually removing the entire UI dependency from it. 

As part of this work we re-examined how to handle events, in order to use them as building blocks for our domain.

## Considered Options

* Event-oriented APIs (Synchronous and Asynchronous)
* Request/Reply APIs

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Event-oriented APIs (Synchronous and Asynchronous)".
Because we think that this approach helps to keep the message queue resilient to system failures.

This is further motivated by the fact that it allows for messages to be delivered out-of-the-box, which provides 100% predictability and allows for business to make use of this aspect of their domain.

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### Event-oriented APIs

* `+` can be used synchronously and asynchronously
* `+` does not tie messaging to request/reply patterns
* `+` message queue can be resilient to system failures, e.g., RabbitMQ or Kafka
* `-` message queue implementation is not native to Go
* `-` 100% predictability of timing of calls (due to asynchronous nature of messaging)

### Request/Reply APIs

* `+` messaging is tied to the same request/reply pattern that Domain layer follows
* `+` request/reply is easier to handle for a Go program
* `+` message queue implementation would not require custom implementation, e.g., RabbitMQ or Apache Kafka
* `-` could introduce more coupling between UI and domain if used incorrectly
* `-` it will be difficult to separate the logic to handle messages from the logic of handling requests in the domain

## Context and Problem Statement

Maps and spatial data are used throughout the EASi application. Currently, our spatial data needs to be accessed via the EASi backend API. The backend API also accepts location and radius searches as parameters. As a result, a user in the field using the EASi application is currently required to send their location and a search radius to the EASi backend in order to use the map layer. Additionally, there is no indication of how best to implement an autoscroll to a particular location. 

## Decision Drivers

* Development velocity
* EASi functional requirements

## Considered Options

* Option A - Implement autoscroll in EASi backend API. 
* Option B - Implement autoscroll in EASi Frontend Client

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Option A", because per the EASi architectural principles, the EASi frontend library is not to be used as the single place of truth for the user and backend applications. The EASi backend API will remain a single place of truth and all other clients will accept and forward requests to the EASi backend. To achieve this, a forward URL will be sent from the EASi frontend to the EASi backend API when a location is selected and a search is performed. The user will then not be required to manually send the location to the EASi backend. 

### Positive Consequences

* As a result of sending the location and radius to the EASi backend, we will be able to keep the EASi frontend free of logic related to how an autoscroll is implemented. 
* As a result, we will be able to send the location and radius as a JSON object as part of the GET request body to the EASi backend and remove the need for a forward URL.
* As a result, the EASi Frontend will continue to serve as a single point of truth for API requests (initially at least) and the EASi Backend will remain the single point of truth for spatial data.

### Negative Consequences

* The backend will need a POST endpoint to support adding new locations and updating the location associated with a particular application.

## Context

There are two strategies I am aware of for handling time based tests:

 1. Introduce a `time` method/field into the model, through which all time based logic would flow.  A common weakness of this approach is that to make sure the time moves forward for all tests, the app would need a view model to introduce the concept of current time and move it forward after each view change.

 2. Rely on a time function, which can be used to check that some operation eventually occurs.  As well as checking that something happens in the future, this approach could be extended to check that something happens in the past.  To illustrate the second point, a common use of this approach is to test that an `enabled` status eventually becomes `disabled`.

It is clear that the best way to handle time based logic is to integrate a time API, as I'm not aware of any time based test that doesn't introduce some way of changing the time (usually after some interaction with the view).

## Decision

This project will introduce a `time` method into each model, through which time based logic will flow. I am aware that some of these models may have two, and only two, usages of this method, but as I only have 3 models, this is acceptable.

This project will not introduce any external dependencies for time based logic (i.e. any time libraries). As this project continues to evolve, and should the need arise to implement things like time based email reminders, this project may become dependent on an external source of time, in which case this decision will be updated.

## Consequences

As described in the Context section, this decision does introduce a `time` method into every model.

## Status

## Context

### Background

#### Block and Transaction

Blockchain technology provides two ways to think about recording transactions and their history over time. This enables a method for communicating a trust model as a part of the infrastructure.

The first way is that of blocks of transactions. Transactions will typically refer to another object, a transaction hash, and this is used to maintain a chain of blocks as a history of the network.

The second way is that of events. All transactional activity, and other notable activity on the network, can be recorded as an event. These, too, can be used to maintain a history of the network and are useful for communicating trust to users.

#### Current Use

Currently, there is not a way to query events within the application as a chain of hashes. It would be possible to maintain this chain as a function of query parameters to a particular endpoint, but to have a method for communicating trust through this way would require a similar development to adding events in Tendermint.

### Use Case

We want to develop a method for staking users to update a commitment to the past that is a part of the system as a whole. This would require a mechanism for validating the commitments of all parties to the network to the past to be an accurate representation of the network as a whole.

### Considerations

#### What events are notable enough to record?

At the protocol level it is not possible to require the recording of every event that is done on the network. This will leave it to the application level to judge what events are noteworthy and should be recorded.

We believe that if we record:

-   The allocation of tokens to users (and thus their stake)
-   All transfer of tokens between users (and thus the transactions they commit to)
-   Block heights to which events are committed to as far as notable.

This will be enough to require a method for queryable re-commitments to past events as a part of the protocol.
Adding additional events in a speculative future may extend its usefulness beyond a stake system.

#### Storing the past

Commitments to the past will be stored on the blockchain as a part of the network's history.

A commitment to the past is something that can be updated with a new block header for a new commitment to the past to the application's current best guess of the distribution of tokens (and hence stake) on the network (and hence a new stake commitment).

#### Consequences

The application will be able to provide a method for querying all events that have been committed to the blockchain.

### Decisions

**The hashing algorithm is SHA-512/256.**

The reason for this is simply that it is the current blockchain's standard.

To build the event hash a SHA-512/256 hash of the string representation of the events is built using the following logic:

-   When events are specified in the block header the hash is built using the current best guess of the distribution of tokens (and hence stake) on the network (and hence a new stake commitment)
-   When events are specified in the block body the hash is built using the actual distribution of tokens (and hence stake) on the network (and hence a new stake commitment)

**The transaction event is specified as the hash of the encoded transaction event.**

To encode a transaction event an `events` json array is constructed using the following logic:

-   When an event is a transaction the encoded transaction event is the transaction itself
-   When an event is another event the encoded transaction event is the encoded transaction event of the other event

## Context

The [phpAPI](https://github.com/php/php-api) project currently defines all its APIs
as HTTP Resource APIs. This is an architectural style very closely related to REST
but is not quite the same. In this sense the project will take the REST paradigm in
some key aspects, but not to the extent of the more REST-oriented project the
[phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client). This is in contrast to the [phpClient]
project which takes REST to the point of introducing the concept of representation
and Resource object. In this sense the [phpAPI] project takes the other direction of
using resources in some key aspects while using a less strict REST protocol overall.

A basic motivation for this different approach is probably a desire to have more
control over what gets exposed rather than forcing the project to do more or less
than the API user intends. Thus exposing APIs is treated more like creating resources
rather than accessing the same through endpoints.

## Decision

I decided to implement and use the REST framework with following rationale:

The project is intended to be both a software and a hardware resource, in that many
aspects it will be built, used as and over time reflect new developments in the
hardware it is deployed to.

The [phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client) project is an important milestone
in the journey of exposing APIs as REST resources, but with the following consequence:
in order to handle the variety of REST resources and representations, it introduced
the concept of resource and resource representations, which can lead to confusion
and unnecessary complexity.

## Status

I've used the [phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client) and I am motivated by
the rationale above to implement the phpAPI as more of a resource-oriented API
without, however, sacrificing REST. In doing so I am motivated to also implement
the [phpAPI](https://github.com/php/php-api) project as more REST in the sense of
[phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client).
As I'm using Helix and as phpAPI are based on each other, I will add a [phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client) as well.

## Consequences

A resource-oriented API, like the one in the [phpAPI](https://github.com/php/php-api),
and REST architectures in general, has the advantage of being better equipped to
handle future changes that would be difficult or impossible with traditional REST.
So it can be said that a resource-oriented API is in fact more REST-oriented, even
if this was not the intention of the original author of the [phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client).

This approach is especially useful in the context of [phpAPI](https://github.com/php/php-api)
which I'm envisioning as a library of functions to produce and consume resources. In
this sense the [phpAPI](https://github.com/php/php-api) is the phpClient and a library
to be able to implement the [phpAPI](https://github.com/php/php-api). I will add an
[phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client) and call it also phpAPI. I will not make
any attempt to implement resource-oriented [phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client).

## Conclusion

As stated above, the intention of the [phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client) project is
probably not creating resource-oriented [phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client). It is
quite likely that the reason for introducing resource objects and resource representations is
in order to have a common abstraction for handling the representation of the [phpAPI](https://github.com/php/php-api).
There is also reason to think that the [phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client) project
can still benefit from the use of [phpAPI](https://github.com/php/php-api). I'm planning to
use [phpAPI](https://github.com/php/php-api) as both a PHP resource api library and a
REST client, but leaving to the user (e.g. in the [phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client))
the choice of what is the best representation of their [phpClient](https://github.com/php/php-client)
resources. I'll leave

## Status

Superseded by [ADR-003](003-create-de-versioned-code-bases.md)

## Context

Our node package `moj-frontend` is currently deployed to several environments and contains [a semantic version bump](002-create-version-file.md).

In the near future, we expect to start hosting the code as part of a monorepo (along with services, common code and data). This will lead to having multiple versions of `moj-frontend` in parallel.

This is not ideal for a number of reasons:

- It's a build complexity issue in itself - for every new release, we'll need to create a new branch, create a release tag to point to the branch, tag and do another build step.
- It's confusing to users who have different system requirements and use one particular version of `moj-frontend` in production, and we have three other versions deployed on the market.
- It is unsustainable as we add more code in parallel to the main branch.

## Decision

This ADR is an interim step for having a single, unchanging, versionless codebase of `moj-frontend`.

## Consequences

Having a versionless codebase will change the version requirements in production as well as development. These two concepts will need to be made clear by publishing practices:

- `moj-frontend-config` will no longer be required and will become a sibling of `moj-frontend`. This will be used to provide environment-specific configuration values when `moj-frontend` is installed via NPM or yarn.
- `moj-frontend-service` will no longer be required but could be used as a mono-installation (read: local development) of `moj-frontend`.
- `moj-frontend-service` will remain in production and when `moj-frontend` is installed via npm or yarn, `moj-frontend-service` will be used as before. This means that in order for `moj-frontend-service` to remain completely free of breaking changes, whenever `moj-frontend` changes in a backwards-incompatible manner a new release tag will be required (see [ADR-003](003-create-de-versioned-code-bases.md)).
- If we add any development-only functionality which could possibly be useful to users in production (and we don't expect to do this), this will be added in `moj-frontend-service` and the above rules will apply.

## Status

Proposed

## Context

We will be receiving a lot of functionality coming from our integration with Workday. Most important of these are:
* Organisation management functionality
* API integration
  * Taxonomies
  * Entities
  * Taxonomy entity data
  * Entity data
  * Relations (Organisation to Taxonome and among entities)

As of v22.11, we will also be able to create, edit and delete organisations, hierarchies and taxonomies in Workday. 
We want the same simplicity, consistency and minimal effort in maintaining Workday data as we have on the platform.

## Decision

We would like to create a set of API-driven views, in order to translate the information contained within Workday API calls into something more familiar to the MoJ.
For example, a taxonomy of Services, Service Types and Organisations will be reflected as a Service Taxonomy, with each Service mapped to a specific type and Organisations linked to the taxonomy. 

The information contained within the Workday taxonomy entity will be reflected in a Service Taxonomy Entity, and so a Taxonome to Service relationship that is captured in the Workday taxonomy will be reflected as an Organisation to Service relationship in the service taxonomy.

This approach reduces the amount of API calls made by the integration, and provides a more familiar way to think about the data structure which the platform needs to operate with.

### Exceptions
* Taxonomies or Service Types that we don't want to appear as a Service Taxonomy will be distinguished by their presence as an additional entity in the integration - ie. Organisations which have custom taxonomies will have their own taxonomy, but no service taxonomy. This will be used for the creation of some one-off migrations and the initial administration of service taxonomies.
* There will also be some Service types which are too complex to be reflected by our current integration logic in a Service Taxonomy. These will have their own entity in the integration, and will only be reflected in the service taxonomy via the API calls which link the service to a taxonomy.

## Consequences

* New code will need to be written to support the logic outlined in this Decision, and to translate API calls into our data model.
* The existing integration will need to be extended to support the new logic, and the creation of the first Migration to apply the Logic and data from the existing integration.

# ADR012: Haproxy healthcheck

## Context

There are two main [Haproxy](https://hapt.io/) servers that are configured as standalone
machines that provide several services:

 - A single page application frontend for the Alfresco 5.2 "Haze" UI and API application.
 - An Alfresco 5.2 "Haze" API application that provides endpoints for the Alfresco 5.2
   "Haze" UI and API application.
 - The Alfresco Application Services (AAS) server for Alfresco 5.1 and 5.2; this serves
   the Alfresco 5.2 "Haze" API application by means of a reverse proxy.
 - An Haproxy-Ingress server which is part of the Alfresco Application Services (AAS)
   server and extends it to provide additional routing functionality, including
   conditional HTTP and HTTPS routing, rate-limiting and stickiness.

These Haproxy servers should only be accessible over HTTPS using port 443 and this
needs to be configured using the [https://certbot.com/docs/getting-started/](https://certbot.com/docs/getting-started/);
the [Haproxy][haproxy-hapauth] module needs to be used for this.
The user `alfresco` needs access to all of these machines but access to most
Alfresco servers is not dependent on the access of the Alfresco UI frontend server.

In the discussion that happened in #430659346, some options were evaluated:

* [nightmare](https://github.com/nikgraf/nightmare)
* [selenium-scrap](https://github.com/selenium-scrap/selenium-scrap)
* [webdriver.io](https://github.com/gepetto/webdriver.io)

## Decision Drivers <!-- optional -->

* A full-nightmare-like driver in JavaScript would be convenient due to our usage of mustache.js for markdown rendering.
  The option of playwright is interesting but seems to be missing the ability to run headless in browser and could be integrated to a headless browser (Chrome or Firefox) via `--headless`.

* Nightmare offers an API similar to Selenium, which would be easy to translate into a valid test.
  Daydream is a bit awkward because of its reliance on phantom.js which seems rather immature, and its API is less selenium-like in some aspects (e.g. handling of the document and DOM).
  Nightmare seems to have a lead in this space, however, and the usage of phantom.js in it's entirety is the part I'm not comfortable with.

* If a headless browser is used (Chrome or Firefox) there is the problem of not having the same appearance as the one used by developers.
  So if the browser has extensions (e.g. adblock, dark mode), this could also have an impact on the results of the visual regression test.
  On the other hand, this would also be the appearance of the browsers that would have to render the page.
  Chrome or Firefox could be configured to launch with the same extensions (with the ability to override this through environment variables, e.g. `NIGHTMARE_CHROME_FLAGS--kiosk` or `NIGHTMARE_FIREFOX_FLAGS--kiosk`), or puppeteer might work in an automated fashion if we want to cap the options by environment variable (e.g. `NIGHTMARE_CHROME_FLAGS--kiosk --disable-extensions`).

* Puppeteer seems very well known and mature.
  Chrome headless + webdriver.io seems a bit clunky in comparison.

The custom field labels can still be generated from the api, instead of storing it in the database in the `field_content` table.
Some plugins might not use `\Shopware\Core\ContentManagement\Internal\Content\CustomField\CustomerPropertyFieldType` and just directly register them without using the API (which is a bad idea, see #1860).

## Decision

The customer property will continue to be retrieved from the API upon retrieval of the order item.
The `field_content` table is not needed after the custom fields are loaded from the `api` field content.
This could be a simple implementation:
```php
$customFields = [
    [
        'id' => 'shopware_content__custom_fields_label__custom',
        'customer_property' => 'custom_location',
        'customer_property_type' => \Shopware\Core\ContentManagement\Internal\Content\CustomField\CustomerPropertyFieldType::LOCATION_PROPERTY,
        'content_data' => [
            'short_property_label' => 'Custom Location',
        ]
    ],
]
```

- Customer Properties are fast to retrieve from the API, even when they don't live in `\Shopware\Core\ContentManagement\Internal\Content\CustomField\CustomerPropertyFieldType`.

#### Cons

- It could get messy with plugin developing as the `content_data` property can and might be generated by a `content_content_field` via an api, but the customer will not be using it.

## Status

accepted
