The custom field label has to be fetched from the api on retrieval of the customer property and not from the database.

## Context

Our original plans for handling source code transformation were quite extensive. We wanted to handle various tasks that needed to be performed in the pipeline such as:

* resolving versioned names for modules and submodules
* performing a binary search on module paths to find desired files
* merging source trees from multiple repositories
* extracting a single unified manifest for imports
* transforming source code based on certain flags
* doxygen documentation generation
* unit testing on source trees
* running linters on source code

While this ADR doesn't completely abandon source code transformation in `kdb`, it does drastically reduce the scope of what `kdb` does as a build tool.

This proposal is heavily based upon the [Discussion on minimal source-to-source transformations][source-to-source] that took place earlier this year.

## Decision

`kdb` will only perform transformations on a few (3?) different types of source code. We will delegate all other capabilities to independently available command-line tools. These capabilities will be categorized as follows:

### Module handling

* module versioning
* binary module search
* import merging
* extracting unified manifest
* transforming module source code based on flags
* documentation generation

These features will be implemented as plugins in `kdb` and are expected to be relatively straightforward to add.

### File handling

* removing files based on patterns
* replacing files with other files
* extracting files based on patterns

These features will also be implemented as plugins in `kdb` and are also expected to be relatively straightforward to add.

### Source code handling

* perform code transformations based on flags
* generate documentation
* run linters
* generate test manifests
* run unit tests on modules and submodules

These features will be standalone command-line tools which will be invoked from `kdb` using the same command-line paradigms as the previous category of features.

## Status

Approved.

## Consequences

* `kdb` will only perform a subset of all operations currently envisioned for it.
* New operations that require source code transformation will be implemented as standalone command-line tools which can be invoked from `kdb`.
* Creating a new command-line tool is easy to do and has minimal impact on the rest of the system.
* There are no immediate plans to implement any of the "advanced" capabilities like actually _transforming_ source code during build (e.g. based on some boolean flag).

## Context

Ensuring that the code we write is correct is a problem that has never
had an easy, clean, or permanent solution. There are many different
approaches to code verification, however none of them are perfect.

[More formally](https://logic.vienna.ac.at/people/joh/teaching/ecsc/sem1/),
we can re-frame the problem as:
 * given some set of source files, written in some programming language,
 * determine whether these files actually implement a certain intended
   contract.

## Decision

For now, we will use two different strategies for code verification:

1) For correctness of logic, we will use unit tests, as has been our
   practice.

2) For correctness of syntax, we will use a linter.

## Consequences

- Unit tests do not detect syntax errors.
- Linters do not detect logic errors.

Both unit tests and linters are tools, and both can produce false
positives and false negatives. The hope is that by using both, we can
mitigate the problems associated with using either exclusively.

This does not, of course, solve the problem of ensuring that the code
we write is correct. It does, however, solve the problem of ensuring
that the code we write is free of syntax errors.

## Decision

InventoryItems do not have a resource ID field, and are therefore not URLs are not URLs are not resource URIs. The model uses a `List<InventoryItem>` to hold items.

InventoryItem instances do not have an `id` field, but do have a `key` field. The `key` field is an `ObjectId` generated for the use case of storing items in Redis and does not need to be an `id` field. Each type of InventoryItem has its own nested JSON structure for properties based on the use case. The type `ItemValue` is used for generic Item values. The following is for an ItemType as defined for use of the ItemValue type.

## Context

We should be able to identify individual rotations and create or edit a new one without being tied to a set of actions taken on a subject image. To accomplish this, we may or may not support rotated images that are part of a set and need to be edited collectively. The idea is to be able to select either the image with a single rotation, or a list of images that are rotated together. 

#### Rotation Tool

To accomplish this, we should first decide if the rotation tool is only designed to handle single image rotations or if it may also handle sets of images rotated together (e.g. from an original image with multiple crops or sub-sections removed).

#### Temporary Rotations

If the rotation tool can also handle sets of images, it may also be useful to have a way for those rotations to be applied temporarily over a set of original images and then to be removed once they are applied. This is useful for things like rotating and cleaning up an area of a subject before snapping to a specific view of the subject when making a selection (e.g. for the macro classification task). 

#### Macro View

The macro classifier is one example of a task where a temporary rotation tool would be useful: the classifier starts with a default view of the subject set and presents the subject in a single "macro" image from which to select a region of interest (ROI). The ROI boundaries are then applied in the same single "macro" image and used to select individual classification regions for the cropped-out ROI. This same single "macro" image that is used to draw the ROI is also the same image that was rotated when the task was chosen from the main classification flow. It could be useful to have an automated way to apply that same rotation to a new subject set, and then rotate the cropped-out ROI of that new set to the macro-image that was cropped out of the previous set. 

## Decision

Implement two tools for rotations:

1. a **Rotation Tool** that allows for a user to make manual rotations on a single subject image.

2. a **TemporalRotatingRectangle Tool** that allows the user to temporarily apply the rotation from an original subject image over the cropped-out region of interest (ROI) of the original subject in order to annotate and classify the subject. 

## Status

Proposed

#### Consequences

- Rotation Tool:

- Annotate/Crop Tool:

## Consequences

We may have to make subsequent tool changes if/when we support editing multiple images at once (e.g. the crop tool).

The current method for exposing lifecycle events for Interlok is as written in [ADR 0009](0009-lifecycle-management-overview.md), requiring the use of an [annotation](https://api.javacraft.org/javax.lang.model.annotation) to tag an interface with an invocation point and then use an [enum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enum) to reference it.

## Considered Options

* Continue to use annotation based approach
* [Deprecate annotation approach]
* [Use [reflection](http://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/lang/reflect/package-summary.html) ]
* [Use [cogliere](https://github.com/mattlitchfield/cogliere)]

## Decision Outcome

The team has decided to deprecate the use of annotation at runtime in favor of using the enum based approach as the [reflection approach](http://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/lang/reflect/package-summary.html) didn't provide sufficient benefit to outweigh the complexity it introduced. The [reflection approach](http://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/lang/reflect/package-summary.html) was chosen over [cogliere](https://github.com/mattlitchfield/cogliere) as [Cogliere](https://github.com/mattlitchfield/cogliere) is a daemon that has the option to replace reflection code in application. This enables applications to replace the mechanism for exposing lifecycle events.

The proposed `metatags` schema allows publishing information about a Thing in order to enrich search and browse experience in Digital Collections.
In order to accomplish this task, this schema is extended in the `Resource` model.

## Decision

Two extensions are proposed:

### `metatags` schema
The `metatags` schema contains `resource`s that have multiple `metatags`s associated with each other in a `Resource-Metatag` relationship.

```
metatags : ResourceMetatags
description : Metatags for a resource.
name : String (required)
value : String (required)
resource : Resource (required)
```

### `metatags` schema
Since `ResourceMetatags` contains `resource`s and each `resource` contains `metatags`, the two schemas cannot coexist.
If a `Resource` contains `metatags`, the `ResourceMetatags` schema should be used.

## Consequences

If a `resource` contains `metatags`s, the `ResourceMetatags` schema should be used.

A `SimpleMetadataAttribute` has attributes like `name`, `value` and a `metadataHash` that can be represented with a plain key-value object. The given example shows a metadata attribute.
```javascript
const metadataAttribute = {
  name: 'custom-extension-api',
  value: '{"endpoint": "https://{yourdomain.com}/{version}/openapi/openapi.yaml}",
  metadataHash: 'sha256({apiSecret | apiExtension || getApiHashFromExtension | getGlobalSecurityConfiguration}}) === "none"'.toString()
};
```
`apiHash` will be the same as the `metadataHash` for the REST API endpoint if no secure token is defined or undefined.

There are some cases where the value of the metadata attribute is not a simple JSON serializable value. 
Thus the extension is rendered as the actual value and not an object. This is the case of an OpenApi path where the value is a string.
```javascript
const metadataAttribute = {
  name: 'security',
  value: '{"$id": "security", "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-06/schema#"}',
  metadataHash: 'sha256({securityExtension | getGlobalSecurityConfiguration}) === "none".toString()'
};
```
In this case a JSON object can be parsed with the `MetadataAttributeResolver` in terms of the `value` to resolve the secure token.
Another example is to use the `oauth` extension.
```javascript
const metadataAttribute = {
  name: 'oauth2',
  value: '{securityScheme: "oauth2", 
            server: [{
              url: "https://{yourdomain.com}/oauth2",
              securityUser: {
                username: "string"
              }
            }}',
  metadataHash: 'sha256({securityScheme | getGlobalSecurityConfiguration}) === "none".toString()'
};
```

## Decision Drivers

* Should be transparent for an extension whether the value is a JSON serializeable type or not.
* Should be transparent to the user how to resolve the metadata attribute.

## Considered Options

* Use `SimpleMetadataAttribute`
* Create a `ComplexMetadataAttribute` that inherits from `SimpleMetadataAttribute`
* Add `getValue()` and `setValue()` methods to `SimpleMetadataAttribute`

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: "Create a `ComplexMetadataAttribute` that inherits from `SimpleMetadataAttribute`"
This is done as this will lead to having one `SimpleMetadataAttribute` that can be called for any `ComplexMetadataAttribute`.

The Docker image we build and push to the Docker hub contains everything needed to run the "Hello World" app. This includes a `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml` and the `index.js` file (empty but required by `nunjucks-template`). This directory structure could be rendered as a Unix filesystem by a Windows host. This can be done using a tool such as Docker for Windows. The `Dockerfile` would be evaluated by the Docker system, the necessary steps would be carried out, and the resulting filesystem would be rendered by a Windows tool such as `dir` or `roboto` (RoboCop). A `docker-compose` file would be executed by `docker-compose` (not Docker for Windows), which is used internally by Docker for Windows to start the containers. Finally, the `index.js` file would be loaded by `nunjucks-template`, which would render the contents into an HTML file. This whole process can be automated by a single command.

## Decision

The main `Dockerfile` would be updated so that when evaluated by a Windows tool, it would run the command to create a `directory.json` file. This file would be then passed to `nunjucks-template` which would render the contents into an HTML file. A `nunjucks-template.yaml` would be added to the `Dockerfile` to specify the configuration for `nunjucks-template`. A `build-and-deploy.ps1` would be added to the root of the repository to contain the command to build and deploy the app. This script would be updated regularly to deploy the latest build of the app.

## Consequences

The main `Dockerfile` would be updated to add `nunjucks-template.yaml` and `build-and-deploy.ps1` as well as a `directory.json` file that would be passed to `nunjucks-template`. The build process would be automated and separated from the deployment process, but both would be triggered by the same command.

## Context

A lot of systems require the concept of roles, for instance to delegate administration or view access to different users. This ADR defines roles in the context of the Datalabs project.

### Terminology

- **User** - An authenticated user of the system.
- **Role** - A group of users that have the same access to the system. Roles are a subset of users.
- **Privilege** - An action that can be performed by a user on a given resource.
- **Permission** - A privilege that is restricted to a certain role.

## Decision

#### Roles

Datalabs will use two roles:

- Local Administrator
- Researcher

#### Privileges

Every user is assigned a default set of privileges. These are as follows:

- Use the graphical user interface to view data
- Use the command line to add or edit samples and/or subjects
- Use the command line to upload data
- Query data via the user interface
- Use the command line to query the experimenter API
- Use the command line to reset the Experimenter database

Privileges will be assigned dynamically via the `roles` table in the experimenter database.

#### Roles and Privileges

A list of predefined privileges is maintained in the `privileges` table. Each privilege corresponds to a certain action.

Roles will contain a set of privileges. A user is assigned privileges dynamically, either by the `roles` table if the user has already been assigned roles, or via a given command.

## Status

Under review

#### Consequences

- By giving certain privileges to every user, Datalabs will not be restricted for usage in scripts that are run by users.

## Context

The Financial Times has several Applications that will be migrated as part of the Modernisation Platform project.

Historically the different Applications have followed separate paths for building their API:

- Some use Events as the central part of their API:
  - E.g. Alpha - reads *EventStream*s (i.e. reads historical log data). The 
  - Alpha API is built around the consumption of these EventStream*s.
- The majority of the FT Applications read *EventData* (i.e. read 
  high-level *Event* data). There is little understanding of the logs
  underlying these events and no provision is made for reading the
  historical log data that underpins the *EventData*.
- A few Applications are deployed outside of the main application stream:
  - E.g. The application provides a console based tool for loading and
  - viewing *EventData*. The loading is done through an RFC file
  - provided via a web application.
  - Some *EventData* are generated in the backend through API calls (to
  - create a financial product instance in the Alpha API).

There is a concept in the FT (and the Financial Industry in general) to
"Event-driven application". This builds upon the ideas around Event
Sourcing and can take the form of:

- Retrospective: understanding what changes have happened over time, using
  *EventData* to create reports on past behaviour.
- Proactive: reading and processing *EventStream*s to modify their application
  e.g. generate and act upon alerts based on the historical log events in
  a *EventStream*.

## Decision

- All new applications must define an API which is event-driven and/or
  event-sourcing.
- If there is only one application to be migratied (eg Alpha) - EventSourcing
  should be built as a first class citizen, as this application serves
  as the API reference.
- There will be separate *EventStream*s and *EventData* in the application
  database.
- *EventStream*s will be read in order and create *EventData*s
- The *EventStream* will be rebuilt when creating each event. *EventStream*s
  will not be created in-memory.
- When adding EventSourcing to an existing application - see ADR 0004.

## Consequences

- There will be more than one database.
- All Applications will be more complicated.
- Future development will have a higher learning curve in understanding
  how different events impact the *EventData*.
- We will be taking full advantage of the EventSourcing/EventDriven
  principles.

## Context

There's a trade-off between "default" and "named" exports (e.g. `export const foo = 42;` vs `export { foo as bar }`) and it might be useful to document here's a decision on trade-offs.

### When to use default exports

- when you have named imports everywhere and they aren't doing anything special
- when you're having trouble getting a function or class to export properly

### When to use named exports

- when you need to import only a function or class and not their defaults
- when you're running a microservice architecture and having issues with REST transports

### Trade-off and alternatives

- default exports often mean using `this.default` or `this[Symbol()]`; it feels better to make use of named exports which then can be given default values
- defaults exports are easier to work with in the AST nodes of a parser, however, named exports are easier to manage in the final compiled code
- it's also easy to use a Babel plugin or something similar to transform default exports into named exports.

## Decision

We will, by default, use named exports wherever it's easy to do. This might mean some extra setup but it'll be worth it in the long term.

As we released the first version of the Gaia specifications in [this](https://github.com/zdb-community/gaia-specs) repository, we made it available in multiple other version control repositories, along with a script to automatically update each of those repositories to point to the latest version. These scripts were also updated to make the process of releasing a new Gaia version straightforward, in two steps:

1. `cd repo/develop/apps/gaia-specs && sh release-v1.0.0`
2. `cd ../master/apps/gaia-specs && sh release-v1.0.0`

This was done in several repositories over a couple of months, and so we now have several Gaia specifications versions concurrently in the versions control repositories associated with each release.

The process we used for each release involved extracting the artifacts from the release and packaging them into an RPM. This RPM is then pushed to a personal GitHub account which is configured to be able to upload the RPMs to the repositories.

We have now finished this process using the last release, and are moving on to the next release. This is taking the form of the `2.0.0` release, and we will make changes to the file structure of the package to reflect this.

This document covers how we will handle the multiple versions of Gaia in the various repositories concurrently.

## Decision

After moving to the `2.0.0` release, we will use this process, which is now in `master`:

1. `cd repo/develop/apps/gaia-specs`
2. `cp -r ../master/. ./`

## Context

For the Raspberry Pi we had two choices of operating systems, Debian and Ubuntu.
Debian uses the debian packaging system with its own set of repositories,
while Ubuntu uses the ubuntu packaging system with its own set of
repositories.

The advantage of Debian is that you can get an operating system that supports
all the latest releases, using a debian-specific repository. The
disadvantage is that you lose out on some software that is in the standard
Debian repositories. For example, there are no official Raspberry Pi drivers
in the Debian repositories.

Ubuntu uses the ubuntu packaging system, and comes with their own set of
repositories. Ubuntu generally ships with the latest versions of software.
Ubuntu also supports installing additional repositories to get even the
latest versions of software. Ubuntu also supports installing .deb packages that
are created for the Ubuntu system. Because of this, there are plenty of
Raspberry Pi drivers in the Ubuntu repositories.

In the past, installing additional repositories using the personal private archive
(PPA) was the only way to get the latest versions of software on Debian.
However, the advantage of Debian over Ubuntu is that the software in the
Debian repositories ships with debian-specific packaging, which is advantageous
over the ubuntu-specific packaging shipped with Ubuntu. Because the
Debian-specific packaging uses standard files for packaging, it is easier to
install and remove the personal private archive when you are done with it.

There is an official Ubuntu repository for Raspberry Pi that makes it easy to
install the latest version of Ubuntu by using the personal private archive
(PPA). This solves the problem of out-of-date drivers. However, this
repository only contains the base operating system, and doesn't include any
additional repositories for additional packages.

## Decision

We will use Ubuntu 18.04 as the operating system for our Raspberry Pi.

## Consequences

Our container images will be based on Ubuntu, and we will use the official
Ubuntu repository for Raspberry Pi to ensure that our container images contain
the latest versions of all packages.

Using the Ubuntu repository will make our container images more bloated, but
the trade-off is worth it. The ability to keep our container images up to date
with the latest versions of packages is a higher priority.

Installing additional software will be easy with the Ubuntu repository.
Installing new software will be easy once we get the build process working
with Docker and the buildpack.

We feel that there are several reasons to want to support multiple
resolutions and sizes in a game:

1. The game could be developed to be interesting across a large number of devices
1. This option could be made available to end users as they make purchases or
sign up for a subscription
1. This may offer a solution to the problem of providing interesting game content
via mobile platforms
1. A user could select their preferred resolution and scale down or up to
adjust the visual presentation (useful for users on low-power devices)

# Decision

We decide to use SDL with the `Renderer` type (as opposed to `Window`) to provide
multiple options to the end user, that the end user will then apply to adjust the
scale (both zoom and pan) of the game (the end goal should be that the game and
rendering process is already scaled to the smallest suitable resolution).

# Status

Accepted

# Consequences

**Pros:**

1. Allows us to create many types of content to appeal to many users
1. Provides a solution to the problem of having low-bandwidth content available
via mobile platforms
1. Allows for a simpler and easier-to-understand UI to make selecting these
options easier (we expect that it will be fairly straightforward for the
end user to decide on their preferred resolution and scale)
1. The end user can adjust their preferences (as above) to provide the optimal
experience for them
1. Scale() will make it easy to create content that can be easily re-used at
multiple scales

**Cons:**

1. We will need to support rendering at multiple scales
1. We will have to handle the logic of mapping resolution-specific features
(such as scaling and positioning)
1. We will have to be careful to avoid introducing scaling or positioning
issues when we need to scale everything up or down via `scale()`

- <https://stackoverflow.com/questions/14480988/scaling-graphics-via-sdl>

Taurus appears to come from a testing tool set originally created by Scalera and this seems to be a testing consultancy organization. - _Client technology_: I'm not in a rush to use Selenium or another external tool but I can see a path from Locust to Selenium reasonably easily.

## Considered Options

- The decision is made and we are going to implement Taurus!
- Delay this and experiment more with Locust and see if I can make any progress on getting the tests to run in parallel.

## Decision Outcome

- The first option is chosen.
- I can provide a demo of Locust that should take 3 hours or less. I will need to write some code to create a second endpoint (http://example.com/new-locust-test) for sending commands with some parameters and then I will need to write some code to parse the Locust API response.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Configuration can be used to tailor an application to specific circumstances, for example, to provide options for users, or to override default settings for an application deployed to a specific environment. In this document, we will define what global configuration is and what it should do, and how it is configured and used, so that the application provides the right options in the right circumstances.

## Decision

There are two kinds of configuration. The first is for domain logic, that determines how the application behaves, what it does, and how it responds to actions. This configuration is for internal application use only and should never be made available to users. Domain logic should always provide sensible default values for all configuration options, and provide a well-defined and easily understood mechanism for overriding them.

The second kind of configuration is for user-facing options. These settings allow the user to customise how the application behaves, and provide alternative ways of doing things. This configuration should be readily accessible to the user, and allow them to be changed easily and safely. Changes to domain logic should never require changes to user-facing configuration, and vice versa.

## Consequences

It may be tempting to use global configuration to allow the user to tailor the application to their own circumstances. It may be tempting to use domain logic to provide sensible default values for user-facing configuration. In both these cases, the temptation is understandable, but the decision-makers must be wary of adding unnecessary complexity and moving configuration options between domain logic and user-facing options.

## Status

## Context

Previously we've used the `/publish` endpoint to list items from multiple feeds, combining results from each feed into a single JSON object that is returned to the requesting function.

We are starting to receive several calls with the option of publishing with "null" content. This behaviour makes it easier to combine elements with different data for different uses. 

### HTTP method

Using `null` for the value for the POST parameter `fields` is not a REST-compliant method. POST calls should have an optional body. 

### HTTP codes

Currently if `null` is passed `200 OK` is returned. As a `POST` request in REST use cases where something can be returned:

- `200 OK` when data is received
- `201 Created` when data is appended
- `204 No Content` when nothing is returned (and expected)

### Query parameters

If there were query parameters to select fields the request would be something similar to `/publish?fields=[id,title,description,category]`

Currently these parameters are merged into the request body, resulting in `fields=[id,title,description,category,feed]`

## Decision

We have updated the `/publish` endpoint to meet REST best practice. This includes:

- Accepting a POST request with an optional body
- Expecting a JSON-encoded body that is merged into the query parameters if present
- Returning appropriate HTTP codes based on the success or failure of the operation

## Consequences

- There are several places where endpoint responses are being expected that no longer is the case. For example if a request has `fields=[item1,item2]` but the query parameter is `fields=[item3,item4]`. This situation can result in a `400 Bad Request` being returned as none of these `fields` will be processed.

## Status

Accepted

## Context

Phosphorylation is a common step in many enzymatic pathways.
As an additional constraint, we will consider only
single-substrate, single-product enzymes.
(There are still many interesting issues to consider,
namely for dealing with multi-step reactions.)
In this setting, the enzyme's activity
can be captured by an enzyme's kinetic parameters,
$k_cat$ and $k_a$.

## Decision

The rate law for the enzymatic reaction(s) is
described by the Michaelis-Menten equation:

$V(s) = \frac{k_cat s}{K_m + s}$

where $V(s)$ is the velocity at substrate $s$.

The Jacobian matrix is:

$J = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{d(V_1(s))}{ds} & \frac{d(V_2(s))}{ds} & 0 \end{pmatrix}$

$J(s) = \begin{pmatrix} k_cat / (K_m+s) & k_cat / (K_m+s) & k_cat / (K_m+s) \end{pmatrix}$

The rate equations are then:

$\dot{x}_1 = -\frac{k_cat}{K_m + s} x_1 + \frac{k_cat}{K_m + s} V_2(s)$
$\dot{x}_2 = -\frac{k_cat}{K_m + s} x_2 + \frac{k_cat}{K_m + s} V_1(s)$
$\dot{x}_3 = -\frac{k_cat}{K_m + s} x_3 + \frac{k_cat}{K_m + s} V_1(s)$

The enzyme's kinetic parameter $k_cat$ should be chosen such
that the enzyme's maximal velocity $k_cat \cdot \delta$ is 1,
where $\delta$ is the "distance"
(or other mass action) of the two enzymes,
$1/\delta = K_m$.

(Note that other choices are possible, e.g.
if $1/\delta$ is set to a different value).

## Consequences

The enzyme's maximal velocity is 1,
which can be arbitrary;
by scaling $k_cat$ by a factor of 1/K_m
the enzyme's activity becomes 1/(K_m^2).

If $K_m$ is known then $k_cat$ will be known by 2.
The resulting enzyme will have $k_cat$
(i.e. its activity) set to 1.

As the number of enzymes will be a part of the user's command
the user will need to know the enzyme to use to implement the desired phosphorylation.
Also, $1/K_m$ is set as a constant and as it is not provided to the function as a parameter,
the default value must be chosen by the user.

4. We will use IAM to authorise and configure network access to the service.

Yes, we use Typescript as we have used it for several months without problems.

# 2. VRS Type

Date: 2019-05-21

## Status

Accepted

## Context

We are building a VRS application and need to decide what data types to use.

## Decision

We will use the following types:

- `Any` - Base type for all types
- `String` - Text or characters
- `Number` - Integer or floating point
- `Bool` - Boolean
- `Null` - Represents a null value
- `Undefined` - Base type for nullable and undefined values
- `Object` - A collection of properties without a fixed structure
- `Array` - An ordered list of items
- `Map` - An unordered collection of key-value pairs

## Consequences

There may be additional overhead for serialization and deserialization.

# Deprecate DynamicServiceLocator

* Status: Deprecated
* Date: 2021-10-31

## Context

The `DynamicServiceLocator` was introduced in [#274](https://github.com/istio/docs/issues/274) and has been deprecated. It was part of a
decision to replace the custom way of wiring resources in the istio-netes-sidecar into a proper Kubernetes resource.
A decision was made to instead use the existing RESTAPI of the GRM. We also wanted to provide ability to change the endpoint used to
contact the restapi.

## Decision

* Deprecate `DynamicServiceLocator`
* Use `RestAPI` endpoint that is provided in the `GRMCorp` RESTAPI module.

## Consequences

* We will start to deprecate the DynamicServiceLocator
* Deprecate the RestAPI module
* We will merge the endpoint that was used to contact the restapi into the `RestAPI` module.

## Future

* We will need to deprecate the route53 endpoints that are configured to provide routing to the restapi and create new
endpoint resource.
